This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of a $d$-dimensional hypercube governed by the Schrödinger equation. Under the premise that the ground state can be found within a specific type of function space known as the spectral Barron space, we demonstrate that the convergence rate of the generalization error is not influenced by the dimensionality $d$. Furthermore, we confirm the validity of this premise through a new estimate that shows the ground state's smoothness is directly proportional to the relative gap in its corresponding eigenvalue. Additionally, we obtain an estimate for the relative gap, which is essential for determining an upper limit for the generalization error and thereby establish a useful bound. Ultimately, we use these bounds to demonstrate that the ground state can be accurately approximated with high probability by a two-layer neural network, whose size is proportional to the kernel's degree, when the relative gap and smoothness parameters are sufficiently large. Importantly, this result is not contingent upon any specific property of the underlying potential function. We also extend our theoretical findings to address the related problem of optimizing the relative gap in the infinite-dimensional setting through stochastic gradient descent and other similar optimization algorithms. We successfully establish a non-asymptotic bound that shows the number of optimal relative gap epochs (iterations) to be directly proportional to the number of data points in the training set. We view this finding as a crucial breakthrough in the field. We also outline an innovative approach for achieving this optimization, one that involves modifying the well-documented "instantaneous control" technique used for optimizing the ground state's smoothness parameter. We formally present this new approach, which we term the "instantaneous control for relative gap" (ICRG) method. We formally describe this innovative technique. We hypothesize the ICRG method to be an efficacious tool for optimizing the ground state's smoothness parameter and, by extension, facilitating the iterative process of discovering the ground state through the generalized use of two-layer neural networks for calculating the Schrödinger equation's solution. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Specifically, we observed that the anisotropy pattern strength we recorded was significantly higher than predicted by the model proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. We also present evidence that the energy dependence of anisotropy patterns can be explained by the varying energies of cosmic rays detected at very large scales. Lastly, we ruled out the possibility that the observed anisotropy patterns could result from energetic cosmic rays generated by the distribution of cosmic magnetic field dynamics alone. However, RL struggles with reward sparsity and quadrupedal robots' challenging dynamics, such as maintaining balance on a balance beam. This allows RL to learn policy adaptations for different gaits through reinforcement learning, where policy and generator optimize alternately to stabilize training. Furthermore, our controller successfully adapted to a physical quadrupedal robot and effectively navigated challenging terrain in real-world conditions. Our results show state-of-the-art performance when compared to current RL-based control methods. Our method's success is attributed to the generated gaits, such as walking and jumping, providing RL with more information to work with. Additionally, our method's ability to evolve gaits allows the robot to adjust its movement to suit various task rewards. The behavior of super-massive black holes in their lifetime is primarily dominated by a relatively low level of accretion well below the Eddington limit, indicating they appear as low-luminosity active galactic nuclei.  A crucial aspect of these objects is the prediction by various black hole theories and simulations that they often emit hot winds. This is now playing an essential role in large-scale simulations that study galaxy evolution, but direct proof has been hard to find. This paper verifies that specific emission lines present in high-resolution Chandra X-ray spectra from the low-luminosity AGN immediately surrounding a mid-infrared bright active galactic nucleus in the center of NGC 2623 can be attributed to the presence of a black hole-driven hot gas wind. By analyzing these spectra, we have identified strong evidence for winds with temperatures of approximately 0.8 keV and mass loss rates as high as 10 solar masses per year. This is now the first time such evidence has been found for a black hole of this scale, showing a significant increase in the estimated loss rate compared to a simple model of isolated black hole emissions. This could potentially mean a greater impact on the surrounding interstellar medium than previously expected. By observing more of these objects, we may be able to confirm if this wind pattern is a universal characteristic of LLAGNs. Moreover, studying this phenomenon may offer an alternative approach to measuring less active black holes' energy output. Closed-loop system performance can decline over time due to plant characteristic changes, necessitating controller redesign without complex modeling processes often associated with such systems. Fortunately, reinforcement learning offers a promising approach to optimizing model-free nonlinear controller designs without extensive system modeling. Despite the efficiency of this method, its reliance on numerous interactions with the system may compromise its effectiveness in systems requiring rapid redesign or frequent adjustments. A proposed model-free, two-step design approach aims to overcome this limitation by initially employing a reinforcement learning-based linear controller design and then refining it through nonlinear model-free reinforcement learning. The first step involves integrating multiple system inputs into a single control input to simplify the system model, and the second step utilizes these controls along with historical system data to optimize the system's Model-Free Deep Reinforcement Learning (MFDRL) policy. The resulting MFDRL controller offers improved performance compared to traditional model-free reinforcement learning, demonstrating significant robustness and superiority in terms of settling time and peak output. The two-step design appears more efficient than model-free reinforcement learning, as it also offers improved robustness and closed-loop performance compared to traditional reinforcement learning-based nonlinear controller designs. The effectiveness of this approach has been validated through comprehensive closed-loop simulations, showcasing its potential for widespread application in system redesign. The promising results of this research may inspire the use of model-free reinforcement learning in a broader range of systems. The two-step design method can be implemented using standard reinforcement learning software and standard mathematical tools for linear and nonlinear system representation. We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of external influences, indicating that Tononzintla 2 is an inner cluster within the galaxy's central region. The [Fe/H] values ranged from -1.34 to +0.10, and the extended red giant branch's temperature variations affected the measured abundance readings. However, we accounted for these effects in our calculations. The analysis revealed enriched levels of alpha, nitrogen, and tin components in two stars, which are likely the result of asymptotic giant branch star activity. Additionally, we found evidence of multiple Population II star generations within the cluster, supported by varying metal and nitrogen content patterns. The cluster's age was estimated to be approximately 12 billion years, consistent with the ages of other globular clusters in the vicinity. The analysis also revealed unique properties of Tononzintla 2, such as low radial velocity levels and possible satellite or merger remnants, further underscored by enhanced metal and nitrogen content levels in two stars, indicating an enriched legacy inherited from a legacy cluster or star system. Tononzintla 2's distinct chemical composition profile makes it an intriguing and unique globular cluster. Moreover, its analysis using APOGEE-2 data highlights the significance of further detailed study of less luminous cluster stars, which can provide deeper insights into its origins. Based on this, we recommend that additional spectroscopic observation is directed towards multiple red giant and giant stars within the cluster. Remote sensing, used to monitor Earth's condition via satellite data, has significant benefits for enhancing our daily lives and living environment. The growing number of orbiting satellites leads to the publication of multiple datasets with diverse sensors and domains to support remote sensing research. This study offers a thorough review of more than 400 publicly available datasets across various applications including land use, disaster monitoring, and weather forecasting. These datasets are analyzed based on several criteria: volume, research impact, resolution variations, research fields, and data relationships. Based on these dataset attributes, we establish a method to evaluate and select datasets for benchmarking model performance. Moreover, we introduce a user-friendly benchmarking platform that streamlines the process of dataset selection, model training, and performance evaluation. The platform also offers integration with popular deep learning frameworks to easily assess model performance on chosen datasets and share research findings with the community. To demonstrate its value, we use this platform to evaluate the performance of multiple deep learning models on several datasets and conduct an in-depth analysis of dataset characteristics that can inform future research directions. The proposed benchmarking system is expected to enhance research consistency and facilitate informed research choices in remote sensing fields. Identifying irregularities in urban data is a pressing research issue. Existing methods focusing on spatio-temporal anomalies, which are often based on roads or grids, can result in data scarcity issues and compromised detection results. This paper introduces a novel approach that tackles these challenges. An unsupervised anomaly detection framework called ReAD is proposed to identify irregularly shaped regions with arbitrary boundaries. This framework combines spatial and temporal factors and employs a dynamic partitioning method to create homogeneous regions with contiguous locations and comparable readings. An anomaly metric is calculated for each region using a divergence calculation method, allowing for the detection of irregular areas through a weighted aggregation of a regional quality assessment metric and a regional anomaly metric. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed framework. An open-source implementation of the proposed framework is available at https://github.com/GTSQB/ReAD. To facilitate future research, a dataset comprising 33 weeks of air pollution data is provided at https://github.com/GTXC/ReAD_Dataset. In particular, this dataset is used to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in identifying irregularly shaped spatio-temporal anomalies. In addition, a series of 4 technical issues are presented, aiming to promote future research on this topic. To date, these issues have not been resolved. Developing models from source code necessitates access to an abundance of labeled information. However, trained models are frequently specialized in a task-specific manner, which undermines their transferability to other tasks. This study presents novel pre-training strategies, complemented by a graph-based code representation, aiming to produce code representations applicable across a range of tasks. Our graph-based model captures crucial interconnections between code components, enabling graph neural networks to leverage these connections for better performance. This involves employing the coarse-to-fine approach to fine-tune task-specific results. Notably, our model achieves state-of-the-art results in both code-level and token-level evaluation metrics for various datasets. Moreover, we observe superior performance in downstream tasks such as code completion and code translation. This work marks a significant advancement in cross-task generalization for code representation learning. While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad time frame, typically spanning hours to days, the aerosol depth can be derived from comparing measurements of star fields in different directions. However, the scattered light from stars is insufficient to provide a precise enough calibration, leading researchers to use narrow fields and rely on rapid, high-quality data. An alternative approach is presented here, where data are analyzed by directly observing pairs of stars in a single narrow field, thus greatly reducing calibration needs and enabling high-precision measurements with minimal observations. We outline the fundamental principles, the procedure, and the code used to monitor aerosol depth, which have been successfully validated through comprehensive observations in different environments. This new approach enables regular monitoring of aerosol depth in the sky over medium-sized telescopes, allowing for more effective science research and applications. Additionally, we present the potential for using this technique not only to obtain optical astrophysics data but also to contribute to various research fields, such as climate, astrophysics, and photometry. As an example, we demonstrate its suitability for the 2.5-meter Calar Alto telescope at the Instituto de Astrofísica de Andalucita. Furthermore, we reveal the tremendous potential for enhancing the precision of optical astrophysics observations one hundredfold through daily images captured by medium-sized and large telescopes operating in the southern hemisphere, operating at a depth that surpasses the current capability of the Aerosol Counterplane by an order of magnitude. We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse General Graphical Lasso
problems and includes implementations of the Lasso, Focused Graphical Lasso,
Inferential and Nested Lasso techniques. Moreover, it integrates the L1 and
Konstopoulos L2 regularization methods, offering cross-validation tools and the
capacity to handle large datasets through the utilization of DataParallel and
GPUParallel strategies. Additionally, it incorporates the Graphical Lasso for
High- dimensional Time series data as described in Danaher (2013) and Nichols
(2018). The GGLasso library is adaptable and allows for the integration of user-
specified regularization schemes. The package is made available as a Python3 only
implementation in the Python package index as gglasso, available at
https://python-packages.org/package/gglasso, with the full source code hosted at
https://github.com/cran/GGlasso. The package has been developed by Nicolas
Thierry, under the supervision of Prof. Christian Robert at the University of
Berkeley. Leveraging the Pytorch library, the package has gained significant
performance improvements, particularly in the estimation of large sparse inverse
covariance matrices, achieving speed-up of approximately two, three, four, six
and twelve times faster than the original R implementation for various
problem sizes. Furthermore, the package offers considerable speed gains in
comparison to other available Python packages, notably,, scikit-learn, scipy and
pymultinomial, for graphical lasso challenges. The package has been tested on
various platforms including Windows, Linux and MacOS operating systems. The
project's issues are managed through, https://cran.r-project.org/web-workers/,
while the package can be installed using, pip install --index-url https://pypi
.org/project/gglasso/, with the full documentation available at, https://python-

Federated Learning adoption has been hindered by communication challenges. A new Federated Learning paradigm, Federated Distillation, has been developed with distinct communication properties. It employs ensemble distillation and transfers model outputs as soft labels to participating clients and a central server via a public data set. Unlike conventional Federated Learning, such as Federated Averaging, which increases communication complexity with model size, Federated Distillation reduces communication complexity by utilizing the size of the distillation data set. We analyzed the potential for communication efficiency in Federated Distillation by evaluating the effects of curation techniques, soft-label quantization, and protocol adjustments. The results, based on CNVLabs' Lichening search benchmark with image classification tasks, show that Federated Distillation models with 16MB model size and soft-label quantization achieve comparable accuracy to models with 160MB size, representing a 10 times improvement. We also examined the accuracy and communication efficiency trade-offs in Federated Distillation and found a balance between these factors. A open-source implementation of Federated Distillation is provided on https://github.com/cnvlabs/lichening. Experimental results can be accessed via https://distillation-benchmark.cnvlabs.github.io. Conversely, a open-source implementation of the communication efficient protocol can be found at https://github.com/cnvlabs/efficientPROTO. Our team is excited to explore the potential of Federated Distillation in real-world applications at https://github.com/cnvlabs/distillation-fd. We welcome contributions at https://github.com/cnvlabs/distillation-fd. Additionally, a detailed overview of our work, including motivations, methodology, and findings, is available at https://github.com/cnvlabs/distillation-fd. We are confident that Federated Distillation will serve as a foundation for future research in efficient Federated Learning. Nonetheless, our work also presents difficulties, such as a increased privacy risk due to the utilization of soft labels. Consequently, additional research into privacy preservation strategies is required. Furthermore, the potential for data manipulation through the utilization of public data sets also necessitates further investigation. Therefore, we suggest future research into Federated Distillation should concentrate on tackling these challenges. The conventional approach in multi-objective optimization assumes a pre-defined utility function, or it's learned through interactive feedback or a complete Pareto front determination. This assumption is too narrow, given the utility function's subjectivity and the practical limitations of obtaining explicit expert feedback. Instead of directly learning the utility function, our method learns the constraints associated with its possible values. This top-down constraint-based method doesn't require a utility function and doesn't assume a perfect understanding of the problem's variables. It uses generalized utility functions as constraints to represent the known utility function's range logically. This approach allows for the discovery of partially ordered variables and partially defines the utility function, providing better insight than typical local utility learning methods. We showcase the performance of this novel technique in two real-world scenarios. Recent findings in reinforcement learning indicate that agents can be exploited using specially crafted malicious examples. Our investigation demonstrates that these vulnerabilities can be expanded from attacks that have knowledge of the agents and their training processes, to situations where no information is available. We employ sequence-to-sequence models to predict actions of trained agents based on sequence data. Our results reveal that these models effectively anticipate the future actions of RL agents across a broad range of scenarios, suggesting that these agents can be vulnerable to black-box attacks. Moreover, modifying these attacks to adapt to changing environments has proven successful. We utilize these models to launch attacks on RL agents in two applications, a power system and an industrial process, targeting them with malicious goals. Our analysis shows that these attacks can shift the RL agents from optimal to safety-critical behavior, as evaluated by an independent safety specialist. These findings suggest that a black-box attack could potentially cause RL-based power grid autoregulators to malfunction and induce instability, leading to a significant reduction in reliability. Our safety specialist's evaluation reveals that these attacks could cause an industrial process RL agent to safely halt in order to avoid damage to equipment and humans, but fail to do so due to being compromised. These studies highlight the necessity of developing cold-start defenses against black-box attacks for the safe deployment of RL in critical systems. This paper presents a unified approach to addressing certain complex optimization challenges. Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, a more manageable formulation is required. This paper introduces such a formulation, dividing the solution process into two parts. Firstly, a series of time-series data is generated within predetermined time intervals through discrete modeling. Secondly, an algorithm is applied to process the data and produce continuous signals. Notably, the proposed method is adaptable to various optimization algorithms, including model predictive control, extended Kalman filter, and minimum variance optimal controller. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to a series of case studies. Ultimately, this work offers a practical strategy for tackling continuous-time optimization problems when analytical solutions are not available. Moreover, this framework provides a fundamental understanding of the relationship between discrete models and their continuous counterparts. This knowledge holds potential for further improvements in modeling efficiency. The associated software can be found in the MATLAB File Exchange under the identifier MP4.

A rational map $f$ from the Riemann sphere to itself is bicritical if it has precisely two points where the derivative is zero. We identify the groups that can be formed as groups of deck transformations of iterations of such bicritical maps, providing a comprehensive classification up to isomorphism. Additionally, we offer proof of a specific case of a conjecture initially proposed by Matzke. This bicritical structure corresponds to a specific type of topological object called an Sibirskii graph when examining the local behavior of $f$ around its critical points. This provides a geometric representation of these groups, which can be used to identify their presentation in cases where the graph has a finite number of vertices. This presentation can then be used to determine the group's structure. We establish that the group of deck transformations is finitely presented whenever the Sibirskii graph has a finite number of vertices. Conversely, if the graph has an infinite number of vertices, the group of deck transformations is not finitely presented. A bicritical map will have an absolutely infinitely branching Sibirskii graph if and only if it has a point where the derivative is zero that is mapped to itself, known as an attractive point. We show that the group of deck transformations is compactly discrete if and only if it has an absorbing point. Notably, this occurs in cases where the map is hyperbolic, as defined by the definition of hyperbolicity. When examining the properties of groups of deck transformations in specific cases, it is helpful to know the group's structure. We use Erlenmeyer-Poulsen's algorithm, which is based on a method originally proposed by Garside, to identify the groups of deck transformations associated with specific bicritical maps. This algorithm works by breaking down a given group into its subgroups, particularly those that correspond to specific geometric objects known as braid groups. This research introduces three indices for characterizing online signature templates based on distinctiveness, complexity, and reliability. 
Distinctiveness is evaluated through statistical analysis and a random signature assumption on a set of user signature examples.
Complexity is determined by examining the features of user signature examples.
Reliability, on the other hand, is estimated by assessing a validation set of user signature examples.
These three indices serve as indicators for measuring the performance of online verification systems against both random and intentional forgeries as well as the performance of genuine users providing valid signature examples.
Through experiments using different verification algorithms and three online signature datasets plus one keystroke dataset, the validity of these measures and their applications have been confirmed and demonstrated. 
Additionally, the study utilizes reliability as a validation metric to compare and evaluate the performance of different verification algorithms. 
Ultimately, the study proposes a utility function integrating distinctiveness, complexity, reliability, and accuracy as a comprehensive guide to helping online verification system designers optimize their solutions. 
The study's findings highlight the distinct advantages of different validation methods and genuine user contributions in enhancing the performance of online verification systems. 
Specifically, the study shows that algorithms utilizing a user-independent validation process by multiple genuine users achieve the best results in resisting both random and intentional forgeries. 
Additionally, the study reveals that genuine user contributions with high reliability and complex features are highly beneficial to online verification systems, and these contributions should not be considered as attacks but rather as valid signature examples. 
These findings will surely provide valuable guidance to online verification system designers in effectively utilizing signature examples from genuine users to boost their performance and achieve the best possible results. 
The study's outcomes are meaningful and useful for online verification system designers, showcasing the benefits of using reliable signature examples with high distinctiveness and complexity to resist both random and intentional forgeries.

These theories are represented as two asymmetric orbifold versions, one of order two and the other of order three. We demonstrated that the perturbative spectrum and the one-loop amplitudes are preserved under a symplectic group with Hurwitz and Eisenstein quaternions. Furthermore, we established the constraints on supersymmetric couplings in the effective theory and speculated about the non-perturbative properties, such as the completion of six-derivative couplings through rank-one theta functions, and the associated BPS states spectrum. We also explored the decoupling limits in which the T-folds reduce to singular backgrounds, namely the orbifold limit and the zero coupling limit, and analyzed the properties of the previously found spectrum in the six-derivative couplings. Lastly, we connected our findings with the recently proposed 'duality web' that links string theories in the six-derivative couplings sector. We determine empirical limits on nitrogen's nucleosynthetic yields by integrating nitrogen enrichment into a previously developed galactic chemical evolution model. The model considers two types of nitrogen yields: one that depends only on a star's mass (not its metal content) from massive stars, and another that depends on both the star's mass and metal content from AGB stars. As time progresses, model zones don't follow the [N/O]-[O/H] relation but instead first increase in oxygen to hydrogen ratio at a constant nitrogen to oxygen ratio, and then move upward in the [N/O] ratio via nitrogen produced by secondary processes. By selecting specific nitrogen yields that are in line with the mass of massive stars ($y_N^{CC} = 3.6 \times 10^{-4}$, consistent with stars that are rotating quickly), and AGB star yields that are linearly dependent on both the mass of these stars ($y_N^{AGB} = (9 \times 10^{-4})(M_*/M_\odot)(Z_*/Z_\odot)$) for a given mass of metals produced, our model is able to replicate observed trends of the [N/O]-[O/H] relation in the gas within galaxies. Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. By developing standardized datasets and models, we can better address complex societal problems and draw insights from related domains, such as domain adaptation, sentiment analysis, hate speech detection, and code-mixing monolingual tasks. Ultimately, this work serves as a primer for NLP researchers on these critical issues and offers a dataset of Hindi-English code-mixing sentences for data-driven modeling. This research was motivated by the 2021 IJCA special issue on relevant topics, offering a comprehensive overview of existing work and a set of recommended explorations for the NLP community. Hypothetically, this paper posits several additional research outcomes if NLP researchers focused on related areas, such as domain adaptation, sentiment analysis, hate speech detection, and code-mixing monolingual tasks, could be applied to these critical issues. Additionally, this research presents a new dataset of Hindi-English code-mixing sentences. In contrast to standard monolingual code-mixing tasks, this research tackles a more challenging problem by combining two language combinations, English and Hindi, as well as Hindi, an agglutinative language with various suffixes and prefixes, posing challenges for NLP model development. To address this research's goals, we propose developing standard datasets and models, leveraging related domains, and conducting empirical studies on code-mixing tasks. To this end, this research offers a new standard dataset of Hindi-English code-mixing sentences. In contrast to prior studies, this research differentiates between two types of code-mixing: monolingual and bilingual, with a focus on bilingual code-mixing. To develop this dataset, we used Google's Ngram data, the Wikipedia encyclopedia, and the Indigo corpus, finding that most available corpora did not meet our standards due to their small size or absence of relevant information.

This study reveals that sharing images online can compromise one's privacy, prompting the development of Graph Privacy Advisor - an image privacy classifier. This classifier leverages visual details and the number of objects in an image to predict its privacy level, by adapting a sophisticated model, reducing its complexity and improving performance through feature refinement. In particular, the classifier identifies the most relevant image characteristics to use for privacy evaluation and replaces complex, high-dimensional image data with simplified features, thus reducing its complexity. Moreover, the classifier tackles the issue of preconceived biases by modeling the likelihood of objects appearing together, rather than the frequency of individual objects. Experiments demonstrated that the classifier effectively detected private data in uploaded images, outperforming existing image classification models. This research is ongoing and the trained models, as well as additional information, can be accessed at https://github.com/princetonadvsys/GPA. In the future, the classifier will be integrated into online platforms to automatically flag potentially private images, thus informing users and protecting their privacy. Building on Griffiths' model of a quantum radiator, I expand upon it by developing theoretical models that can represent high entropy levels in physical systems for extended periods of time, eventually converging to pure states. These quantum radiation models are grounded in fundamental quantum principles and provide abstracted models of real-world phenomena as well as unusual spacetime configurations such as black and white holes and alternate universes. An in-depth examination of these models indicates possible avenues for experimental research into the underlying intricacies of quantum mechanics including interference with a particle's past, the influence of quantum entanglement on entropy, and residual connections between particles even at great distances. Additionally, I explore the implications of these models from an ontological perspective, particularly in relation to the concept of object identity over time. By comparing the ontological commitments required to understand these quantum radiation models, I suggest that the one based on entanglement offers the most compelling and consistent vision of what quantum mechanics demands of physical reality. To facilitate clarity and ease of understanding, I have chosen to minimize technical complexities in my explanations and instead employ clear, approachable language relevant to audiences with limited expertise in quantum mechanics, including philosophy students. Furthermore, I hope the underlying ideas and questions raised by these models will encourage further investigation and debate into the intricate nature of quantum mechanics and its profound ontological ramifications. \end{abstract}

Small solar eruptions known as nanoflares may hold the key to explaining the solar corona's high temperatures due to the potential release of vast magnetic energy, which could also lead to the emission of hard X-rays. The quiet Sun's faint HXR emission has not been directly observed so far; research using the Magellan Baade Telescope to study the corona's faint emission has yielded negative results for direct detection, but an analysis using a different statistical approach has indicated there may be faint HXR emissions present. Secondly, we aim to explore the effectiveness of a novel image processing technique, the Multi-Scale Fast Linear Independent Component Analysis (MFLICA) algorithm, in retrieving physical properties of the loop plasma from simulated images of the region. The findings from our study suggest that self-absorption can result in cooler apparent loop temperatures and also produces a reddish chromospheric response in the FUV images, as well as an underestimation of the surface pressure when using MFLICA-derived densities. The proposed MFLICA technique shows great potential for future applications in observing the solar corona and other astrophysical phenomena. Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in state or operator complexity investigations. A key advantage of this approach lies in the ability to easily manipulate boundary conditions and dual tensors, thus providing valuable insights into the geometric structure of complexity in quantum field theories. In this spirit, we thoroughly examine the complexity of boundary states and specific operators within the universal sector of a chiral CFT, effectively reducing the problem to a pure Hilbert space problem. Furthermore, we develop and support a theoretical framework for complexity in FQFT through the adoption of Adler-Bell-Jackiw charges, thus providing additional evidence for our claims. An interesting aspect of this analysis is the detection of a scaling relationship between complexity and the central charge of the CFT, specifically in the context of entanglement complexity. Moreover, a clear distinction is observed between state or operator complexity and the associated entropy generated in this process. Lastly, we extend our study to the dual holographic theories, specifically exploring the complexity of dual tensors and demonstrating that the associated complexity, expressed as a function of the dual tensor's contraction, is directly related to the amount of bulk matter ejected during the process, thus providing new insights into the mechanisms underlying complexity variations in quantum field theory. This theoretical work offers a comprehensive framework for the task of estimating object pose from total least squares, where features from point clouds are employed as vector observations of landmark features. Initially, a structured optimization model is introduced that extracts observation vectors from these features, followed by the derivation of associated error-covariance expressions. Utilizing this framework, solutions for object orientation and position are proven to achieve Cram\'er-Rao bounds under an approximate analysis of angle measurement errors. Several approaches for minimizing this error are presented, including a simple analytical solution and a modified Newton-Raphson algorithm, both of which are evaluated in simulation studies and found to outperform existing methods. Furthermore, an interesting finding from this research is that utilizing observation vectors directly in optimization leads to an approximately Cram\'er-Rao optimal solution, which is notable given the computational ease of this approach. This work extends earlier research on pose estimation to consider various error factors, provides closed-form solutions for minimizing related covariance expressions, and validates the efficacy of proposed methods through simulation studies. Additionally, key results from this research have been implemented in the ViSP meta-package for vision algorithms. This note examines the possibility that in models of supergravity and string theory, sectors driving dark matter and additional Higgs fields exist in hidden layers, which are disconnected from the standard model sector. We investigate how these hidden sectors can remain undetected while consistent physical laws are preserved. We then explore the possibility that dark matter is solely responsible for its own interactions through secondary processes, such as dark matter-induced decay of hadrons from dark form radiation, or through the interaction of dark matter with other dark sector particles that eventually decay into it. We specifically calculate the rate of dark matter-induced dark form radiation in the Milky Way galaxy, and our analysis indicates that it could be detectable by upcoming experiments. We also consider an alternative scenario where a dark sector particle decays into dark matter, leading to an observable rate of dark matter-induced gamma-ray emission from distant galaxies. Experiments may also be able to observe an isolated dark matter particle in a hidden sector through the observation of long-range interaction between standard model particles, such as electrons and muons. We have calculated the strength of this long-range interaction and found it to be within reach of up-to-date experiments. Finally, we have found that a hidden sector composed of dark matter and an almost massless particle can explain an observed anomaly in the data collected by the BABAR experiment. This anomaly involves a slight disparity in the number of di-leptonic events observed in certain energy ranges and is estimated to be a statistical anomaly if interpreted as a physical phenomenon. This discrepancy can be attributed to the interaction between a dark matter particle and an almost massless particle in the hidden sector, leading to an observed deviation in the predicted Standard Model results. We have found that a particular set of parameters in this model can account for this anomaly and predicts a future detection by the CRESST experiment. Researchers have discovered an instance of same-sign W boson pair production in proton-proton collisions. We examined the performance of six cosmological models by utilizing a dataset of three pairs, each of which included Planck data, lensing data, and non-Planck data, to analyze spatial curvature in three-dimensional space. In half of these pairs, the parameter governing lensing consistency, A_L, was treated as a variable; in the other half, this parameter was assumed to be 1. Our analysis revealed discrepancies in parameter estimates derived from Planck data versus non-Planck data when lensing consistency is fixed. Notably, these discrepancies favored models of a non-flat universe when examined separately, but these disparities disappeared when analyzing combined data, particularly when lensing consistency is allowed to vary freely. In the case of a dataset consisting of Planck, lensing, and non-Planck data, the estimates revealed a preference for A_L being larger than unity, by a significance value of 2.7 sigma. In light of this, the authors propose a new parameter, phi_L, which measures the deviation of lensing consistency from its standard value in Lambda-CDM models based on radial basis functions, where a significance value of 2.7 sigma favored values greater than zero. In models which treat spatial curvature as a variable, the estimates revealed a significance value of 2.4 sigma indicating a preference for negative values. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring an abundant amount of target domain data and being susceptible to contamination from a foreign domain, as well as having an overly broad target domain data requirement. This paper introduces a novel paradigm called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles the challenges of data scarcity in multiple domains by incorporating several domains into the recommendation process. MSDCR utilizes a multi-target framework to simultaneously optimize multiple domains by leveraging a dense tensor representation for each domain, thereby addressing the aforementioned issues. Experimental evaluations on four real-world datasets firmly establish MSDCR as a highly effective method, outperforming current state-of-the-art CDR methods across diverse metrics. Additionally, visualizations and analytical inspections confirm the logical coherence of the MSDCR framework. In particular, MSDCR excels in scenarios involving extremely sparse domains, such as a dataset with a 7% density level, significantly surpassing the performance of the second-best method by 43%. The source code of MSDCR is available at https://github.com/aimware-rc/Multidomain_Recommendation. The reconstructed video for the paper is accessible at https://www.youtube.com/aimrc. We are focusing specifically on how local moments behave in insulators that have disorder, and we are finding that the correlations associated with the spin slowly decrease over time in these materials. This is in line with what is expected in the random singlet phase, and it is also confirmed through numerical tests. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Shwartz for Sn. This study investigates kink soliton patterns within scalar field interactions, specifically involving two fields in 2D and 4D dimensions, where one field exhibits a broken symmetry while the other exhibits a unbroken symmetry. We derive a generalized form of the sine-Gordon model, originally proposed by Bakulev and Larkin, that demonstrates kink soliton patterns in a theory with couplings that are proportional to the difference between the two fields. We then examine how these kinks behave as the symmetry breaks gradually, either partially or completely, in both 2D and 4D dimensions. In addition, we discuss how these kinks can be interpreted as a result of a topological hidden symmetry. Furthermore, we derive a generalized form of the Manton equation, which governs the behavior of these kinks in a rapidly moving frame of reference. Lastly, we examine how these kinks can be stabilized through a gauge boson mass generated by the Schwinger mechanism. Our findings reveal that the development of a mass gap in the 4D theory can occur through a rapid collapse of the kink, which in turn is induced by a gradual decrease in the symmetry breaking parameter. Conversely, in the 2D theory, this transition is non-instantaneous. However, by introducing an auxiliary scalar field, we demonstrate that a mass gap can occur both slowly and suddenly, depending on the interaction between this field and the two primary fields. Our study thus sheds light on the behavior of kink solitons in theories with multiple interacting fields and reveals novel stabilization mechanisms, including one based on a gauge boson mass generated by the Schwinger mechanism. Our findings also suggest that these solitons could serve as powerful tools in the exploration of such complex theories. Ultimately, our analysis may find application in the study of certain microscopically induced phase transitions in condensed matter physics. Our study also raises the possibility that these solitons could be used to model analogous phase transitions in fluids. Conversely, by integrating the Higgs mechanism into the theory, we discover that the resulting solitons can be unstable and potentially stable, where this dichotomous behavior is induced by the interplay between symmetry breaking and the duration of the phase transition. Our study also uncovers an intriguing analogy between this behavior and that of kinks in theories with three interacting fields, where the interplay between symmetry breaking and the duration of the phase transition gives rise to a dichotomous pattern of kink stability. Our discovery of this analogy opens up new avenues for research

Robots that learn from observations in real-world environments using inverse reinforcement learning can face obstacles when experts' demonstrations are marred by extraneous data from their surroundings. This unwanted information is usually eliminated in controlled settings, but when impossible, it needs to be filtered out. However, tracking down the source of this extraneous data is a challenging task, especially with large amounts of data involved. A new approach utilizes a hierarchical Bayesian model to analyze both expert and extraneous data, effectively acknowledging the diverse range of observations a robot may encounter. Building upon an existing algorithm, it extends to handle a variety of observations, including partial occlusion and extraneous data, as seen in a simulated environment. Our model outperforms comparable methods in a sorting domain and nearly achieves optimal results when given extensive training. Moreover, it successfully removes distractions in a robot navigation task, allowing it to discover a relevant reward function. This rewards function aligns with an expert's intentions, indicating a potential solution to a common problem in robotics. Given a subgroup $H$ of the fundamental group of a space $X$, we develop the concept of a strong $H$-SLT space by adapting the definition to the relative version. This extension allows us to investigate the existence of a covering map for these spaces, and under certain conditions, a semicovering map can be regarded as a covering map when the space satisfies the strong $H$-SLT property. Our study further explores when the whisker topology coincides with the lasso topology on $\widetilde{X}_{H}$, and examines the correspondence between open subsets of $\pi_{1}^{wh}(X,x_{0})$ and $\pi_{1}^{l}(X,x_{0})$. Additionally, we provide illustrative examples to demonstrate the validity of the concept and further research of strong $H$-SLT spaces. Finally, we present the main theorem involving functorial properties of strong $H$-SLT spaces on open subsets of $\pi_{1}^{wh}(X,x_{0})$. Our work offers new insights into the existing article by Anan'tu et al., extending their results, and providing answers to posed questions within that publication.\\

Keywords: Strong $H$-SLT space, covering map, semicovering map, whisker topology and lasso topology.\\

There are many complex control problems in both theoretical and practical settings, where current automated reinforcement learning techniques struggle to find a suitable policy. The path from initial observation to final action involves two primary challenges: identifying a relevant action from many options and ensuring the chosen action leads to a beneficial outcome. A new algorithm, called Directed Action selection using Local Optimization (DALO), tackles these issues by decomposing the decision-making process into two manageable stages. Firstly, DALO focuses on selecting the most relevant action using an unsupervised model without considering the consequences of each option. Secondly, DALO employs a local optimization to refine the selected action. The effectiveness of DALO is demonstrated through its success in solving a difficult navigation problem on a 10x10 grid and a challenging robotic joint control problem with 28 DOFs, where all associated dynamic models are unavailable. Moreover, DALO's performance is compared to the state-of-the-art n-step Q-learning and a recent action selection algorithm in the 10x10 grid setting. When DALO's optimized actions are used in a stable and stable-free setting, its average episodic returns significantly surpass the average episodic returns obtained from the state-of-the-art n-step Q-learning. The source code for DALO is publicly available at https://github.com/visual-reinforcement-learning/dalo. The associated video can be found at https://youtu.be/7e4D7TPxMTk. Binary matrix datasets are widespread in scientific research and analyzing them often involves identifying complex structures, such as dependencies and relationships, through various statistical methods. In order to study binary matrix data, researchers employ randomization tests to investigate specific hypotheses concerning the matrix's structural properties. One such test is the permutation test, specifically tailored for binary matrix data, known as the binary matrix sampling (BMS) test. The BMS test has been proven effective in detecting significant clusterings within binary matrices by utilizing an efficient swapping algorithm that exploits the matrices' sparse properties. However, our investigation reveals that the presence of structural zeros in the matrix affects the test's critical significance levels, leading to elevated Type I error rates. In order to address this issue, we present two modified versions of the BMS test that are capable of detecting a broader range of meaningful clusterings beyond the original implementation's limitations. The first variant involves the use of computational optimization to identify effective clusterings, while the second involves a heuristic approach based on the matrix's sparse properties. Through numerical experiments and real-data analyses, we demonstrate the enhanced effectiveness of these new algorithms in detecting important clusterings within binary matrices. In addition, we have implemented these algorithms in R package available at https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/BMS/index.html. Anyone can utilize the BMS function to generate the figures presented in this study, found at the bottom of this page. Our work aims to facilitate the detection of significant clusterings within binary matrices by providing these algorithms as supportive tools. Generating synthetic cell shapes realistically can contribute to developing training datasets to enhance cell tracking and segmentation capabilities in biomedical imaging. For effective cell shape synthesis, a compact yet flexible representation is required, however current methods involving voxel-based and polygon mesh approaches have limitations for high-resolution and topology changes such as growth and cell division. Our proposal utilizes level sets of signed distance functions to represent cell shapes. By training a neural network to implicitly generate signed distance function values at any point in three-dimensional space over time, conditioned on a latent code, it is possible to create new and realistic spatial cell shape sequences. The effectiveness of our approach was evaluated both qualitatively and quantitatively through comparisons of synthetic cells with actual cell growth, mitosis and lung cancer cells exhibiting complex protrusions. Our results demonstrate the generation of synthetic cells with similar characteristics to real cells, including the production of plausible cell shape sequences in three-dimensional space over time. The implementation of a conditional implicit generative model of signed distance functions also facilitates the creation of synthetic cells with predetermined topological characteristics such as cell splitting. Moreover the representation is suitable for the synthesis of a broad range of spatial cell shapes including those with flat membranes and those that have undergone extensive cell shape changes such as cell lobe formation. Last but not least our approach offers an opportunity to train a neural network to learn cell shape evolution profiles for real cells which can be used to prompt cell shape synthesis. To evaluate the efficiency of event-chain Monte Carlo algorithms for complex systems, we thoroughly examine the alchemical perturbations of linearized ECMC, a simplified variant of earlier ECMC algorithms. Our analysis explores four types of alchemical perturbations: volume, temperature, chemical potential, and concentration variations. We observe that linearized ECMC remains asymptotically reversible in these scenarios and that differences between its differences and reversible Metropolis algorithm's differences diminish as the update size becomes progressively smaller. Moreover, the speed at which linearized ECMC converges to the target distribution is significantly faster than that of the Metropolis algorithm. We also compare its differences with those of another ECMC algorithm, which uses univariate linearizations, and find that it remains asymptotically reversible despite taking a different approach. Comprehensive testing validates the efficacy of linearized ECMC in simulating the behavior of complex systems through alchemical perturbations. These findings provide a foundation for applying linearized ECMC in various scientific applications, including materials science and physical chemistry. By way of example, we apply linearized ECMC to investigate the phase behavior of the hard-disk fluid and accurately map out its phase diagram, particularly in scenarios where first-order phase transitions occur. Our analysis supports the use of linearized ECMC as an exceptionally powerful algorithm for performing detailed simulations of complex systems, either in isolation or in conjunction with Metropolis algorithm for finer-scale investigations. We additionally outline a variant of linearized ECMC that operates in three dimensions and showcases its potential in various applications. Furthermore, we examine its application in slab geometry and observe that it remains asymptotically reversible despite the presence of boundaries. Additionally, we explore its use in canonical ensembles and observe that it exhibits asymptotic equivalence to a thermodynamic benchmark in the flatland limit. As a further extension, we apply linearized ECMC to investigate the thermodynamic properties of mesoscopic particles in canonical ensembles. Our results provide a foundation for future research in this domain. Moreover, we examine the application of linearized ECMC in simulations involving multiple particles and observe that it remains asymptotically reversible despite the presence of interactive dynamics. To further optimize its performance, we have also developed an accelerated variant of linearized ECMC, which integrates the univariate approach of another ECMC algorithm and is shown to be exceptionally powerful. As a concrete example, we apply linearized ECMC to investigate the thermodynamic properties of nanoscale particles in canonical ensembles and obtain highly accurate results by matching differences with a thermodynamic benchmark. Time-frequency analysis heavily relies on spectrograms, being a crucial tool derived from the short time Fourier transform (STFT). The underlying theory's rigor is influenced by the properties of a zero set of a Gaussian analytic function, making it particularly challenging to handle. Despite this, spectrograms have proven invaluable in various practical applications. On the positive side, they offer highly effective ways to extract features from signals. Therefore, it's essential to develop more intuitive and mathematically sound approaches that take into account the inherent inaccuracies inherent in spectrograms, ultimately leveraging their benefits in signal processing applications. This research focuses on the approximate spectrograms of signals with uncertain origins, aiming to provide a framework that uncovers their underlying features. A key contribution is the establishment of a spectral low-complexity criterion that enables the identification of optimal spectrograms. This criterion serves as a foundation for a convex optimization problem, facilitating the construction of spectrograms. Spectrograms derived from this approach exhibit improved time-frequency resolution, compared to traditional ones. Furthermore, there's a subtle connection observed between approximate spectrograms and a Gaussian analytic function's zero set. Consequently, spectrograms still possess limited accuracy but demonstrate significant utility in feature extraction tasks, as demonstrated through an extensive evaluation of various signal processing applications. Specifically, it's Iliev's conjecture that the zero set of a Gaussian analytic function has a diameter of approximately $0.89\bar{3}$. Consequently, spectrograms may not provide completely accurate frequency estimates but do offer precise time-frequency relationships, crucial for feature extraction. Ultimately, spectrograms successfully demonstrated their potential in numerous practical signal processing applications, firmly establishing their value in scientific and engineering fields. Evidence suggesting the demographic characteristics of massive black holes is accumulating, spanning a broad spectrum of galaxy types, from large clusters to solitary stars. Despite this, the original paths of massive black holes remain shrouded in uncertainty. We have discovered a potentially significant indicator of massive black hole formation in isolated dwarf galaxies, which could help reveal the origins of these enigmatic objects. We have found that massive black holes in isolated dwarf galaxies often reside within a densely populated stellar environment known as a core or bar pattern. This distinctive feature can be seen in all galaxies hosting a massive black hole, including NGC 205, Segue 1, and F568-1, in which it was discovered using the Hubble Space Telescope's high-resolution images. These patterns are thought to be the residual effect of a massive black hole's gravitational influence on the host galaxy, specifically on a massive accretion disk or bar that formed during a key period in the galaxy's evolution. Thus, this phenomenon may serve as a critical indicator of massive black hole formation in isolated dwarf galaxies, one that is consistent with theories involving disk-based feedback mechanisms. In contrast, we did not observe this pattern in galaxies that are galactic pairs or those thought to be the remnants of galaxy mergers, such as Leo I, which might indicate a distinct origin for massive black holes in these types of galaxies and a different impact of massive black hole feedback in these systems. Further research is needed to confirm these initial findings and explore potential links between massive black hole evolution and the observed demographic characteristics of these enigmatic objects. Ultimately, this could help reveal a clear picture of massive black hole origins, one in which different formation paths are reflected in distinct observational signatures.} \end{abstract}

To each multiplicative linear logic proof structure, we relate an ideal that encapsulates its logical meaning through polynomial equations. We demonstrate how cut-elimination in multiplicative proof nets parallels specific applications of the Buchberger algorithm, a method used for computing Gröbner bases in elimination theory. This connection equips multiplicative proof nets with a decoder, which verifies the correctness of net interpretations and provides a useful tool for decomposing complex nets. Furthermore, we show how this decoder can be adapted to model interactive systems defined using the lambda calculus with explicit substitution as described by Krivine, with additional axioms potentially present. We suggest an alternative method for the decoder to function without relying on the axioms' solvability. Finally, the paper explores an algorithmic strategy for the axioms' solvability, which may lead to further research opportunities. Overall, this paper highlights a range of new tools for the study of multiplicative proof nets that not only align with cut-elimination in type theory but also offer various additional tools. We detail an implementation of the presented methods and an example of its use in a problem involving planarity, which shares similarities with a problem previously studied by Jonsson. We successfully applied the methods to solve this problem as well as other related examples. A sophisticated time series analysis tool called cross-correlation analysis is used in this study to explore the interconnected behaviors of time series, with a focus on financial markets. A novel prediction method for determining the future synchronization state of two related time series has been developed. Cross-recurrence plots are applied as a non-linear approach to measure the coupling between the time domain of two series, thus establishing their synchronization status. A deep learning strategy is employed to address the task of predicting synchronization states, utilizing dynamic sampling of cross-recurrence plots as key features. Experimental results from multiple stocks, including significant S&P 100 constituents, have been gathered to test the efficacy of this method. Findings indicate that synchronizing predictions for time series pairs can be challenging, yet achieveable with substantial accuracy for certain stock pairs. Current click-through rate (CTR) prediction models are largely dependent on behavior IDs that are based on past user-ad interactions. However, using behavior IDs is impractical when predicting CTR for new ads without prior interactions. To overcome these limitations, our approach utilizes ad visuals to enhance the performance of CTR prediction models. We achieve this by converting each ad into a set of visual identifiers that reflect its content. These identifiers are then used to generate visual embeddings, which can improve CTR predictions. The process of generating these visual identifiers is cast as a supervised quantization problem. Due to the absence of labels for commercial images, we instead utilize text descriptions to optimize our image extractor and create effective visual identifiers. Since traditional hard quantization operations are non-differentiable, we employ a softened quantization approach to support end-to-end network training. The resulting visual identifiers can then be paired with historical user-ad interactions to learn corresponding embeddings. Notably, the embedding derived from the visual content of an ad can effectively generalize to new ads. When used in conjunction with traditional ad behavior IDs, our approach leads to significantly improved performance, with average CTR increasing by 1.46% and total revenue rising by 1.10%. The enhanced performance is particularly evident when predicting CTR for new ads without prior interactions. When used alone, the visual content of ads can effectively substitute the traditional behavior ID, resulting in an 8.62% improvement in total revenue. Moreover, our approach has the added benefit of reducing network complexity by diminishing the size of ad embedding vectors. To achieve this, we employ the same softened quantization technique to reduce the number of units in the last fully connected layer of the CTR model. Notably, our approach offers a more effective way to decrease model complexity than traditional network pruning techniques. The resulting configuration can significantly lower the cost of training CTR models while also reducing memory usage during inference. The improved performance resulting from our approach is validated by our analysis of both advertised visual content and the generalized embeddings representing user interactions. Additionally, we examine the impact of the number of visual identifiers, their representation capacity, and the network complexity on CTR prediction performance. Furthermore, we provide an efficient implementation of the softened quantization approach that is currently unparalleled in the field. The improved generalizability of our CTR models means they can be more easily transferred to new ads, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of online advertising systems. Research has shown that combining resting-state functional MRI data from multiple sites can potentially introduce systematic biases in connectivity measures. In this research, we studied how site-to-site effects impact our ability to detect individual and group differences, and our analysis suggests that multisite studies are feasible when utilizing large sample sizes. Our data collection was based on actual, rather than simulated, fMRI datasets from N=345 young, healthy subjects, acquired across eight scanning sites, all of which utilized 3T scanners and varied scanning protocols. Our findings demonstrate that commonly observed functional networks are consistently present across all sites, and inter-site effects were relatively minor. Through Monte-Carlo simulations, we evaluated the effects of data combination on our ability to detect changes and predict group differences, revealing that large sample sizes can compensate for any resulting loss in power due to multisite effects. Our study provides empirical evidence that multisite research is feasible and viable, and can contribute significantly to our understanding of brain function in large-scale studies. Building on previous work, where a directed graph equivalent of the Ricci curvature was developed based on the Chung Laplacian, this note focuses on deriving a characterization of our lower Ricci curvature bound by applying a heat semigroup gradient estimate and a heat flow-based transportation inequality. This will serve as the basis for establishing a concentration of measure inequality for directed graphs with positive Ricci curvature. Our work is largely analogous to Kozlov's methods in the context of undirected graphs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the lower Ricci curvature bound can be expressed as a concentration of measure inequality and that concentration of measure inequalities imply a certain characterization of our lower Ricci curvature bound. Lastly, we provide an example illustrating that an incomplete directed graph can possess curvature bounded below, yet fail to have a characterizable concentration of measure inequality. This is in contrast to the scenario in the context of undirected graphs. 

In this updated version, we have incorporated additional insights and an alternative proof for the gradient estimate and the transportation inequality, which relies on a different approach. This approach uses a different formula for the gradient estimate and the transportation inequality and requires an approximation by completion of squares for directed graphs, which is analogous to the methods employed in the context of undirected graphs. 

We have also provided an alternative characterization of our lower Ricci curvature bound by applying a different approach, which is based on an approximation by completion of squares for directed graphs. This approach uses Bonnet's formula and involves an approximation and an interpolation technique, which is similar to the methods employed in the context of undirected graphs.

Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained considerable attention, 
mainly driven by the widespread use of language blending in social media across 
multi-lingual countries such as India, Mexico, Europe, and parts of the USA. 
Given their importance, developing word embeddings for code-mixed languages has 
become a pressing concern. A major obstacle in achieving this goal is 
overcoming the limitations imposed by language switch points. Statistical models 
are unable to efficiently capture the characteristics of these transition points 
owing to the high variability in observed data examples. This research paper 
investigates the effectiveness of applying switching point-based positional 
encoding methods to process code-mixed languages like Hinglish, resulting in only 
marginally improved outcomes relative to state-of-the-art models, although 
initial findings suggest that positional encoding could be a valuable technique 
for training sensitive language models that account for position-based language 
usage patterns in mixed texts. Notably, positional encoding may offer crucial 
insights into the tactical language switching strategies employed by social media 
users. Hinglish was chosen for this study due to its widespread use in online 
communications, particularly in countries like India and the Maldives. This paper 
presents a comprehensive analysis of word2vec, FastText, and BERT models used in 
code-mixed settings, identifying areas for improvement and proposing a data 
augmentation technique to address the data scarcity issue that affects model 
training. Overall, the research provides a theoretical argument for the role of 
positional encoding in training sensitive language models, even though the empirical 
outcomes were only mildly positive. As a result, further studies are recommended 
to verify the proposal's validity and explore other encoding techniques to 
effectively capture the characteristics of code-mixed languages. Additionally, the 
research offers a novel data augmentation strategy, which could be applied to 
other datasets to address data scarcity challenges encountered during model 
training. Currently, the proposed method's efficiency in handling scarcity issues 
is unknown and requires verification in follow-up studies. Nonetheless, the 
research makes a significant theoretical contribution to the NLP community, 
especially in the context of code-mixed languages, offering valuable insights into 
the language switching patterns of social media users. As social media continues to 
grow in importance, the likelihood of social media text becoming a primary data 
source for NLP model training and language understanding analysis increases.

Fisher developed the Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection using the concepts of average excess and average effect, where he initially defined these ideas somewhat abstractly. However, some experts believe that reframing his theories using statistical methods such as covariance and regression would clarify these concepts, both are part of classical statistical analysis. We propose an interpretation where Fisher's average excess and average effect are intended to represent a fundamental distinction between statistical correlation and causality, and according to this understanding, the average effect specifically measures the weighted outcomes of a physical change in the genes of a homologous pair. We show that this apparent conflict can be resolved if specific relationships are maintained between gene frequencies and residual non-additive components, and also discuss the idea that maintaining causality as part of Fisher's original framework has certain advantages in the field. Fisher's key distinction between statistical correlation and causality holds crucial importance in the field of evolutionary biology and also for genetic studies of phenotypes. We explore some of the implications of this distinction, such as the fact that in the case of sexual populations with shuffling of homologous pairs, correlation and causality can often be considered equivalent. However, this presentation of the key concepts of evolutionary biology also highlights the need for a clear distinction between statistical correlation and causality, and perhaps most importantly, it clarifies the fundamental difference between correlation and causality that is essential for making accurate claims about biological phenomena. We also touch on some intriguing implications of this distinction, such as the fact that in the case of sexual populations with shuffling of homologous pairs, correlation and causality can often be considered as equivalent. However, the key importance of Fisher's key distinction between statistical correlation and causality lies in the fact that it facilitates the accurate formulation of causal claims that are both necessary and sufficient for making accurate claims about biological phenomena. We also discuss some of the potential implications of this distinction, such as the challenges it poses in inferring causal relationships from statistical data, particularly when dealing with complex phenomena such as the diversity of life on Earth. We conclude by highlighting some of the key areas where further research could contribute to our understanding of the key concepts of evolutionary biology, and perhaps most importantly, it clarifies the distinct value of Fisher's key distinction between statistical correlation and causality in the context of evolutionary biology. This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking assisted by thrusters using a closed-loop feedback system. By assuming that supervisory controllers are properly set, we will concentrate on refining joint trajectories to meet specific performance requirements. To achieve this, we will create a mediator filter utilizing reference governors to ensure that performance constraints are met. Due to the impacts and adjustments made during the gait cycle causing deviations from desired periodic orbits, we will ensure robust hybrid invariance through the application of predictive methods within a short timeframe. To maintain hybrid invariance, we will leverage the distinctive features of our model, the thrusters, to our advantage. The key benefit of our approach is that unlike other optimization-based nonlinear control methods, performance-related constraints are met during the single-support phase without reliance on costly numerical methods. Furthermore, the proposed thruster-assisted gait control framework allows for the utilization of performance and robustness-enhancing capabilities during particular phases of the gait cycle, a previously unreported aspect. Experimental results confirming the efficacy of this strategy are presented. This work was partially presented at the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems, Vancouver, in 2017, and partially presented at the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation, Phoenix, in 2018. Due to differences in quality and relevance, some of the contributions from these conferences have been incorporated into the current version but with significant alterations, hence being considered as substantially new contributions.
