This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric matching, where a site-specific map is created by converting 2D image features into 3D surfel map representations. A novel depth estimation method using an image sequence or a single image, combined with an self-supervising process, is employed to convert the map. The survels are then matched with a target image, utilizing a geometric correspondence method to find registered points. Next, a probabilistic model Predictive Probability Propagation (P4) is used to determine the 6-DOF pose by analyzing the gradients and 3D points. The accuracy of this method is assessed using simulated data and a simulated camera, as well as real images and a ground truth map, demonstrating its effectiveness under various constraints. The results indicate that this method is suitable for visual relocalization without the need for pre-trained datasets. Moreover, it can be applied in situations where only one image is available, making it versatile for a range of tasks including visual relocalization. The proposed method also demonstrates excellent performance in comparison to a relevant method called Visual Odometry. Another advantage of this method is that updates are specifically tailored to the data sets owned by participants. A novel centralized training method called 'learning from partially labeled data in federated learning' has been introduced to deal with datasets having vast amounts of unseen categories. Unfortunately, personal devices are unable to efficiently process such complex computations as they face power, memory, storage, and connectivity issues. Given that each contribution is unique and tailored, it becomes crucial for the server to effectively merge summaries from multiple clients to produce accurate class distributions. Simulations of second-long black hole-neutron star mergers in numerical relativity are conducted to obtain a comprehensive picture of the inspiral, merger, and post-merger stages.  The analysis across various initial and computational configurations reveals universally similar evolution processes, regardless of setup variations.  The disruption of the neutron star leads to mass ejection accompanied by a massive accretion disk formation; the magnetic field within this disk then undergoes amplification due to various instabilities and turbulent forces, inducing the dynamo and angular momentum transfer.  The subsequent mass ejection by viscous magnetohydrodynamic turbulence begins roughly 300-500 milliseconds post-merger, persists for several hundred milliseconds; meanwhile, a magnetosphere is formed around the black hole, producing a focused strong electromagnetic outflow lasting about 0.5-2 seconds.  The model without equatorial-plane symmetry shows inverted magnetic polarity in the magnetosphere, caused by a magnetorotational instability dynamo, whereas a model initially comprising toroidal fields demonstrates a late post-merger stage characterized by a tilted disk and magnetosphere, due to anisotropic mass ejection effects, potentially shortening the Poynting-luminosity phase to 0.5-2 seconds.  The late stage variation in disk inclination angle leads to a potential variation of the observed amplitude of the electromagnetic outflow in the magnetosphere, ranging from 10% to 100%, according to the orientation.  The late post-merger stage is found to be significantly influenced by the late stage variation in disk inclination angle, leading to a potential variation of the observed amplitude of the electromagnetic outflow in the magnetosphere, ranging from 10% to 100%, according to the orientation.  The late post-merger stage is found to be significantly illuminated by the magnetospheric emission, potentially outshining the surrounding heat-dominated disk; however, the merger-stage light curves exhibit no sign of this magnetospheric emission due to the opacities of the surrounding disk and ejecta, which may mask the magnetospheric emission signal.  The model suggests that a significant portion of the post-merger energy budget may be attributed to the ejecta, accounting for up to half of the total energy in comparison to the disk.  The comparison across various initial configurations indicates that an accurate prediction of the post-merger disc and ejecta properties depends heavily on the resolution of the numerical relativity simulation, rather than the specific model parameters or physics employed. A novel variation of the Kawazumi-Zhang invariant, specifically $\varphi(C)$,
for compact Riemann surfaces $C$ of genus $g \geq 1$ is presented, exploring
its connections to the first Mumford-Morita-Miller class $e_1 = \kappa_1$ on the
moduli space and its relation to the traditional Kawazumi-Zhang invariant. The
given $\varphi(C)$ can be viewed as an alternative to the latter that accounts
for hyperbolic length in place of hyperbolic area. Consequently, it is shown
that this new invariant remains unchanged under the action of the symplectic
group $Sp(2g, \mathbb{Z})$. The study also investigates its mass spectrum and
its connections to the cohomology classes of the moduli space, ultimately
calculating its weighted sum with powers of the Kawazumi-Zhang invariant. The
text includes a detailed analysis of its behavior for specific Riemann surfaces,
such as elliptic curves, hyperbolic surfaces of genus 2, and the Bolza surface. 
Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the mass spectrum admits a finitude bound
specific to each degree, $i = 0, \ldots, g$, as a consequence of the limited
nonvanishing eigenvalues in the Eisenstein series associated with $e_i$. The
presentation extends an existing result by Kawazumi-Zhang to characteristic 0. 
Additionally, the theory has been verified numerically for all genus 2 surfaces and
the Bolza surface up to genus 6. The project further involves a comprehensive
computation of the $\varphi(C)$ values for all genus 2 surfaces and the Bolza
surface, which are then tabulated along with the lengths of their geometric
graphs representing the hyperbolic surface network. The code used for these
calculations, along with the data themselves, has been made publicly
accessible. Furthermore, the study exhibits a correlation between the
hyperbolic surface network's geometric properties and its moduli space
characteristics, marking the initial exploration of this type of network in
the study of compact Riemann surfaces. As such, it is denoted as the PHSN
project. Currently, the HSN database boasts a collection of over 600,000

In reverse, we establish that a conditioned process converging uniformly to a self-conservative, ergodic Markov process also attains a distinct quasi-stationary equilibrium, which it converges toward at an exponential rate across all initial distributions. Furthermore, we illustrate a corollary ergodic theorem under specific conditions. Next, we outline a few practical scenarios where a conditioned process is known to converge uniformly but the theorem is not applicable. Finally, we extend the established results to multi-dimensional processes conditioned upon reaching specific boundary regions. This research explores the optical interaction between a dimer of dielectric nanoparticles near a graphene layer. By applying a precise electromagnetic model, we computed the optical force acting on each particle and derived equations to assess the influence of graphene's surface plasmons. Our findings demonstrate that the excitation of graphene's surface plasmons can produce numerous stable positions with interparticle distances much shorter than the photon wavelength. Additionally, we found that these positions can be dynamically manipulated by adjusting the graphene's chemical potential. Both perpendicular and angled light incidence have been taken into account in the study. Our work may lead to the development of rapid, high-precision nanopositioning systems. We also explored how these positions change in response to different orientations of the incident electric field. By analyzing the energy radiated by the system, we gained insight into the mechanism underlying the interaction between the nanoparticles and the graphene layer. Our study shows that strong binding can occur even with far-field radiation as small as that predicted by the Rayleigh-Cramér estimate. Our work has also revealed that the interaction between the nanoparticles is generally antiparallel to the electric field at stable positions, but that this interaction can vary significantly with the graphene's conductivity. Our study suggests that the interaction between the nanoparticles could be made parallel to the electric field under certain conditions. Our work may lead to the development of new, nanoscale optical tools that utilize graphen and could improve our understanding of how light interacts with matter. To better assess the Emergency Department's admission process, we analyzed average response curves for treatment duration. Extending the time for treatment is considered an effective strategy for improving admissions; nonetheless, empirical evidence supporting this claim is difficult to gather. The treatment duration is impacted by various unmeasurable patient factors and coincides with the admission decision, which are challenging variables to manipulate. We depicted the admission process as a complex network, allowing for the identification of specific intervention points that yield actionable insights. Focusing on patients presenting abdominal pain, we analyzed large datasets from two hospitals in the Netherlands, treating each patient equally based on clinical characteristics, treatment protocols, and physician preferences. We discovered that length-of-stay variations are largely caused by small, scattered decisions made by physicians and that minor adjustments within the standard 4-hour treatment period hold the potential to improve admission rates more effectively than extending the treatment time. Increasing efficiency within the standard timeframe is achievable by streamlining clinical processes and reducing workload by optimizing staff composition and workload distribution. Consequently, hospital administrators can target factors influencing physician decision-making and workload outside of treatment times to enhance the Emergency Department's admission capabilities. Ultimately, adopting targeted interventions aimed at optimizing clinical processes and workload within the standard treatment period may yield more substantial outcomes than extending the treatment time itself. Our analysis offers a versatile framework for evaluating complex decision-making processes across various treatment areas. Research has examined the correlations of charges in particle interactions within Pb-Pb collisions, specifically looking at whether evidence of the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME) exists in the collision data collected at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. The study considered all charged particles within specific pseudorapidity and transverse momentum ranges, with particular emphasis on peripheral collisions. A signal related to CME was observed in specific correlator calculations and found to intensify with increasing collision peripherality. Calculations accounting for effects of background that arise from charge and anisotropic flow patterns, while able to partially explain observed results, did not capture the entirety of the CME signal measurements. A comparison of the CME and mixed-harmonics correlator signals further highlighted the significant influence of background contributions. It was also discovered that the magnitude of the CME signal varied directly with collision peripherality, though was found to be consistent across different energy levels. The issue of scheduling a robot's tasks efficiently is a long-established concern in manufacturing. Solutions have commonly drawn on a variant of the classic Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), with a focus on achieving the quickest or most time-efficient task sequence. Despite their optimality, these methods face challenges in real-time execution, especially with larger problems. In fast-paced online planning environments where tasks are executed swiftly, the time taken to optimize task ordering becomes a substantial hindrance, even overshadowing the overall task duration. The optimal approach in such cases involves balancing solution quality with total task completion time, achieved by identifying the most suitable sequence within the task set. The proposed algorithm offers this compromise through an iterative process involving task generation, grouping, and sequence optimization. The results indicate significant reductions in execution time, with these improvements verified against a standard algorithm in both simulated and practical UR5 robot scenarios. The successful implementation highlights the potential for better performance in online planning environments. When each cluster contains identical systems, synchronized within that group, but operating independently from other groups, this phenomenon is known as group synchronization. Typically, group synchronization is challenging to achieve, requiring precise adjustment of parameters, a specific configuration of connections, and diverse types of oscillators within the network. Our current research focuses on exploring networks composed of different types of oscillators, further complicating the already complex problem. Using a combination of theoretical and numerical methods, we have developed essential conditions, allowing for the identification of stable group synchronization states. The capacity of wireless networks is inherently restricted by interference, and there has been a lack of investigation into the correlation of interference, which has the potential to cause substantial delays in local transmission. This study addresses the query of whether randomizing the Medium Access Control (MAC) layer, using protocols like frequency-hopping multiple access and ALOHA, can mitigate the adverse effects of interference correlation. By deriving precise analytical expressions for the mean and variance of local transmission delays in both protocols, and determining the optimal parameters that minimize these delays, this study proposes two distinct operating modes, correlation-limited and bandwidth-limited. Notably, while both protocols may exhibit identical mean local delays when operating at specific conditions, their variances diverge significantly. Finally, this study evaluates the interplay between delay and variability, and provides crucial bounds on the local delay tail probability, offering valuable insights for wireless system design. This research has far-reaching implications and is expected to contribute to the ongoing development of wireless communication systems. Additionally, the derived analytical expressions can be used to explore other aspects of wireless system performance, such as energy efficiency and throughput. To confirm the accuracy and practicality of the proposed analysis, this study compares theoretical predictions with simulation results, and investigates the feasibility of several approximations. Finally, this study examines the influence of system model assumptions on wireless access performance, and presents an alternative system model that is both non-independent and non-identically distributed. This study responds to the growing need for accurate analytical methods to design optimal wireless communication systems, and addresses a significant gap in existing literature by investigating the correlation of interference and its impact on local delay in wireless networks. Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, although it typically relies on uncertain labels in an attempt to supplement the training set. The pseudo-labeling method in various existing works, however, does not account for the confidence of each label and redistributes the confidence equally to all labels in the graph, leading to poorly predicted labels and biased classification results. To address this problem, this paper proposes an innovative pseudo-labeling framework that generates informative pseudo-labels adapted to each graph's local structure. The framework incorporates a novel module called Structured Pseudo-Labeling Module, which assigns pseudo-label confidence to each node based on the local structure of the graph, utilizing the node features and the graph's degree distribution. The module is then integrated into various graph neural networks and has demonstrated impressive results on limited-label datasets, outperforming existing baseline methods with improved robustness. The proposed GNN model has also achieved state-of-the-art performance on limited-label datasets and showcases its superiority over traditional GNN models through a rigorous comparison of efficacy. In video processing tasks, precise identification of recognizable objects at a low computational cost enables real-time video analysis on devices.  To accomplish this, we develop an efficient model called PatchNet for accurate and real-time object detection in videos.  By dividing each frame into multiple localized areas or 'patches,' we train the network to extract distinguishable features from these patches at a reduced size, thus alleviating the burden on computational resources.  Unlike traditional methods that train on entire images, PatchNet offers a patch-based training approach that enhances generalization and accelerates inference.  Through extensive experimentation on various datasets, we validate the robustness and efficiency of our model, achieving impressive performance at a remarkably low computational cost that outdoes existing methods while requiring minimal memory.  Notably, our model achieves a 15.0 NMS score on Ren30k and a 28.7 mAP on Kinetics-600 with an inference time under 10 milliseconds.  We envision PatchNet as a pioneering technique for real-time video analysis on mobile devices, paving the way for innovative mobile AI services. We examine the one-dimensional discrete-time asymmetric exclusion process with periodic boundaries, using parallel updating rules. For the exclusion process with a variety of starting conditions, we obtain a formula for a multi-time distribution. This involves complex mathematical calculations based on integrals of determinant functions. Under specific assumptions about the initial conditions, we are able to determine how this distribution evolves over large time and distances in the system, particularly in situations where geometry impacts the system's behavior. These assumptions are verified for certain basic starting conditions. As a consequence, we are able to determine the probability distribution of the exclusion process on the entire integer lattice by considering large enough systems, effectively removing boundary effects. Furthermore, we calculate the probability distribution of the exclusion process on the lattice at large times for a specific starting condition. Notably, we find that certain properties of this distribution are similar to the probability distribution of a Markov process in a system with a defect wavefront. Based on this calculation, we are able to determine the probability distribution of the exclusion process on the lattice at large times for a different starting condition, which confirms earlier predictions based on scaling analysis. These calculations are particularly complex and have not been seen in similar studies of the exclusion process. Finally, we determine how the exclusion process behaves in certain large systems and discover that its properties are similar to those of a system with a defect wavefront in a different phase of the exclusion process. To facilitate our complex mathematical integrations, we create a computer program to calculate the probability distribution of the exclusion process at large times and distances, which is available online along with a summary of the code's functionality. Furthermore, we examine the exclusion process on smaller systems and discover that its behavior is often unpredictable and varies greatly depending on the system's details. Based on these findings, we suggest that certain properties of the exclusion process, such as its ability to determine its own boundaries, are inherently linked to the exclusion process itself rather than being a general property of systems with a defect wavefront. Ultimately, we conclude that studying the exclusion process on large systems with periodic boundaries is particularly effective for understanding the exclusion process and can reveal valuable insights about the system. As a byproduct of our studies, we are able to determine the probability distribution of the exclusion process on large systems with different starting conditions and confirm similar predictions based on scaling analysis. Laparoscopic surgery has limitations due to a narrow field of view. Smoke produced by laser ablation in such operations obstructs the surgeon's visibility, highlighting the need for smoke removal to ensure a clear view. To apply smoke removal techniques effectively, it's essential to accurately distinguish between smoke and non-smoke images, which poses a challenge as current methods are incomplete. To overcome this issue, we have developed an image enhancement technique that extracts crucial information from RGB images to differentiate between smoke and non-smoke content. Leveraging a weighted least squares optimization framework, we employ statistical features derived from bivariate histograms and specific image characteristics, which are then used to train a classifier for binary classification of smoke or non-smoke content. We have tested our approach on the Cholec80 dataset and achieved notable results, demonstrating a 4% improvement in accuracy and F1-score over standard RGB image performance, as well as enhanced performance compared to existing methods. Notably, our technique offers a 3.5 times increase in F1-score over Cholec80 without the use of additional data. We have made our source code available on GitHub at the address provided. Experimental outcomes suggest that this method can effectively differentiate between smoke and non-smoke content in surgical scenes, paving the way for successful smoke removal applications. Given its versatility, this technique can be applied to various image-based medical tasks beyond smoke removal. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a frequency-proof entanglement diagram. Additionally, we explored the balance of gate accuracy and duration by implementing a method that adjusts the duration based on a predefined criterion. This method can serve as a general framework for developing robust gates capable of withstanding sudden frequency changes. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach for a two-qubit gate with a Jonson-Sorensen ratio of 64, achieving a high degree of accuracy within a 200 kHz frequency margin. Moreover, we showed that a specific setup can execute nearly fault-tolerant single-qubit operations over a similar frequency range. Our work paves the way for frequency-independent quantum gates with long-lasting coherence, which can be crucial for the development of practical quantum computers utilizing trapped ions. Moreover, this approach may also be adaptable to other types of quantum systems. Early stages of this research were carried out in collaboration with Joel Greene and Benjamin Clary. Benjamin Clary made significant contributions to the project, including the development of an advanced tool for visualizing 3D trajectories, as well as the creation of an efficient algorithm for balancing gate precision and duration. Existing quantum processors are prone to errors and have limited lifespan due to
imperfect gate operations. To work effectively with these processors, compilers
must optimize programs to run within the device's coherence time, translating them
into the most efficient version possible to extract maximum value from the hardware.
We have developed new, deterministic methods to schedule short-term programs within
a specific time frame, ensuring they complete just once and in the optimal sequence.
We utilized a novel short-term scheduling approach, built upon the concept of conflict
free graphs, to successfully demonstrate the feasibility of our determinant time scheduling
method. We further expanded upon this idea, creating the first efficient deterministic
algorithm for conflict-free scheduling, which we then integrated with an optimized compiler
toolkit to demonstrate a substantial 4.4 times performance boost for programs compiled
using our approach, compared to a random compilation method, across a variety of quantum processors. 
The determinant time scheduling method we developed is highly versatile and can be applied
to various types of quantum processors, beyond the ones we initially tested, as long as they
employ a reiable instruction completion mechanism. We have made the source code for our
compiler toolchain available.

We have developed a message-passing algorithm designed to accurately determine the location and track of mobile objects within areas with multiple signal paths that may experience blocked or obstructed visibility. The proposed adaptive probabilistic algorithm estimates a mobile device's position by leveraging data from multiple anchors, taking into account the timing and amplitude variations in signal components and associated uncertainties. Utilizing an adaptable noise model, the algorithm enables accurate estimation of the agent's position, even without precise knowledge of the surrounding environment. The algorithm dynamically adjusts its operation in real-time according to changes in signal strength and the likelihood of direct line-of-sight visibility with each anchor. Numerical testing demonstrates that the algorithm remains effective in areas with intense signal interference and temporary obstructions. The results show that the algorithm outperforms existing location estimation methods, yielding positions that are significantly closer to the true location. In interior point methods (IPMs), where an iterative method is employed to solve a linear equation system, speeding up convergence often involves developing optimal preconditioners for the linear solver. However, standard termination criteria for the solver frequently cause excessive 'oversolving' by insisting on sufficient residual reductions. This paper presents an alternative approach to interior point methods that utilizes an inner termination criterion not dependent on the residual, as well as indicators for premature inner iteration cessation informed by IPM demands. It also modifies this criterion to accommodate Conjugate Gradient and Minimum Residual algorithms, and demonstrates substantial performance enhancements in computational experiments for quadratic optimization problems, which translates to considerable time savings in IPM solution. This improvement has the potential to greatly accelerate solving linear systems in IPMs and other numerical techniques. This work is subject to a patent application. The principle underlying the renormalization group bears a strong analogy to gradient flow, especially in scalar field theory where the RG and gradient flows share a direct connection through the ERG formalism. To generalize this connection in Yang--Mills theory while maintaining gauge invariance, we propose an ERG equation based on a similarity principle and further extend it to lattice gauge theory from the continuum theory context. Using an example with a non-interacting gauge theory, we demonstrate that the proposed ERG can effectively restore the transversality of the vertex function. Additionally, we outline strategies for applying the ERG in more complex situations. As an initial application of the ERG, we investigate how gradient flows and the RG flows diverge as the flow parameter increases, within an SU(Nc) lattice gauge theory context. Our findings indicate that the RG and gradient flows indeed converge for large gradient flow parameters and suggest an ERG approach as a means to access the conformal window of Yang--Mills theory. This research paves the way for an extensive study of the Yang--Mills theory via an ERG approach. Future projects will focus on an in-depth analysis of the ERG and related techniques as well as their interplay with other methods such as lattice simulations and continuum Yang--Mills theory. As an alternative to these methods, the ERG offers a means to access the renormalization group properties of the gauge theory without relying on an expansion in the coupling constant. This contrasts with the functional renormalization group approach developed by W. Kurtz et al., which we will also seek to leverage and contribute to as the approach bears significant overlap with the proposal presented here. Furthermore, we will investigate how the ERG can be generalized beyond Yang--Mills theory to more complex theories such as supersymmetric Yang--Mills, QCD with heavy quarks, and two-dimensional lattice gauge theory, thereby significantly expanding the scope of the proposal. Lastly, we will outline an extensive plan for simulations that can be conducted using the ERG, which will enable precise determinations of many key physical quantities such as the nature of spectroscopic states in the mass spectrum as well as the behavior of gauge theories in the conformal window. This research will significantly contribute to our understanding of the fundamental properties of Yang--Mills theory and QCD. Current business process monitoring methods mainly concentrate on one process model. However, in some scenarios, it is necessary to analyze multiple process definitions at the same time. These specifications can be operational, rule-based, or a combination of both. For example, in the medical field, a treatment guideline might not cover all co-factors a patient can have and therefore supplementary restrictions might need to be considered. Sometimes, these constraints may conflict with existing guidelines, requiring either the guidelines or the constraints to be violated. To address this issue, we suggest a solution to monitor hybrid process definitions expressed through a combination of (data-aware) Petri nets and temporal logic rules. During the process execution, the monitoring system can handle conflicting specifications by possibly violating some of them, and can even provide recommendations for the next course of action based on a violation cost model that minimizes the total cost of violations. To determine whether an arbitrary hybrid process meets a specified hybrid process definition, we first demonstrate that the monitoring problem can be redefined as a decomposed problem involving two separate monitoring tasks, one for each type of specification, and then finally prove its decidability in the context of (data-aware) Petri nets. A prototype has been implemented to verify the proposed decomposition method's effectiveness. Finally, the concept of checking hybrid process definitions is tested using a simple case study from the medical field.

Quipper, a domain-specific language, enables the description of quantum circuits by embedding in Haskell, resulting in a highly functional and practical language. Yet, its embedded nature in Haskell hinders the development of a formal semantics and restricts the type system. The absence of linear types in Haskell makes it simple to write quantum state-cloning violating code. The Proto-Quipper family addresses this issue through research languages designed to ensure the type-safety of quantum circuit fragments. Specifically, this paper examines Proto-Quipper-M, which employs a categorical quantum circuit model and incorporates linear types for compile-time cloning property verification. The study then develops a small-step operational semantics by transforming its corresponding big-step model and proves subject reduction using coinduction. The resulting paper paves the way for a formally defined and type-safe quantum programming language. The associated Haskell code is available at https://github.com/tweberj/proto-quipper-m. Assembling a complete genome from short, overlapping DNA sequences is a critical task in genomics. With the rise of long-read sequencing technology by PacBio and Illumina, along with the increasing size and quality of resulting reads, the core genome assembly problem has evolved. Since most sequences lack overlapping reads, correcting errors becomes particularly challenging, leading to the prevalence of misassembled genomes. Our research presents a novel, high-performance genome assembly framework, guided by an efficient graph construction approach, an improved error detection system, and an optimized post-processing strategy. Evaluations using 21 real-world genomes demonstrate that our system surpasses existing approaches in accuracy, surpassing the current state-of-the-art by 15% to 50% in Canu terms, while also showing superior speed and scalability on up to 128 CPU cores with up to 10 TB of available memory. Furthermore, our framework successfully assembles the largest genomes to date, including those of Encephalitozoon biospurus, Encephalitozoon cuniculi, and Trichomonas vaginalis. Our system is now available on the web at https://cabigy.ucr.edu/cabigy/Software/cabigy.html. A modified logistic equation, previously known as Hutchinson's or Wright's equation, originally aimed to model oscillating ecological phenomena. However, it received criticism from modelers for the lack of a direct biological explanation. Our study proposes an improved logistic equation with a clearer biological foundation based on cell population dynamics, incorporating discrete and distributed delay terms. The model's global dynamics are fully analyzed and proven to converge to a unique positive equilibrium in an octant, characterized by stability through linearization and spectral analysis, and ultimately proven using a Lyapunov function method. The model's two key non-oscillatory solutions are examined, one corresponding to the extinction of the population and the other representing sustainable growth. The model is also found to exhibit oscillatory behavior under specific conditions, specifically when the delay term meets a certain criterion, ultimately converging to a stable limit cycle. The study validates the model's validity through numerical simulations, aligning with the original equation's behavior. A key distinction lies in the model's capacity to be classified as a non-oscillatory solution, leading to permanent extinction or sustainable growth, depending on initial conditions and delays. The model offers an alternative to the original equation, providing a more accurate and interpretable mathematical framework for oscillatory phenomena in ecological dynamics. The study is partially based on a previous research paper with the same key findings, differing mainly in the presentation and organization of the results. The study is part of a broader project, aiming to investigate and explain oscillatory behavior in ecological dynamics, exploring the fundamental nature of these phenomena, and the importance of delays in triggering oscillations, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of ecological complexity and the diversity of oscillatory patterns in the model. Achieving maximum engine performance involves leveraging quantum effects. In this investigation, two strategies for creating the most efficient engines are considered, specifically (1) using hybrid quantum systems capable of performing multiple beneficial tasks, and (2) minimizing random fluctuations in these tasks. In classical devices, eliminating random fluctuations requires high entropy generation as dictated by thermodynamic uncertainty principles. Here, these principles are extended to hybrid thermal machines with multiple terminals. In quantum conductors, these limitations are bypassed, and we demonstrate this for a setup comprising a double quantum dot and normal metals in contact, powered by an entangled Cooper pair generator. Furthermore, we show that hybrid quantum batteries can function as cooling devices and that this can be accomplished by using a series battery-recharger configuration to reach maximum performance. In contrast, classical batteries can only be recharged if they have a thermal component. Finally, we examine the performance of quantum random number generators in thermal machines and find that these generators can improve the efficiency of these devices. In particular, we find that hybrid quantum generators with two outputs can be used to create machines with maximum cooling capabilities that surpass any classical device. These findings provide a unified understanding of the fundamental physical limitations of thermal machines and suggest novel approaches for creating more efficient devices. In particular, we find that using half-metalized normal materials in contact with quantum dots or Josephson junctions can be an effective way to implement these more efficient devices. These materials are commonly used in everyday computer chips and are currently widely available. In contrast, devices based on quantum coherence cannot be used to generate random numbers. Instead, they require an external source of noise, such as thermal fluctuations, to function at their best. In fact, we show that the best random numbers can be generated by devices with the lowest possible cooling efficiency, such as those based on micromechanical tunnelling. In particular, we find that these devices can produce the best random numbers with an efficiency that approaches the maximum possible, even when the devices are very small, as predicted by the fundamental principles of thermodynamics. In fact, we show that the fundamental limits of thermal machines and random number generators are closely related and can be understood through a common understanding of these devices. Researchers have introduced an innovative technique for accurately measuring the masses of extremely short-lived, unusual atomic isotopes over a wide range of frequencies. This method utilizes the principle of isochronous mass spectrometry, combining real-time ion velocity and trajectory analysis at the Lanzhou CSRe particle storage facility. Dubbed Bρ-defined isochronous mass spectrometry, or Bρ-IMS, this technique enhances precision and sensitivity, paving the way for new mass measurements. Specifically, in a single test setting, precise mass readings were obtained for $^{46}$Cr, $^{50}$Fe, and $^{54}$Ni with exceptionally low margins of error. This breakthrough technique will serve as a crucial tool for evaluating the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa quark interaction matrix and for further refining the measurements of highly rare, shortest-lived atomic isotopes. Furthermore, this new approach may expand storage ring-based isochronous mass spectrometry into a higher frequency range. Research is currently underway to increase the technical capabilities of the Bρ-IMS method, which shows great promise for future explorations in this field. This tutorial notebook exemplifies a novel technique for generating Boltzmann distributions of lattice field theories through normalizing flows, a subset of machine learning models. The underlying concepts presented in papers arXiv:1904.12072, arXiv:2002.02428, and arXiv:2003.06413 are summarized, accompanied by a detailed, concrete implementation of this approach. The tutorial showcases its application in a lattice scalar field theory and U(1) gauge theory contexts, which particularly incorporates gauge symmetries into its flow-based method for the latter. The tutorial's interactive format is best experienced with the associated Jupyter notebook, which we highly recommend utilizing. The code used in this tutorial is highly adaptable and can be easily modified to accommodate a wide array of theories. The underlying concepts and generic framework make this tutorial suitable for a broad theoretical physics audience. The benefits of using this approach, in terms of the resources required to achieve a desirable level of precision, are compared to traditional Monte Carlo methods. The technical details of implementing this method are presented in the accompanying paper, titled "Machine learning Boltzmann distributions in lattice field theories". CITE arXiv:2003.06413. The associated code can be found at https://git.lip.pt/jpbaldan/flowbased_lattice_field_theory/-/tree/flowbased_tutorial. The repository includes additional essential resources, which are listed in the appendix. The presentation covers an introduction to normalizing flows, a summary of the conceptual framework, the gauge theory extension, the rationale behind choosing specific machine learning models, the remediation of ultraviolet divergences, the integration of this method with existing Monte Carlo methods, and the future prospects for this approach, along with an overview of the tutorial's structure. The technical details presented in the presentation are essential for understanding the methodology's underlying architecture. The presentation also hosts a JupyterHub interactive session, accessible at https://git.lip.pt/jpbaldan/flowbased_lattice_field_theory/-/tree/flowbased_tutorial. The future updates to this tutorial are intended to incorporate new developments in this emerging methodology. CITE arXiv:1904.12072, arXiv:2002.02428, arXiv:2003.06413. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at 5.02 TeV, utilizing 42.7 microbarns of integrated luminosity. Top quark events were identified in both the single-top and top-pair categories using 2015-2018 data, totaling 279 million minipublications. Signals above the 3-sigma threshold were detected for the first time in the single-top and top-pair decay modes, and the observed and predicted cross-sections were quantified as 45 nanobarns and 63 nanobarns, respectively. Additionally, top quark event measurements were made in high-pT systems, and the top quark pair cross-section was found to exhibit dependence on charged particle multiplicity. The observed and predicted cross-sections were found to agree within statistical uncertainties for events with high multiplicity, but showed a significant 4-sigma discrepancy for events with low multiplicity. The results were corrected for acceptance and sensitivity losses due to jet identification biases. The cross-section was found to change by 10% when the fastest jet's pseudorapidity was shifted from -3 to 3, and exhibited a 20% variation in relation to charged particle multiplicity in top quark events. The ongoing LoTSS survey is conducting a thorough observation of the Northern sky to better understand how the large-scale structure of the Universe changes and develops. Although only 1% of the sky is covered in the LoTSS DR1 data release, analysis shows fluctuations that need to be clarified. In this research, we simulate future LoTAR data to examine the auto and cross-power spectra of galaxy density, galaxy size, and redshift using the CAMBE galaxy clustering model. Our LoTAR simulation is based on the predicted large-scale structure patterns from the KiDS-1000 data. Our research reveals that future LoTAR data will be capable of accurately determining the galaxy-halo connection, reducing uncertainty in redshift and angular size measurements by a factor of two compared to the KiDS-1000 data, and allowing a more detailed analysis of galaxy and galaxy cluster distributions across vast cosmic areas. Our simulations also indicate that future LoTAR data will be sensitive to patterns of Baryonic Acoustic Oscillation at a radius of around 140 million light-years, although this will depend on the specific characteristics of the LoTAR telescope and data processing methods used. Our research further finds that future LoTAR data will be capable of detecting around 600,000 confirmed galaxy cluster candidates with masses in the range of 10^43 to 10^47 erg/s, and an additional 300,000 uncertain candidate clusters. Our simulations also predict the potential to identify around 60,000 candidate galaxy groups with masses in the range of 10^42 to 10^43.5 erg/s using the concentration function and richness as the primary detection method for these galaxy clusters and groups. In conclusion, our research indicates that future LoTAR data will provide significant insights into the nature of galaxy and cluster distributions in the large-scale structure of the Universe. Our future plans include participating in the data release and analysis process of the LoTAR survey, and contributing our expertise to the ongoing research of the LoTAR community. In the mean time, our research presents the first prediction of the large-scale structure patterns in the sky and fibre assignments of the LoTAR survey, and makes our simulation code and data release available to the public through the use of Github. Our research further outlines the strategy for participating in the future data release and analysis of the LoTAR survey, and makes our simulation code and data release available to the public through the use of Github at the following address: https://github.com/CCarrota/LoTAR

The High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDR Lasso) model offers a computationally efficient solution to handle complex data analysis. Introduced as a parameter-free and robust method, HDR Lasso has been shown to outperform other approaches in various applications. Mathematically, HDR Lasso is represented by an optimization problem consisting of two terms: a Lasso term and a generalized loss function, while incorporating penalties for coefficients and a covariance matrix. Notably, the Lasso term is broken down into additive parts to accommodate complex structures such as low-rank matrices, tensors, and other features. By employing the Charlier-Mehler series, an explicit reformulation of the HDR Lasso problem is achieved, enabling the coordination of model parameters through the Karhunen-Loève expansion. Employing this series, HDR Lasso is successfully extended to include multi-way data, sparse structures, and prior information on coefficients and the covariance matrix. Numerical experiments, conducted using both simulated and real data sets, demonstrate the efficacy of the HDR Lasso approach in extracting underlying structures from complex data. As a result, HDR Lasso has promising applications in numerous fields such as medicine, biology, and finance. Due to its computational efficiency, HDR Lasso can easily handle large data sets, even those involving imaging or signal processing applications. Thus, HDR Lasso offers a versatile and effective technique for various data analysis applications. As a result, the paper contributes several innovative extensions to the HDR Lasso model while providing a resource that is accessible to a broad audience. In particular, the paper targets statisticians, data analysts, and researchers who focus on advanced statistical methods for signal and image processing applications. Identifying whether an optimal solution is localized or universal is particularly challenging in complex optimization problems. This work addresses that challenge by demonstrating the existence of a single, optimal, and universal method for achieving the lowest possible rate of entropy production in fast and sluggish driving processes. This outcome is verified by proving the functional convexity of the entropy production rate in relation to a key controlling parameter, which further confirms its monotonous progression in such scenarios. This contrasts with our previous research findings where the rate of entropy production was not consistently positive throughout all stages. Our analysis demonstrates that an analytical technique previously employed is, in fact, effective in determining the optimal solution, which is subsequently verified by comparing it with results obtained through genetic programming's global optimization method. Ultimately, the study presents a valuable tool for solving complex optimization problems by indicating that functions exhibiting a single, sharp minimum, known as inflection points, can be solved with the aid of an analytical method, while functions with multiple, more gradual minima may require alternative, more robust methods for accurate solution determination. This study introduces an error control strategy for a Boussinesq model with adaptive coefficients, where temperature-dependent properties of heat transfer and fluid viscosity are taken into account. The coupled system of the Navier-Stokes and heat equations is solved in a unified manner. The primary goal is to utilize the dual-weighted residual method for estimating the errors of various goal functions with the help of an adjoint problem. To localize the errors, we utilize a partition-of-unity method within a weak formulation framework that is well-suited for solving coupled problems. This approach enables the implementation of adaptive algorithms that are validated by a range of numerical experiments, including one benchmark problem and two further investigations inspired by laser material processing. The efficiency and robustness of the developed framework are confirmed by the observed reductions in errors and effectivity indices. The study shows that the partition-of-unity method is capable of efficiently solving complex problems involving strong and weak discontinuities, even when coupled phenomena are involved. The introduced framework is versatile and can be easily adapted to a wide range of other problems in fluid flow and heat transfer. Furthermore, the developed error control technique provides reliable indications that further refinements of the model could be unnecessary. The numerical computations were carried out using free open-source software that is included in the methodology section. Additional information about the problem can be found in Ph.D. thesis [1]. Kinderlehrer in [2] investigated similar problems, as did Benner et al. in [3]. Relevant work by Caputo et al. can be found in [4,5], while an overview of the method's applications is provided in the introductory parts of the thesis. The presented work was influenced by the research conducted by Crouzeix in [6] and Ravi Artola in [7]. Relevant studies on laser material processing can be found in [8-11]. The nonlinear stability of similar problems was investigated in [12], while relevant work on the same topic can be found in [13-15]. Specifically, the 'd-Set Matching' problem for integers 'd', involve identifying a set with 'k' elements that matches 'b' number of edges in a given 'b-d-vertex graph. Researchers have shown that for 'd being 2' and certain values of 'k', there exist kernelization algorithms with size limitations. Nonetheless, no such algorithms were found with size limitations below the 'k^2' threshold. In this study, it is proven that no such algorithms exist below the 'k^(1+o(1))' threshold as 'k' approaches infinity. Furthermore, it is shown that linear constraint satisfaction problems along with several combinatorial optimization problems follow a similar pattern. This study explores how opinions are shaped and social connections evolve in a complex system, governed by a delicate balance between friendly and hostile relationships. We have developed a model that captures how individuals with limited confidence in their judgments form opinions based on their personal relationships. We considered scenarios with one and two distinct aspects of opinions, and found that our framework consistently leads to the separation of agents into two distinct groups, characterized by distinct opinion sets. Depending on the level of trust, these groups either develop uniform views or multiple distinct perspectives within each group emerge. In the case of opinions based on a single dimension, the two groups have opposing views, forming a 'left' and 'right' category. In scenarios with multiple dimensions, the two groups are separated by a dividing line in opinion space. We have demonstrated that our results can partially explain a phenomenon previously observed by other researchers. Our work has implications for understanding how political ideologies become fragmented and how new parties might emerge. Similarly, in a society with diverse views, our model can partially explain how distinct cultural groups might arise and how internal differences within these groups might develop. In addition, our model has implications for understanding how new religions might emerge and how they might lead to the separation of faithful into distinct groups. Different genes exhibiting similar activation patterns may show distinct mRNA expression levels at different time points due to variations in transcription duration, RNA breakdown speed, and processing rates. The impact of RNA splicing on delaying mRNA production cannot be ignored. We developed a model combining transcription dynamics and RNA accumulation to estimate the parameters of transcriptional activity, RNA production lag, and RNA breakdown rates. The model uses sequencing data from start and end sites of mRNA molecules and is applicable to single-cell and population studies. The approach enables the determination of active gene numbers, transcription rate, RNA production delay, and breakdown rates all along the RNA sequence without requiring prior knowledge of transcription factors. The method has been validated with simulated data and applied to actual cell cycle CTLC data, showing its effectiveness in inferring RNA production delay, detecting transcriptional activity shifts, and breaking down complex systems into distinct cellular events. Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked a first in Ni isotopes. This unique configuration, often seen in even-even nuclei, was found to persist in 64Ni, and the presence of a collective 2+ state so close to a high-energy prolate state, provided strong evidence for a distinct excitated 0+ state, often indicative of superdeformations. An older suggestion by Bars and Yankielowicz to match the theory's 't Hooft anomalies with those of free fermions is revisited, resulting in novel constraints for the large N limit. We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure. We freely provide our source code and the dataset employed in our study. Our introduction includes a newly created probabilistic logic network type, the amnesia network, which according to our knowledge, has not been described before and is particularly useful for modelling long-term forgetting phenomena. Our analysis reveals that FABE becomes feasible only when the problem size exceeds the memory capacity, due to an analysis of various parameters, as detailed in our supplementary materials. The visual appearance and auditory qualities of an object provide dual insights into its material properties.  In everyday situations, information from vision and hearing arrive simultaneously, but the integration of asynchronous cues is essential, as seen when we locate an object dropped on the ground after hearing its fall.  In this paper, a controlled environment for studying 3D object localization in real-time is established, involving an embodied robotic agent, a camera, and a microphone that identify a dropped object in a room.  The robot achieves this by synthesizing audio and visual cues along with the principles of physical mechanics.  A dataset called Fallen Objects has been developed for studying this complex challenge.  The dataset is based on the ThreeDWorld platform and includes over 8000 simulations of various object types in 64 settings.  As an initial step toward resolving this problem, different agent architectures based on imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and modular planning are designed and evaluated to provide an in-depth analysis of this new task.  The research sets a baseline for 3D object localization and provides an evaluation framework for other approaches, along with the implementation details and an expanded version of this paper available online. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a framework for understanding shear thickening through the lens of nonlinear elasticity and elasticity instability. To support this idea, they investigated the behavior of sheared, particle-like units in a dense mixture, observing that near the shear thickening point, the nature of interactions within these units shifts from hard to soft. This study investigates the fluctuating electricity consumption in Ghana's period of power shortages by applying Markov switching models, namely MS-AR and AR. The data, comprising hourly electricity usage from January 1, 2014 to December 31, 2014 provided by the Ghana Grid company, helped determine the best-fitting model as MS(2)-AR(4) based on different evaluation criteria. The parameters of this model were then estimated using an expectation-maximization algorithm, indicating that the likelihood of experiencing low electricity consumption is 87%, with the low consumption period expected to last around 7.8 hours a day. The model outperformed traditional AR models by effectively modeling peak and varied consumption patterns and identifying distinct regime changes during the power crisis periods. The results of this study can aid power sector stakeholders in planning, while the model itself can be used for other time series analysis tasks. Automatically creating programs from detailed specifications is a task called program synthesis. A novel framework for generating code based on flow charts is presented, where a deep neural network called GRCNN is trained to accurately interpret these visual specifications by identifying their graphical structures. By being trained end-to-end, GRCNN is capable of simultaneously predicting node and edge details in a flow chart. The framework's results reveal high levels of accuracy in synthesizing programs at a 66.4% rate and also demonstrate robust node and edge recognition at rates of 94.1% and 67.9%, respectively. Furthermore, program synthesis occurs in approximately 60 milliseconds. The framework's efficacy is confirmed by comparing it favorably to a recent approach in the field. We propose several innovative strategies to enhance program synthesis, including utilizing multiple visual views and incorporating attention mechanisms during node prediction. The framework's source code and program synthesis datasets are made publicly available. The research demonstrates significant advancements in program synthesis via deep learning methods, especially for specifications with controlled structures and clear mapping relationships between visual and textual forms. The results can be found at the link: https://ymy-sec.github.io/GRCNN/. Radiation oncologists' goal is to target tumors accurately while shielding surrounding vital organs, specifically the stomach and intestines, from x-ray beams. The incorporation of MR-Linac systems allows real-time tumor positioning, enabling precise radiation dosage adjustments based on shifting cell populations. The manual process of identifying these organs and calibrating X-ray beams can be lengthy, extending treatment times up to one hour a day, making automated techniques with deep learning essential. A recent paper explores the use of deep learning-based automation to streamline this complex task and provide faster access to treatment for a greater number of patients. The research specifically evaluated whether automated imaging and calibration tools can provide comparable results to those obtained by experienced medical professionals. A comprehensive set of challenges, known as the MR-Linac Automation Challenge, was developed with data from 382 patients and 13,382 images to test the robustness and accuracy of these automated techniques. Notably, the selected challenge focused on imaging the stomach rather than other organs, as it was deemed critical for radiation therapy planning. The participants were tasked with estimating stomach volume and calculating corresponding calibration scales in axial, sagittal, and coronal planes. Following the analysis of submitted solutions, it was concluded that automated deep learning approaches can efficiently and effectively replace manual organ identification and calibration methods, resulting in reduced treatment times. The top-performing model achieved a correlation coefficient of 0.963 or higher with medical professionals when determining the stomach's positional scale, meeting the challenge's accuracy requirements. Moreover, it was observed that automated techniques can provide accurate calibrations significantly faster than manual procedures. The top-performing model required only 10 seconds to process an image, a considerable improvement over the 30 minutes it took medical professionals to complete the same task. The success of automated deep learning methods in organ identification and calibration presents promising implications for the widespread adoption of MR-Linac systems in radiation oncology, enabling a greater number of patients to receive rapid and precise radiation therapy. The development of fast and accurate automated techniques has crucial consequences, primarily reducing treatment duration and increasing treatment capacity, thereby enhancing the lives of cancer patients. The MR-Linac Automation Challenge marked a significant milestone in this endeavor by successfully evaluating the robustness of automated deep learning approaches and showcasing their superiority over manual procedures in organ identification and calibration. As cancer treatment continues to evolve, it is essential to investigate the effectiveness of these automated techniques in real-world clinical settings through controlled studies and rigorous analyses, as previously established in the case of image-guided radiation therapy. Compositional data analysis is a technique that deals with complex datasets, which consist of several interdependent components summing to a constant value. Common constant values are 1 and 100%. This data structure is commonly found in disciplines such as biochemistry, geochemistry, and the social sciences. Researchers often examine compositional data in "omics" studies with extremely large dimensions. The method involves calculating logratios – the logarithmic expressions of component proportions. The matrix representation, calculation, and interpretation of these logratios present distinct challenges. This article presents a comprehensive review of a unified framework for a subset of these challenges. Specifically, we'll examine the generalized singular value decomposition of a matrix and its applications to compositional data analysis. The article offers an overview of the theoretical framework, provides step-by-step instructions for matrix calculation, and presents case studies demonstrating its practical applications. These applications cover topics such as data normalization, correlation measures, differential expression analysis, and the identification of biomarkers in "omics" studies with extremely large dimensions. The article offers a comprehensive introduction to these topics, providing readers with a stable software environment for compositional data analysis. The article showcases numerous examples, which demonstrate the practical applications of these algorithms in compositional data analysis. The article also addresses potential future developments and research areas within the field. A theoretical model I propose consists of a single fermion with a high mass, where the lowest energy state of this fermion can be thought of as a boson due to a particular type of interaction it has. This type of interaction can lead to various states at low fermion density, including a Bose-Einstein condensate, superfluid phases, and magnetic phases. The presence of an external influence, such as an electromagnetic field, can cause the phase of the dark matter to change. The property of being immobile doesn't affect the type of electromagnetic fields the fermion can take on, resulting in a contrasting behavior compared to usual dark matter scenarios. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can efficiently solve complex problems that demand memory, error correction, and selection capabilities, outperforming other architectures in constraint satisfaction tasks like Sudoku. Nevertheless, traditional RNNs receive information from all memory locations equally, resulting in increased training time, excessive data requirements, and poor generalization capabilities in large-memory settings. To address these issues, we developed locality-masked RNNs (LM-RNNs), a class of RNNs that only allow information exchange between adjacent memory locations. Experiments revealed that LM-RNNs can learn efficiently within a relatively short training period, and they emerge with superior performance after being trained on substantially smaller dataset subsets. As a result, LM-RNNs can be trained and applied up to 12 times faster than their conventional counterparts. Our research also shows that two distinct formulations of adjacency-masking yield comparable outcomes and lead to notable performance improvements in various memory-intensive tasks. By leveraging an accelerated training pipeline and a compact model, we achieved state-of-the-art results on numerous dataset subsets and matched the original model's performance on larger datasets. Our work is accompanied by an open-source implementation accessible at https://github.com/ai4r/LMRNN. Our research highlights the potential of locality-masked RNNs as a versatile AI tool, offering unique advantages in terms of training efficiency, data requirements, and performance. Our innovation may be applied in various domains where RNNs are widely used, including natural language processing, where they are instrumental in modeling dependencies, generating text, and performing language translation. We categorize nilpotent algebras by dimension with a focus on their commutative, commutative nilpotent and anticommutative properties. Our findings reveal the irreducibility of corresponding geometric spaces, allowing us to accurately calculate their dimensions and establish general families of algebras associated with each space. Additionally, we address the commutativity properties within these families. Furthermore, we identify relationships between these nilpotent algebras and solvable Lie algebras in a comprehensive manner. Our study also provides a thorough analysis of anticommutative nilpotent algebras, including a full classification by dimension. Lastly, we explore links between commutative and anticommutative properties in nilpotent algebras. These results contribute to an expanded understanding of the classification of these algebras. A key aspect of our work involves introducing novel elements, such as flag varieties for commutative algebras and nilpotent Lie algebras, as well as generalizing the concept of Borel subalgebras to nilpotent Lie algebras. These discoveries may be found intriguing by mathematicians working in related fields. Our proofs are rigorous and heavily utilize the theory of coherent sheaves over affine spaces, along with the concept of nilpotent algebras as developed by Shestakov-Zelmanov School. A thorough explanation of these theories is provided for the sake of mathematical integrity. Additionally, we introduce an axiomatic description of nilpotent algebras which facilitates their classification, thereby making the axiomatic description a valuable resource for mathematicians working with these specific types of algebras. Our study also yields correlations between this description and the cohomology of Lie algebras. These results are particularly relevant to solvable Lie algebras. A comprehensive overview of the significance and structure of this work is presented in the introductory sections alongside historical context and related mathematical conjectures. A notable mention among these is the nilpotent Galois theorem for anticommutative algebras. Our work is dedicated to the memory of two distinguished mathematicians, Valentin Lomonosov and Vladimir Dolgopolov. $1/c^2$, considering a generic spacetime foliation defined by $c$, the speed
of light. We achieve this through the application of a suitable 'pre-non-
relativistic' geometrical parametrization, thereby facilitating an
analytical $1/c^2$ expansion of general relativity. Ultimately, this method
permits an in-depth examination of the Einstein-Hilbert action expansion up to
its next-to-next-to-leading order. Additionally, we reassess the physical
significance of quantum effects within the frameworks of perturbative quantum
gravity and effective models of modified gravity. Moreover, we outline the
potential utility of our method in studying black-hole dynamics and
semiclassical states. Further, we briefly investigate how the expansion can
be adapted to include spinor particles within the framework. Lastly, we discuss
the possibility of extending our method to address non-globally hyperbolic
spacetimes, thereby facilitating an exploration of compact objects and
cosmological phenomena through an 'expanded' effective-model approach. We
conclude by highlighting the potential future applications of our method to
investigate quantum effects in cosmological scenarios and compact objects. Due
to limitations imposed by the choice of parametrization, we do not delve into
the quantum origin of inertia but suggest an outlook on this pivotal issue.

This study presents an enhanced approach to 3D image features that incorporates invariance to discrete symmetry by considering inversions of spatial axes and image contrast.  The proposed descriptor includes a binary feature that distinguishes between the sign of the Laplacian operator's results, making it immune to image inversion and 3D transformations that reverse spatial coordinates, achieving SP-symmetry or SP-invariance. This generalization of symmetry applies to arbitrary scalar image fields and encompasses well-known CP-symmetry seen in charged elementary particles. Local feature orientation is represented as a set of independent states accounting for possible reflections, irrespective of image intensity inversion. Two key axis vectors are derived from observed image data, along with a third axial vector defined by the right-hand rule. Adding the sign component to the traditional geometry of local features (location, scale, orientation) generates descriptors that are robust to coordinate and intensity inversions. These enhanced feature properties are integrated into symmetric kernel-based point-wise registration, modeled using binary feature correspondence. Empirical results obtained from experiments using the CPD algorithm demonstrate the high precision and speed of the SIFT-CPD kernels in image registration, particularly for complex datasets such as human brains, CT scans, and MRI images, even when they are inverted or contrast-reversed. This approach provides a general framework for designing descriptors with SP-symmetry or SP-invariance that can be applied to various image modalities beyond 3D medical imaging. Its potential applications include image analysis, biomedical processing, and particle physics. In numerous machine learning models and tasks, the implementation of global pooling operations is often based on experience rather than a thorough theoretical understanding. To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been developed through the lens of optimal transport theory. We demonstrate that most current global pooling methods are essentially specialized solutions to an unbalanced optimal transport problem. By allowing the parameters of this problem to be learned, various global pooling methods are unified within a single framework. Consequently, a generalized global pooling layer for neural networks called UOT-Pooling (UOTP) has been proposed. To implement this UOTP layer, the classic Sinkhorn-scaling algorithm is employed. Furthermore, a new model architecture based on the Bregman ADMM algorithm is designed, which offers better numerical stability and improved ability to reproduce existing pooling layers. The proposed UOTP layers are then tested across several applications, including multi-instance learning, graph classification, and image classification, and are found to be capable of either mimicking conventional global pooling layers or developing novel, performance-enhancing pooling mechanisms. The proposed framework, model architecture, and source code are made available for public use at https://github.com/jindongxuming/UOTP. The primary objective of this research is to examine aspects of the validity of the active galactic nucleus unification theory. Our focus lies on AGN host galaxies which, according to the unified theory, should not exhibit systematic differences depending on AGN classification. We used the SDSS catalogue up to a redshift of 0.2, and the Galaxy Zoo Project catalogue which classifies galaxies into two broad Hubble types, and examined elliptical and spiral galaxy subcategories. Our analysis reveals distinct variations between the galaxies based on AGN classification, particularly in the context of spiral galaxies where Type 1 Seyfert nuclei are more common and larger spiral arms are associated with these nuclei. Our results contradict the unified theory and suggest alternative explanations such as for example, a connection between large spiral arms and an unstable stellar disk. We also found that spiral galaxies associated with Type 1 Seyfert nuclei are more similar to barred spiral galaxies than unbarred ones, and that they share characteristics with giant elliptical galaxies which, as reported in the literature, also host active nuclei. In contrast, non-active nuclei reside in galaxies that lack prominent bars or other structural features that could fuel nuclear activity. Our analysis also reveals distinct variations in elliptical galaxy characteristics depending on AGN classification, particularly in the context of galaxy size and shape, and that these variations are consistent with existing research. Our study's findings are inconsistent with the hypothesis that AGN bias could significantly influence these results, and that certain processes such as for example, host galaxy interactions, may influence nuclear activity. Our study's findings could imply that certain processes such as for example, host galaxy interactions, may influence nuclear activity rather than a single unified mechanism. Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset. Top-notch approaches
traditionally rely on image classification for pre-training, a method which can
be marred by uncontrollable biases. To investigate a more effective method, we
proposed that depth estimation using untagged videos might be a better choice
for pre-training. Although this method lacks any meaningful scene details, we
assert that calculating the three-dimensional geometry of scenes is closer to
the goal of semantic segmentation than assigning broad image classifications.
Lacking an analytical method for validating our hypothesis, we conducted an
experimental evaluation that demonstrated our pre-training scheme produced an
improvement of 5.7% mean intersection over union and 4.1% pixel accuracy in
comparison to classification-based pre-training. Notably, although we were able
to bypass annotation during pre-training, it is indispensable for assessing our
proposed scheme's effectiveness. To validate our findings, we employed the
popular KITTI (outdoor) and NYU-V2 (indoor) benchmarking datasets and also
detailed the benefits and shortcomings of our pre-training protocol in relation
to alternative methods like unsupervised, self-supervised, and semi-supervised
training approaches. Ultimately, we share our implementation to enable other
researchers to build upon our work. A Python-based repository is available at

The ability to provide detailed explanations for complex time-series data is
crucial in intelligence analysis and knowledge navigation, yet current methods
often result in difficult-to-understand interpretations that lack specific details.
In response, we present TCube, an innovative approach that uses a knowledge-
graph embedded in a neural network to create clear and precise time-series
narrations, incorporating essential context and parameters. By leveraging neural
networks, TCube enhances the accuracy and richness of narratives while also
improving their coherence and logical flow. Furthermore, TCube's modular
design facilitates ease of use and facilitates integration with existing systems. 
Evaluations demonstrate that TCube consistently outperforms existing methods, 
notably for intricate and difficult-to-narrate data sets. Although our primary 
focus has been on time-series data, TCube's design is versatile and could be 
applied to other narrative tasks with minimal modification.
