This study focuses on a class of strictly hyperbolic equations with coefficients experiencing mild blow-up. It demonstrates how these equations can be categorized into distinct spectral clusters based on a parameter $t$. This classification leads to the identification of several possible outcomes for the solutions, including rapid decay, a constant high-frequency behavior, and a determining function related to the equation's coefficients. Additionally, it shows that in the case of a single spectral cluster, the solutions exhibit a smooth (in time) $L^2$-decay. A notable distinction is drawn between equations with coefficients exhibiting moderate blow-up and those that are essentially hyperbolic throughout their domain. Finally, an essential role is identified in the blow-up of the equation's large-frequency end, leading to the conclusion that the equation can become degenerate due to the effects of its high-frequency components. To support these conclusions, a number of key methods are employed, including an investigation into the equation's spectral clusters and the behavior of its residual operators. Specifically, it is demonstrated that the latter can be broken down into a locally constant function and a decaying component, ultimately facilitating the proof of the identified outcomes. In particular, a crucial step involves establishing the connection between the equation's solutions and a family of non-autonomous elliptic equations, for which a number of well-known results can be applied. Additionally, the most commonly referenced reference regarding the $L^2$-decay of the solutions is listed as [64], which is readily accessible through the provided reference list. Lastly, the text is concluded by highlighting some intriguing questions and potential applications related to the equation under investigation. A few of these questions have already been addressed in the referenced literature, whereas others await a future response.

This research introduces a novel application of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to tackle the challenging task of Japanese word segmentation. Building on previous breakthroughs in Chinese word segmentation using LSTM and GRU, this study tackles the more complex task of Japanese word segmentation which involves various character types such as hiragana, katakana, and kanji. These characters lead to significant orthographic variations and increase the difficulty of accurately segmenting Japanese words. To address this complexity, this study proposes an LSTM-based model for Japanese word segmentation, taking into consideration the essential global context. Experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed model achieves exceptional accuracy when evaluated across different Japanese corpora. Furthermore, this study conducts comprehensive analyses of the model's performance to gain profound insights into its underlying workings. Notably, this research discovers that the model's success is largely influenced by the orthographic variation introduced by hiragana characters in Japanese words. On the Stack Overflow platform, users utilize 11,926,354 external connections to share resources with each other, along with their combined knowledge of programming. This entails a data collection process involving both structured information (questions, answers, tags, etc.) and unstructured data from posts, which requires a thorough analysis. This research focuses on examining the pattern of link sharing activities among Stack Overflow users to understand their behavior. Findings reveal that 94% of link sharing involves external resources and that top domains account for 70% of these shares. Users primarily disseminate content from social media, video sharing platforms, and news sources via these links. They tend to respond to posts that receive minimal engagement and often share content that is not related to the original question. These links rarely include necessary context for users to understand the content's significance. This implies that the majority of links shared on the platform could be reduced in number without compromising their functionality. By recognizing the intent behind the content of the links, Stack Overflow users can reframe their sharing activities to make them more efficient. This study's conclusions advocate for a more balanced approach to link sharing, one that considers both the link itself and the content it targets. Ultimately, the goal is to enable users to better manage their knowledge and reduce the amount of information required to understand the content of the links they share. To achieve this, the research presents several strategies for implementing this new approach, including implementing a built-in ability for users to summarize the content of links, a system-wide initiative, providing users with feedback about their link sharing activities, and promoting the use of other information sharing methods that are more efficient. This initiative aims to increase the awareness of Stack Overflow users about their link sharing activities and promote the use of other information sharing methods that are more efficient. Galactic rotation curves show a range of varying inner slopes. Observations suggest a potential relationship between a galaxy's brightness and its central dark matter, indicating the need for a more comprehensive explanation. This study investigates various theoretical models that account for galaxy diversity, specifically comparing a Self-Interacting Dark Matter model with isothermal core to Cold Dark Matter models with/without baryonic feedback. Contrary to standard CDM, SIDM can form isothermal cores, and its effectiveness isn't largely influenced by long-term baryonic feedback processes. Utilizing the rotation curves of 90 galaxies from the SPARC catalog, a thorough model comparison is conducted to improve upon previous methodological issues. Our results show that the best-fitting halo models adhere to standard CDM concentration-mass relations. Although SIDM and feedback-influenced CDM outperform the non-feedback CDM in accounting for rotation curve variations, a clear preference for any of these models over the others isn't evident when assessed through statistical measures. This study highlights the necessity for further research into galaxy interactions and darker phenomena to explain galaxy diversity. Future analyses should prioritize precision in rotation curve data and statistical model weights to better distinguish competing theories. Additionally, examining isolated galaxies may provide additional insight into distinguishing these models. A thorough examination of a larger number of galaxies could also enhance our understanding of a particular model's effectiveness. Although climate change is widely accepted, meaningful conversations about it are scarce,
resulting in slow implementation of the necessary societal changes to mitigate its effects.
To enhance climate communication and promote individual actions, we are developing a system
that leverages climate information tailored to each person's values. To overcome initial adoption hurdles,
our system employs a vast knowledge base that maps climate causes to specific social injustices and
related value frameworks. We then utilize this knowledge base to craft relevant, personalized climate messages
aimed at encouraging conversations and individual actions. We initially tested these through
two small-scale studies and found that the value-driven climate communication approach performed significantly
better than generic ones in sparking conversations and inspiring action. With further refinement, we aim to
revolutionize climate communication and accelerate individual contributions to a sustainable future.

Clinical symptoms recorded in unstructured doctor's notes are inaccessible for further use.
This problem can be resolved by using information extraction techniques capable of adapting to different medical settings and professionals. 
In this research, we address the issue of extracting symptoms by using pre-trained and fine-tuned models, trained on diverse patient data, medical institutions, and specialties. 
To enhance adaptation, we developed an adaptation framework called AdaptOR, which uses partially filled-in templates to guide raw text analysis. 
The study's objectives are two-fold: to evaluate different models' ability to recognize and fill in templates and to use these templates as a starting point for extracting additional information. 
The analysis reveals that using pre-trained and adapted models improves symptom event extraction while also reducing the need for labeled data. 
Additionally, we found that using AdaptOR facilitates more accurate and efficient template adaptation and shows potential in extracting additional data, thus enhancing our understanding of medical data and facilitating future studies. 
The source code and datasets used in this research are available on GitHub at https://github.com/colemandel/AdaptOR. 
The project is part of the Knowledge-Based Knowledge Guide (KBB) initiative, hosted by Harvard's Division of Medical Science, with Harvard's Division of Medical Science providing funding.

Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm for instructing machines via environmental interaction and adaptive learning from their errors. Despite initial expectations, however, its successful application in the automotive industry remains elusive. Following in the footsteps of notable achievements by Google DeepMind in mastering Atari games and Go, we have developed a comprehensive framework for autonomous driving through deep reinforcement learning, given its relevance due to autonomous driving's inherent complexities and environmental dependencies. In particular, autonomous driving poses significant challenges as a supervised learning problem due to dynamic interactions with pedestrians, vehicles, and road conditions. In view of the relative novelty of the area of study, we begin with an introductory overview of deep reinforcement learning, before outlining our proposed framework in detail. It leverages recurrent neural networks to consolidate information and facilitate the handling of scenarios with incomplete observability. Additionally, we have integrated cutting-edge attention models to concentrate on salient information and minimize computational burdens for seamless deployment on embedded hardware. We have evaluated the efficacy of our framework through simulated experiments, specifically on the simulated racing tracks of ArcRace and the advanced autonomous driving simulator of Carla. Our simulations demonstrate the feasibility of training a policy using deep reinforcement learning without the need for pre-labeling or co-training with a companion network. Notably, we have achieved the fastest known time-to-completion among similar studies, facilitated by the incorporation of universal network architecture designs and the use of modern CPU and GPU accelerators. Our code repository is freely accessible at https://github.com/fatemaharslan/Deep-Reinforcement-Learning-Based-Autonomous-Driving.git. It includes the implementation of our framework and the supporting simulation code for the arcrace.org platform. Furthermore, it also includes the carla.org simulator code modifications necessary for the integration of deep reinforcement learning with Carla. In accordance with open-source ethics, the repository is freely accessible to the public for further modifications and enhancements. Moreover, it is designed to facilitate the integration of deep reinforcement learning with other autonomous driving frameworks such as OpenCV and ADAS, as illustrated through our supporting video materials available at https://youtu.be/Tv3k32i1wM8, as well as our publicly accessible presentation at https://fatemaharslan.com/slides/DeepRL-Based-Autonomous-Driving.pdf. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks, showcasing this concept's effectiveness across real-world classification datasets. Additionally, we provide an innovative algorithm to rapid-learn and refine such a random network based on feedback from target classifiers, which we call the "Random Neural Network learning and adaptation algorithm". Furthermore, we introduce a method for converting any standard neural network into a random neural network counterpart, which we demonstrate can be implemented using a simple spike-based learning algorithm. We explore the potential for employing such random neural networks as low-power classifiers in battery-powered devices, showcasing our findings with a comparison of our model's accuracy and computational requirements to those of existing spiking neural networks. We conclude by outlining promising avenues for further research to fully capitalize on this innovative technology. Overall, our objective is to present a novel, efficient classifying model that leverages the advantages of both random and spiking neural networks, which we refer to as the "Random Spiking Neural Network". While this term may seem contradictory, it highlights the random network's capacity to be translated into a highly efficient spike-based model. Conversely, this concept also enables random neural networks to be designed as spike-based networks with comparable classification accuracy to their traditional neural counterparts. Essentially, we propose a unified view of these networks as a singular technology, with the term "Random Spiking Neural Network" denoting a versatile, efficient, and highly accurate classifying model. As such, it serves as a versatile, accurate, and efficient classifier that surpasses previous spiking neural networks in performance, while showcasing our algorithm's ability to refine such models based on target classifiers. Lastly, it offers promising avenues for further research to fully capitalize on this innovative technology. A surge in personal device ownership offers an immense, yet largely underutilized resource of computational power, making it feasible to utilize it. To harness this potential, we developed Pando, a novel volunteer computing system based on declarative concurrent programming, and powered by JavaScript, WebRTC, and WebSockets. By employing a dynamic network of unreliable, volunteer-sourced personal devices and their browsers, Pando facilitates parallel execution of a function on multiple values, thus enhancing efficiency on compute-intensive applications like animation rendering and image processing. Furthermore, our approach's adaptability is demonstrated through Pando's deployment across a range of platforms, encompassing local networks, Grid5000, and PlanetLab's distributed nodes spanning across Europe. Although inspired by Eugeniq and Linda, Pando's inspiration isn't limited to past work in volunteer computing, encompassing a broader range of inspiration. In an effort to make the underlying mechanism more accessible, we provide a comprehensive, web-based demo, allowing users to interactively explore Pando's functionality. By leveraging its scalable and dynamic capabilities, users can produce a variety of results, including a display of multiple, dynamically changing maps as well as a visualization of data distributed across nodes. In our investigation, we found that Pando's performance is influenced by factors such as network speed, volunteer reliability, and local computation speed. In light of this, we're exploring ways to improve the system's reliability through utilization of techniques like data replication, as well as incorporating additional programming paradigms like state to further expand its capabilities. Ultimately, Pando represents a versatile tool for a wide array of applications, thanks to its utilization of a dynamic network of volunteer-sourced personal devices, thus holding considerable potential for a variety of use cases including, but not limited to, compute-intensive applications, web-based demo, animation rendering, image processing, map creation, data distribution across nodes, and data cloud with a focus on accessibility. In an effort to further illustrate this potential, we've included a showcase of recent projects completed with the aid of Pando. In conclusion, in an effort to contribute to the field of volunteer computing, we're making Pando available under an open-source license, welcoming users to interact with our system, and looking forward to potential collaborations in the future. We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation that incorporates a hole at zero. By employing this equivalence, we obtain a detailed characterization of these transformations, yielding new insights and results in various areas, such as Krieger embeddings, survivor sets, Hausdorff dimensions, bifurcation sets, and badly approximable numbers. We show that certain classes of sets associated with these beta-transformations possess unique properties, specifically that they are winning in Schmidt games and have the countable intersection property. Furthermore, we establish a comprehensive formula for the Hausdorff dimension of a particular class of sets that arise as bifurcation sets, by combining the concepts of Hausdorff dimensions and topological pressure, previously explored in Lindenstrauss and Maheshwary's work on the complex Génon configuration space. Additionally, we extend the concept of beta-expansions of real numbers by introducing a new notion of beta-expansions with a hole at zero, and show that all intermediate beta-expansions belong to a specific subclass of these beta-expansions, which can be characterized using a topological equivalence that incorporates a hole at zero. This new concept allows us to investigate new questions in the realm of real analysis. Lastly, we address the geometric hypothesis concerning the survival sets of beta-transformations, by demonstrating that all survival sets satisfy a geometric property, specifically that they contain a dense subset consisting of numbers with a unique beta-expansion, known as singular vectors. We also calculate the Hausdorff dimension of a particular class of sets that arise as bifurcation sets, by proving a conjecture initially proposed by Boshernitzan and Liao. Machine learning models such as tree ensembles consistently achieve high performance across various benchmarks, yet their intricate decision-making processes are challenging to interpret. A notable obstacle lies in pinpointing how specific characteristics, or subsets of characteristics, influence these models. Our proposal, Disentangled Attribution Curves, offers a unified framework that generates transparent and understandable models, seamlessly applicable to all tree ensemble methods. By representing a convolution of feature effects using orthogonal curves, our framework facilitates intuitive model interpretation and significantly reduces the number of model coefficients. Moreover, DACs are versatile and can be employed in variance reduction, hyperparameter tuning, and result explanation, among other tasks. Our empirical evidence demonstrates that DACs enhance the understanding of tree ensemble models, surpass other models in predictive capacity when tuned appropriately, and effectively reduce computational complexity. Furthermore, DACs outperform existing methods in explaining the mechanisms behind tree ensemble models and facilitating robust hyperparameter tuning. Our proposed approach, implemented in the R package DAC, is thoroughly illustrated through numerous examples and benchmarked using a range of datasets available on datasets.international.org. In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, necessitating novel approaches for mitigation. Recent proposals, rooted in concepts such as multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption, often come at a cost of significant computational overhead, rendering them unsuitable for practical application. This work presents an alternative solution by harnessing the capabilities of Trusted Execution Environments to safeguard data and model interactions, specifically introducing Flatee - an efficient federated learning framework across these environments, that substantially minimizes both training and communication times, while remaining robust against adversarial manipulation. Additionally, an analysis of safety and security within Flatee demonstrates an acceptable balance between these concerns and data confidentiality. Experimental results confirm the superiority of Flatee in its performance and reliability. Further information on the project can be found at https://github.com/argon-2/flatee. As an open-source implementation, Flatee aspires to address the urgent need for efficient and scalable privacy-preserving federated learning solutions. Ideally, this may serve as a foundational groundwork for federated learning applications where data confidentiality is paramount, such as in healthcare and finance, by providing an adaptable and user-friendly toolkit. Ultimately, this may contribute to the widespread adoption of Federated Learning by addressing its critical impediments to privacy and efficiency. The embedded systems industry is massive and ubiquitous, as evidenced by its presence in most of the world's produced processors. Interactions between drivers and external components like sensors and actuators pose significant challenges to embedded software development, particularly during the testing phase, where flaws can lead to damage or injury. To address this issue, a novel test framework is presented, which streamlines the process of creating and executing tests for driver-external interactions. This is achieved by integrating a software model of the interaction protocol, known as the interaction model, into the test sequence. This model is drawn from the Umbee tool, which provides a graphical interface for defining test cases. This way, a test case can be run on a real-world device, much like a model, using the test sequence's automatic conversion into commands. Additionally, the model is used to generate detailed information about the device's behavior during the test, which can be optimized to minimize execution time. To facilitate seamless integration of the interaction model into existing test suites, a plug-in architecture is implemented, allowing each model to be optimized independently without affecting the test framework as a whole. Furthermore, the model's data is complemented with knowledge about the device's functionality and limitations to provide a more comprehensive analysis of the test results. To illustrate the effectiveness of this approach, a real-world example is given involving the development of a driver for a stepper motor. This involved creating four test cases, which showed promising results, along with the optimization of two test sequences that saved execution time without compromising accuracy. Both the test framework and the optimized test sequences are freely available at https://git.uc3m.es/umbee/framework/-/tree/master/docs. Additionally, a video showcasing the test environment's functionality can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HkHKpXKeU7U. Finally, the model used for the stepper motor test, along with its Umbee representation, can be found at https://git.uc3m.es/umbee/framework/-/tree/master/umbee/interaction-models. Additionally, information about Umbee can be found at https://umbee.uc3m.es. Sincere thanks are extended to the sponsors, researchers, and testers involved. To ensure the integrity of the project, a public repository is maintained at https://git.uc3m.es/umbee/framework. Further details can be obtained by contacting the project lead at sergiu@dia.uc3m.es.

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Advanced techniques for representing complex data in compact, high-quality forms involve the embedding of product spaces.
We've identified a new challenge - linear classification in complex product space structures composed of different geometric environments, like Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic spaces.
To tackle this problem, we first establish a framework for defining linear classification models within curved, high-dimensional spaces that generalize traditional vector-based classification.
Next, we demonstrate that, regardless of the geometry of the space, linear classification models are capable of accurately predicting any $d+1$ data points.
We've then formalized the application of these models in complex product space structures and have developed new types of classifiers for such environments, providing solid theoretical backing for their effectiveness.
Moreover, our analysis reveals that these classifiers can learn complex relationships within high-dimensional data, but we've established that they can only handle at least $d+1$ data points. To substantiate these claims, we tested our methods on various synthetic and real-world datasets, observing that our types of classifiers perform well on small datasets but struggle with large datasets. To address this, we proposed a new sparse model that minimizes weight importance, reducing the impact of feature collinearity on linear classification in high-dimensional product space structures. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of this model through testing on various datasets. Finally, we implemented our methods in an open-source library, libspatial, making it easily accessible to the research community. Overall, our research offers new insights into linear classification in complex geometry-based data representations and provides a set of innovative tools for tackling this complex issue. Ancient sundials served as primary timekeepers, leveraging the Sun's daily movement to divide the day into equal parts. This simple, effective device made the Sun's power visible to people from all walks of life, inspiring various innovations across centuries. As European travelers discovered new paths, they brought sundials to distant lands, marking the beginning of a global spread of this ancient technology. This article delves into the significance of sundials within the context of the classical Islamic civilization, intersecting with modern times via advanced encoding methods. It also outlines a novel approach to estimating unknown sundial parts using photogrammetry and deep learning techniques. Furthermore, we explore the potential of employing deep learning models to develop restored replicas of ancient sundials, utilizing only images of their partially restored components. This pioneering application promises a seamless transition from ancient to modern technologies. To illustrate this future, we present two case studies: one for a Roman sundial and another for an Islamic-era sundial in Damascus, showcasing the effectiveness of this innovative approach. Lastly, we highlight promising avenues for further research and development. This work aims to inspire architects, scientists, and historians to harness the potential of combining past and present knowledge to build sustainable, environmentally conscious buildings. By doing so, it aims to promote a revolution in building design, paving the way for a brighter future. Keywords: ancient technology, sundials, Islamic civilization, modern technologies, deep learning, revolution in building design. The cardinalities of finite models for sentences with at least three variables and binary relations are examined in this study.  Specifically, we demonstrate that any such sentence, denoted as $\Phi$, has a corresponding sentence, denoted as $\Phi'$, utilizing the same number of variables and one symmetric binary relation, whose set of model cardinalities increases linearly with $\Phi$'s model cardinalities. Furthermore, we observe that the models of sentence $\Phi'$ are all bipartite graph representations.  Consequently, we deduce that, in order to ensure a sentence's model cardinality does not fall below a specified integer value, we may equivalently investigate the same property in the context of sentences with at most three variables and one symmetric binary relation, thereby broadening the applicability of partial evaluation techniques for first-order logic.  Additionally, we establish a corresponding extension for the computability of fixed-point logic, demonstrating that any given fp-literal will result in a linear increase in the number of variables necessary to obtain a corresponding fp-literal after partial evaluation, thereby enabling us to determine the effective degree of a single variable fp-literal.  This in turn enables the construction of an effective degree theory for first-order logic.  Finally, we note that similar results may also be applied to the realm of parametrized counting problems.  In particular, we deduce that the parameterized Hopcount problem for bipartite graphs is not in PTIME[log(n)].  In contrast, we find the parameterized Hopcount problem for general graphs to be in PTIME[log(n)].  Additionally, we note the existence of an almost complete solution for the current problem set. The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold. Moreover, we show that a phase plate with an optimal fill-factor 
can support an electron intensity of up to 1200 pA in the focal spot, thus minimizing 
its impact on image quality and making it even more viable for TEM enhancement. 
Notably, our research focuses on utilizing ferrite magnets to incorporate a stabilizing 
magnetization within the phase plate design, thereby addressing concerns over 
electrostatic instability. Our findings strongly advocate for the implementation of 
programmable phase plates to surpass the 1 Angstrom resolution limit on uncorrected 
TEMs. Moreover, a phase plate can serve as an adaptable tool to perform diverse 
microscopic experiments including single particle cryoEM, electron tomography, 
and microscopy-based spectroscopy with improved stability and imaging capability. 
Ultimately, our study paves the way for programmatic control over phase plates to

Drawing inspiration from Feynman's and Deutsch's groundbreaking work, we introduce a theoretical framework that assesses computational capability across diverse physical platforms and complexity scales. This framework is utilized to analyze the fundamental principles of quantum computation. Furthermore, this study serves as a precursor to investigating more universal computation models by examining additional physical mechanisms exemplified throughout the paper. The goal of this research is to contribute to the development of a physically universal model of computation by examining the computational capabilities of different physical systems, with a hope that this insight can guide the construction of future physical models of computation. This study focused on determining the general equation for calculating the potential positions of an $n$ step random walk in a $d$ dimensional space with a single unit step size, denoted as $|P_n^{d}|$. Our approach began by establishing a recursive relationship for the count formula: $|P_n^{d+1}| = |P_n^d| + 2\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} |P_k^d|$. We then presented two distinct methods to derive an explicit equation for $|P_n^{d}|$, involving the application of generating functions and Faulhaber's formula. Ultimately, our analysis led to the derivation of an explicit equation: $|P_n^{d}| = \sum_{j=1}^{\frac{n(d+1)}{d+1}} \binom{n(d+1)-1}{d+1} (d+1)^{d+1} \mathbf{d}^j (-1)^{j+1}$, where $\mathbf{d} = \binom{n+1}{d+1}$. This finding provides a significant advancement, as it yields the first explicit general equation for $|P_n^{d}|$. Furthermore, it facilitates the derivation of an explicit general equation for the probability that a random walk remains within a $d$ dimensional cube with side length $r$, denoted as $P_0^{d}(n,r)$. Lastly, our research enabled the calculation of exact counts for particular instances of $(n, d)$, as well as approximate estimates of the potential positions of an $n$ step random walk in a $d$ dimensional space. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. Additionally, the thermal capacity exhibits a temperature-independent, graphene-specific constant that arises from logarithmically divergent interactions among Dirac electrons over short ranges. By projecting predictive variables into a latent space, we have created a generalized framework that: 1) maintains the original model's integrity while performing variable selection, 2) accurately detects relevant structures and retains posterior uncertainties, and 3) extends its applicability to non-Gaussian models within the exponential family. We've rigorously evaluated our approach by comparing it with established methods on various datasets, and the results demonstrate its superior performance in accurately selecting variables and recovering relevant structures. Furthermore, projections predictive inference offers a substantial speed advantage over competing methods. Due to its broad applicability and utility, we've implemented our approach in the R package ppinfer. Recent research has demonstrated that Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to strategically crafted malicious inputs, prompting the development of countermeasures against query-optimization attacks. Our research diverges from previous studies by exploring the vulnerability of DNN models to Man-in-the-Middle attacks. From an attacker's standpoint, conventional adversarial attacks prove ineffective as they necessitate multiple interactions with the model to devise plans, whereas MitM attacks enable a single adversary with access to the connection to implement various forms of manipulation. We propose an approach for generating adversarial examples on a per-class basis, allowing an attacker to craft an array of malicious inputs. Our model, which can be trained simultaneously with the target DNN model during training, exhibits exceptional performance on DNN classification while also exhibiting a high accuracy rate in MitM attacks - specifically, we've achieved success rates of 85% and 95% on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, respectively, with only a single attempt. Our proposed approach outperforms existing deep learning-based models designed to prevent query-optimization attacks while requiring less training time. Additionally, we've found that our adversary's accuracy can be enhanced when the training data includes labels indicating the connection's access history. A solar type-I noise storm is created by particle beams accelerated from active regions experiencing significant changes in their magnetic field configurations. These storms exhibit significant intensity fluctuations in very short time frames and on very short wavelengths. The dynamic evolution of these storm sources remains largely unstudied due to a lack of high-resolution imaging data in metrewave frequencies. By analyzing data from the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA), this research identifies the high-resolution imaging capabilities of four perpendicular baselines that allow for a detailed study of a storm source associated with a microflare. The storm source exhibited two distinct modes of evolution: a rapid contraction followed by a slow expansion, and a rapid intensity increase followed by a slow decrease. These changes occurred within periods of a few minutes to an hour, and are consistent with the effects of two separate processes: the sudden release of magnetic energy in a microflare, and the subsequent interaction of the resulting beams with the surrounding solar atmosphere. These energy releases and interactions are known to significantly impact the solar atmosphere and can last for extended periods. The storm's intensity continued to fluctuate as it expanded, likely due to variations in the energy dynamics or the storm's geometric shape. These findings provide a framework for the understanding of future investigations into storm source dynamics, and highlight the capabilities of interferometric imaging in understanding these complex processes. The study of these storm sources is essential in identifying their relationship to other solar active regions and to particle beams emanating from the sun. The MWA's capabilities in this regard will be essential in future research of this kind. The MWA's sensitivity levels and bandwidths made it an ideal instrument for a detailed analysis of these storm sources. Similar future arrays such as the SKYMAPP prototype will offer improved sensitivity and coverage, enabling the identification and study of many more storm sources and their dynamic properties. The MWA's dynamic capability to image changing structures such as these storm sources holds great promise for future research in this field. The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom that is both accelerated and moving. Additionally, a comparative analysis is performed with a third model in which the atom's magnetic dipole moment is coupled to a vector electromagnetic field also bounded by a plane with different boundary conditions. These evaluations demonstrate that spontaneous emission rates can be influenced by boundary conditions, and an atom in motion or undergoing acceleration will experience altered spontaneous emission rates due to both its velocity and acceleration. However, these phenomena only occur significantly at very high frequencies associated with the electromagnetic nature of the dipole, and under most conditions related to low-frequency activity, the effects of boundary conditions remain secondary to the impact of the atom's velocity or acceleration on the spontaneous emission rate. A longstanding issue regarding massive star origins involves whether these stars always form within dense clusters and, if found in less crowded environments, if they inevitably moved there.  Recent advances in wide-scale photometric surveys enable us to detect massive stars without bias in the less crowded regions of the galaxy.  This study examines forty candidate OB stars discovered by Mohr-Smith et al in the vicinity of Westerlund 2, with locations confined to a 1.5x1.5 degree square area, distinguished by their extinctions and K magnitudes.  Spectra from two extremely hot O stars show they are verified as O4V stars with masses exceeding 40 Msun.  Their velocity relative to Westerlund 2 displays an assortment of patterns, featuring both negative and positive values, at speeds up to 160 km/s.  Also found are eight O-F stars within a 20' radius of Westerlund 2, exhibiting a different character, with all but one confirmed as massive (M > 15 Msun) and in motion relative to the cluster, with some potentially strayed members showing similar properties.  This last group of stars shows an unusual pattern of velocities, moving away from the cluster at a consistent rate, indicating they originated from a different location.  This research indicates a significant non-native O-F star population outside of Westerlund 2, with evidence of massive (M > 40 Msun) field O stars for the first time.  This implies massive stars can arrive in the galaxy through means other than cluster-explosion, with evidence supporting a new theory of massive star origins/evolution that could impact our understanding of the galaxy's stellar evolution.  Further research is suggested to examine the discovered pattern of O-F stars moving away from the cluster, as well as their potential relation to the much larger Gum 31 association.  Additionally, the potential for a massive (M > 40 Msun) field population of O stars, found through recent wide-scale photometric surveys such as VVV, could offer new insights into the galaxy's evolution.  This study paves the way for further investigation into the newly discovered O-F star population and Gum 31 association, as well as their potential relation to each other. To overcome these challenges, we propose an innovative, end-to-end approach utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks that not only restores visual clarity but also improves the overall readability of the documents. This pioneering method differs from conventional binarization techniques, which primarily focus on enhancing visual quality, by integrating a text recognition module to optimize generated output. The effectiveness of this architecture was validated through comprehensive experiments conducted on Arabic and Latin handwritten texts, showcasing improved readability and visual quality. Additionally, our pre-trained model demonstrated exceptional performance on the H-DIBCO challenges, even after fine-tuning on synthetic, degraded text images. This pioneering work offers a groundbreaking solution for restoring and making older documents more accessible. The proposed architecture is expected to provide significant benefits in accessing and preserving older, degraded documents containing vital historical information. The task of automatically coloring an unseen grayscale image using a learned color encoding is referred to as image colorization.  It has seen significant advancements in recent years, employing Generative Adversarial Networks, particularly through the implementation of multi-resolution techniques and the employment of global and local guidance layers in model training.  However, the generation process still faces issues with stability and speed, particularly the repeated rewinding of the network during training, which hampers performance.  To overcome these limitations, we introduce the Contrastive Colorization framework, which uses self-supervised techniques to generate colorizations for grayscale images by leveraging a contrastive loss in the latent space.  This framework achieves colorization tasks more efficiently than existing methods, resulting in faster and more reliable colorization of large images, elimination of image rewinding, and facilitation of unconditional color generation.  Moreover, it allows for the seamless colorization of multiple grayscale images sharing a common underlying structure through the shared learning of that structure.  This capability makes the framework highly suitable for colorization tasks involving seamless image fusion, such as colorizing black and white images or generating dream scenes.  Extensive experimental evaluations conducted on various image datasets validate the superiority of our proposed framework over existing methods in terms of visual coherence and local structure preservation.  Moreover, it exhibits a 5-20 times speedup in colorization tasks compared to the current state-of-the-art methods. We've developed a novel numerical scheme to efficiently calculate Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) weights without relying on tedious iterative processes. Based on the Universal Approximation Theorem, our proposed algorithm rapidly achieves low error rates in the regression and classification of intricate datasets, such as the Griewank function and the MNIST database for handwritten digits. Its mathematical formulation allows it to accurately approximate highly complex nonlinear functions with a minimal margin of error, and it also facilitates the solution of Partial Differential Equations. The approach works by determining the weights for each neuron in localized data subsets where a corresponding approximation matrix remains invertible, thereby rendering hyperparameter optimization unnecessary. As a direct consequence, this minimizes computational speed. Additionally, since the weights are calculated with relative precision, the amount of data required for training can be substantially reduced, and the results are notably less prone to shifting. We've compared our method to established techniques, such as gradient descent, beam search, and random search, and demonstrated that it surpasses them in performance and speed. Moreover, since the outputs are calculated directly without any delay, the reconstruction of missing entries in datasets can be accurately accomplished. Finally, this powerful tool is equally effective both in supervised and unsupervised learning scenarios. We've visually illustrated our findings through comprehensive support and attached the relevant code to our paper for the convenience of fellow researchers. A new architecture for multi-agent LfD is presented which enables the creation of reliable and efficient robotic systems in complex and large-scale environments by leveraging advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI).  This paper introduces a technological innovation that addresses the problems of executing complex tasks and addressing uncertainty in performance by using deep multi-agent reinforcement learning.  A new collaborative architecture for deep multi-agent reinforcement learning is presented which learns task representation, policy, and reward functions through interaction with a demonstration-based simulator.  A new transfer learning approach is presented which utilizes a pre-trained robust and generalizable network to rapidly adapt to novel situations. This research presents a major breakthrough in the field of multi-agent LfD and paves the way for the development of long-lasting and efficient robotic systems. common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-task
approach, training existing relation extraction models alongside knowledge graph
link prediction to ultimately boost the models' overall performance and achieve
predictable gains in accuracy. By conducting this training, we noticed notable
improvements on three distinct datasets, particularly in scenarios involving
domain-specific models or datasets with limited annotated data available. In
k-fold cross-validation tests, we noticed average increases in F$_1$ score of
$3.55$, $2.05$, and $2.00$ for the datasets BN2E, WN2E, and DAC, respectively.
These enhancements indicate the potential for significant real-world
applications, particularly in relation extraction tasks involving large-scale
datasets that haven't yet been annotated. In addition, we noted that knowledge
graph link prediction served as a highly effective regularization technique,
preventing overfitting and allowing models to generalize more effectively in
real-world applications. Based on our study's outcomes, we recommend integrating
knowledge graph link prediction as an essential component of any relation
extraction model, particularly for large-scale datasets. Ultimately, we hope this
research facilitates the development of more effective relation extraction models
capable of generalizing accurately in real-world applications. In support of
this research, the source code and datasets utilized can be accessed via our

Momentum operators are explored in the context of intrinsically curved manifolds. It's established that for Killing vector fields representing these momentum operators, the manifolds are either flat or belong to specific categories: those with a compact structure and a constant sectional curvature or those with a hyperbolic sectional curvature that remains negative and the same throughout. Furthermore, a comprehensive expression is derived for the Casimir operator, along with an in-depth analysis of its spectrum. In the case of manifolds that are compact, it's determined that the Casimir operator is essentially equivalent to the total momentum squared, a finding that also holds true for manifolds that are semi-compact. In addition, a connection is established between the momentum operators and geodesic deviation equations, along with an examination of skew-symmetric killing vector fields. The study concludes by looking at special cases, such as Euclidean spaces, as well as spheres and hyperbolic spaces. Ultimately, this highlights an important distinction between the momentum operators and their inherent relationship with the curvature of the manifold. As such, non-zero momentum operators can indeed be defined on intrinsically curved manifolds, a fact underscoring the physical significance of these operators. It's also worth noting that any Killing vector field can be associated with a momentum operator, a finding that expands the scope of these operators well beyond the realm of flat manifolds. Here, the complex scalar field's', acting as a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson, plays the role of a flavon, which bears a flavor charge. Upon the VEV of the flavon, $U(1)_F$ flavor symmetry is broken. This break results in the emergence of a small parameter and consequently generates a hierarchy between top and bottom quark masses. A flavon lighter than the TeV scale can naturally be introduced, which makes it a completely testable model to understand the flavor hierarchy origins. Furthermore, its effect on the substantial flavor-changing neutral currents arises and gets constrained heavily by flavor precision experiments. Research into the direct search for six particles including the flavon itself is also conducted. Finally, potential prospects related to flavor of future high-energy colliders such as HL-LHC, ILC, CLIC, FCC, LHC-X, and SPPS are explored. Specifically, the focus is on the detection potential of the $pp\rightarrow t\bar{t} \text{A} \rightarrow t\bar{t} \text{B} \bar{\text{B}}$ process at the HL-LHC, where the distribution of the top quark transverse momentum could serve as a distinguishing criterion to identify the flavor-breaking effect represented by the flavon. This analysis represents the first study of this specific search strategy within this particular model. As a result, the detection prospects of the flavon at various future colliders are evaluated, where the highest sensitivity is shown for ILC with $\mathcal{O}(10)-\mathcal{O}(100)$ TeV sensitivity for a 1 TeV < $\Lambda_{6}$ < 10 TeV range. The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR interaction beyond conventional physical limitations by exploiting the boundaries of human perception, subtly guiding users' movements to enhance interactivity. This research examines the dangers of VPPM exploitation, beginning with a conceptual framework that confirms their existence and the ease with which they can be implemented. An experimental investigation of redirected walking manipulation reveals that it can be optimized using individualized physiological parameters to increase its effect on users. An analysis of haptic force manipulation reveals that certain types of stimulation are particularly vulnerable to exploitation due to their association with significant physiological effects. Future research should focus on developing anti-exploitation measures and conducting in-depth interviews to further understand the consequences of VPPM misuse. Additionally, an open-source VPPM implementation library is proposed to facilitate research in this field. Lastly, potential VPPM applications in VR therapy settings are explored. Overall, this study aims to mitigate the risks inherent to VPPMs while promoting responsible research practices. Disclosure: The authors declare no conflicts of interest related to this research.

Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and CARMA telescopes have unveiled previously unknown details of proto-stars in binary systems. Specifically, mass measurements for CB230 IRS1 and L1165-SMM1 revealed a significantly higher mass range ($0.1-0.25 \, M_{\odot}$) than those generally obtained from binary formation simulations, which were around $0.01 \, M_{\odot}$. In response to these disparities, researchers carried out numerical simulations of a core's collapse to analyze how a binary's formation mass is influenced by its parent core's overall mass. In these simulations, they implemented azimuthally symmetric mass seeds within a rotating core, promoting the development of a dense filament, where a binary system might emerge. This binary formation process decreased as the core's mass increased, prompting researchers to amplify the core's variability through different eigenvalues in the hydrodynamic equations, only to find that this didn't yield desirable results. Ultimately, Compressible MHD simulations of a more massive core ($0.17 \, M_{\odot}$) showed some promise, revealing a binary with a mass of $0.013 \, M_{\odot}$, although this was also found to be an sub-system of a larger proto-stellar system. In contrast, CB230 IRS1 was discovered to possess a mass of $0.1 \, M_{\odot}$ by scientists, suggesting that further theoretical research is necessary to explain the observed proto-stellar masses. Additionally, researchers would have to verify whether a similar binary system, L1165-SMM1, was truly a proto-stellar system or just an illusion created by an optical alignment with a proto-star system. In case of an alignment, researchers discovered that CB230 IRS1 presented a mass $10 times$ greater than the binary system itself, a mass which is consistent with a theoretical mass range, $0.1-0.25 \, M_{\odot}$. This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous methods. Although the kernel trick offers a powerful way to tackle non-linearity, its effectiveness can be undermined by a lack of open-source and reproducible kernel implementations, especially in complex datasets. The proposed m-ar-K-FastICA approach uses a readily available and adaptable Python library that facilitates collaboration with scikit-learn, providing a more reliable solution for feature extraction even in data sets with high entropy levels and no need for data pre-whitening. Several classification experiments using open-access datasets from diverse domains have shown significant performance improvements, showcasing the enhanced capability of the proposed approach. Furthermore, a comprehensive comparison has been carried out between the proposed m-ar-K-FastICA and other established approaches for feature extraction, confirming its superior entropy handling capabilities. The proposed technique also offers increased robustness against data manipulation attacks, including noise addition. This paper builds on existing research linking finite model theory to algebraic and propositional proof systems. It's proven that if a logic system can identify unique, non-isomorphic graphs in CPOT, it implies CPOT's solvability in bounded-degree EPC, which in turn has consequences for the latter's solvability in terms of polynomial formulas. Additionally, this research establishes a connection between the two most powerful known algebraic logic systems, CPOT and EPC. Conversely, it's also shown that strong EPC limitations follow from key number theoretic assumptions. Lastly, a new relationship is introduced between the width of EPC proofs and the number of variables in polynomial equations used to define these proofs. Our analysis reveals the depth of EPC to be at least three, assuming a certain hypothesis holds. Furthermore, it's proven that CPOT depth is at least two, provided a parallelism hypothesis is assumed. Our study explores the width and depth of powerful algebraic logic systems, bringing us closer to resolving some of the most fundamental questions in the field. Key technical innovations include introducing extended polynomial calculus with just one alternation, a concept previously explored by Bird and Polk, and leveraging the classification of finite simple groups to achieve our depth results. Additionally, a new width lower bound for EPC through EPC-derivation height follows a previously established similar proof in CPOT. To generalize Bird and Polk's result, it's shown that a system which can identify unique, non-isomorphic graphs in CPOT implies a strong EPC width lower bound, and this result generalizes to various algebraic logic systems when the depth is at least two. Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing an array of views on society. Despite the numerous opinions expressed, verifying their accuracy can be challenging due to their subjective nature. To address this, we aim to condense these posts into distinct narratives, thereby isolating the core assertions linked to specific topics. By gaining insight into and visualizing these narratives, social media debates can become more informed and productive. To establish a systematic approach for identifying underlying narratives, we propose MAST -- a method tailored to social media discourse. MAST utilizes transformer models to analyze raw posts, their normalization, and a narrative segmentation process guided by topic models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by analyzing Twitter posts related to vaccination, effectively extracting targeted messages and overarching themes. Our results reveal the diverse range of narratives contributing to public opinion on vaccination. To facilitate this process, we make our code and dataset publicly available. This enables researchers to build upon our work, and we envision this research to ultimately empower social media users to engage in more reflective behavior. By navigating the complex sea of social media information, users can discover various content narratives influencing public opinion. Ultimately, this research may inspire a parnassus of reflective social media engagement. Our approach aims to assist social media users in exploring the various content narratives impacting public opinion. Utilizing our method, users can gain insight into the narratives driving social media debates. By applying this approach, users can discover the range of opinions on specific topics, such as vaccination, and explore the narratives contributing to global discussions on vaccination, as well as other topics. Our method aims to enhance social media users' understanding of the content narratives shaping global opinions. To facilitate this process, we make our code and dataset publicly available at https://github.com/argentinam/MAST. Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial, particularly for anticipating incidents such as accidents, protests, or breaking news. The dynamic nature of social media data poses challenges to traditional approaches, including ambiguous event timelines and spaces. An innovative solution, this research introduces an adaptive spatio-temporal event detection framework leveraging social media. It addresses spatial resolution ambiguity through a quad-tree based method that segmentates regions based on data density, and uses statistical analysis incorporating the Poisson distribution to highlight anomalies in post density. Furthermore, event duration is determined dynamically via threshold calculation on post density changes. An evaluation using multiple datasets is presented, demonstrating the framework's effectiveness in detecting events. Notably, this framework surpasses existing approaches by exemplarily identifying geographically dispersed events such as Amazon's global fulfillment network and Wikipedia's registered events. New, high-precision data from the cosmic microwave background lensing measurements and tomographic galaxy surveys in progress will soon be released, giving the usual angular power spectrum analysis little to offer in terms of additional information. Instead, this study focuses on the spectral properties of clustered data based on their continuous two-dimensional distribution of angles and pairwise distances, analogous to how spectroscopy dissects remote stars into their constituent elements. The underlying six-dimensional distribution of galaxy counts is broken down into several non-trivial sections, and their patterns are analyzed to assess the inherent bias within the estimates. The degree of bias varies across the various sections, and different sections yield distinct estimates of the underlying power spectrum. When data from multiple depth ranges is utilized, the most influential sections can be selected through a statistical process, resulting in less biased estimates. The technique is initially illustrated with simulated data, and we show that the variance of our estimated power spectrum is comparable to that achieved through traditional methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate the potential of this method to yield additional and more precise information about the cosmological parameters when applied to data from ongoing and future tomographic galaxy surveys. The technique's scalability allows it to operate on data sets much larger than what is currently available. The analysis's computational requirements are discussed in more detail. Ultimately, the technique offers a versatile tool for exploring the spectral properties of data and can provide valuable insights beyond what is possible through the usual angular power spectrum, making it a valuable method for future cosmological surveys. The technique's suitability for classification purposes is also explored, and we find that the categorized spectra remain highly correlated with the underlying power spectrum. Therefore, we can utilize the correlated spectra to estimate the power spectrum more efficiently than would be possible through the usual power spectrum alone. By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to achieve robustness to potential attacks. The method, demonstrated through empirical tests on standard datasets, allows for training BNNs that are both accurate and certifiably secure on challenging datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10, further providing benefits in uncertainty calibration. This innovation facilitates the deployment of BNNs in applications requiring utmost reliability. This technique is versatile and can be applied to other data sets as well. In addition to certification, we observed an improvement in uncertainty calibration when compared with the state-of-the-art methods. This development opens the door for reliable certification and enhanced uncertainty modeling in BNNs.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated a BERT-based predictive model for online rumor identification, leveraging both traditional machine learning algorithms and social network characteristics. When evaluated against COVID-19 pandemic-related data, our proposed model outperformed state-of-the-art baselines with an accuracy rate of 92.95%, additionally achieving significant advancements in healthcare-related text classification tasks. Our research provides insights valuable for understanding the spread of COVID-19 myths and contributes to the development of more efficient public health crisis management strategies. This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. Five methods (PCA, KPCA, ICA, AE, and DAE) are utilized to compress high-dimensional pixels down to 301 dimensions. The resulting pixels are used for classification, allowing a comprehensive assessment of each method's effectiveness based on classification accuracy, compression rates, and reconstruction errors. Our research employed three diverse hyperspectral image datasets (urban, suburban, and forest landscapes), gathered by the Remote Sensing and Spatial Ecosystem Modeling lab at the University of Toronto. Our analysis reveals that PCA, KPCA, and ICA methods preserve pixel signals well but show decreased classification performance beyond 90% compression rates. In contrast, AE and DAE achieve better results at 95% compression but see their performance deteriorate as the compression rate approaches 97%. Ultimately, our findings highlight the importance of considering both compression methods and rates when crafting an effective hyperspectral pixel classification workflow. The associated code is accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/samuelhutchison1/Dimensionality_Reduction_for_Hyperspectral_Images. The associated datasets can be found at https://rsem.utoronto.ca/datasets. The associated hyperspectral images can be obtained at https://rsem.utoronto.ca/data/index.html?dataset=Building&dataset=Mississauga&dataset=Forest. The associated institutional research profiles can be found at https://scholar.google.com. The corresponding author's email address is [shutchison@uwaterloo.ca](mailto:shutchison@uwaterloo.ca). The research presented in this article was carried out at the University of Toronto.

Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated, resulting in the networks often being referred to as 'black boxes.' In contrast, simpler models are more interpretable but they are also much harder to find. Identifying and utilizing a sparse network that can be trained to replicate the same results is a viable option to improve network interpretability. According to the lottery ticket hypothesis, even large, dense neural networks harbor a smaller sparse sub-network that can be trained independently to achieve the same accuracy in the same amount of time. Our objective is to explore the existence of this trainable sub-network in the realm of natural language models, and we will accomplish this by examining and evaluating the most recent model compression techniques, such as quantization, knowledge distillation, and pruning. We will employ the state-of-the-art 55M parameter Transformer-language model as our test case and will attempt to compress it using a 5GB memory constraint. We will also independently verify the existence of the trainable sub-network and evaluate the available compression algorithms. We found that knowledge distillation produces the best results with an accuracy drop of 13% and we successfully identified and verified the trainable sub-network, confirming the lottery ticket hypothesis. The chosen sub-network requires 1.3GB parameters to achieve the same accuracy when trained independently. Furthermore, we found that perturbing up to 99% of the weights of the original model has an effect on accuracy only when using the full model, and we also discovered that the optimal sub-network can be robust to such perturbations without experiencing a significant drop in performance. Our research not only confirms the existence of the trainable sub-network but also provides insights into the relationship between the data and the model complexity. We thoroughly analyzed the importance of the parameters within the model and we found that the importance is unevenly distributed. The optimal sub-network and the pruning of the full model both show a similar pattern of importance, suggesting a possible data-dependent regularization effect. Our research also reveals that the magnitude of the parameters and the difficulty of the tasks are strongly correlated, and we found that the high-magnitude parameters tend to correspond to difficult tasks. We also found that the optimal sub-network can be effectively utilized in transfer learning by identifying the identifying the relevant head network through a systematic approach. Our approach involves evaluating all possible sub-networks and we found that the optimal sub-network can be found within 10 minutes by using a highly optimized gradient descent algorithm. A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, enables fast and precise calculation of crucial chemical shift indicators in proteins, thereby determining the spatial arrangements of proteins. ProCS is calibrated with the results of high-level quantum mechanical calculations, achieving remarkable agreement in predicting the amide proton chemical shifts of a small protein with a minimal error margin of 0.25 ppm (high correlation coefficient of 0.94). ProCS is now compatible with the PHAISTOS protein simulation program and used to determine ensembles of proteins representing experimentally measured amide proton chemical shift values. The ProCS method is used to refine the structures of proteins G, ubiquitin, and SMN Tudor Domain from high-resolution X-ray structures to align their predicted and experimentally measured properties. This study reveals that quantum-mechanical-based predictions of chemical shifts are essential for optimizing protein structures to align them with the observed data. ProCS presents an innovative tool for optimizing protein structural arrangements with immense potential in studying various biological processes like the conformational flexibility in ligand binding interactions. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits mention of the loss function, leading many to assume its efficacy is inherent. We contend that this lack of scrutiny is unwarranted and that the loss function's effects should be subject to examination. In this paper, we investigate the influence of loss functions on the generalizability of DNNs in supervised DNNs. We found that certain loss functions, like the cross-entropy loss, offer safeguards to safeguard against data augmentation, whereas others, like the KL divergence, are more susceptible. Furthermore, we demonstrated that incorporating a regularization term in the objective function can mitigate the adverse effects of certain loss functions. Our study also sheds light on the mechanisms underlying the adverse effects of certain loss functions and proposes a map to guide loss function selection based on data augmentation types. We also introduce an open-source platform for SCDNN training that supports over 500 loss functions. In our experiments, we found that several loss functions can yield superior generalization performance compared to the conventional cross-entropy loss when combined with data augmentation. In addition, we found that the choice of loss function can significantly affect the effectiveness of DNN generalization under different levels of data availability and problem difficulty. We hope this research promotes a greater understanding of the role of loss functions in DNN generalizability, drives the development of optimized loss functions tailored to DNNs, and contributes to the creation of a more precise theoretical framework for the study of SCDNNs. Describing the behaviors of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting elements requires concise expressions for their internal relationships. Ensuring the stability of these systems is the primary focus. Parquet theory is capable of achieving a level of self-consistency that encompasses all strictly pair-based interactions among elements. Grounded in a perturbative framework, the theory is comprised of a series of nonlinear integral equations that describe scattering events at all levels, from individual to collective. Despite its ability to account for a broad range of interactions, the theory is limited in its scope when it comes to its application within models that feature multiple element interactions beyond simple pairing. This paper presents a comprehensive overview of the principles underlying parquet theory, with particular emphasis on its underlying framework and the theoretical models it supports. The authors' aim in presenting this overview is to provide a clear connection to a corresponding computer program that facilitates the construction of parquet equations for a given model. This program serves as a vital tool for evaluating candidate pair-based interaction models that can serve as a basis for future theoretical and experimental work. Its utility is demonstrated through its application to a number of fundamental systems, including the properties of electrons in metals, the behaviors of quantum liquids in metals, and the roles of electron-phonon interactions in determining material properties. The authors' work on this program is an outgrowth of a long-term effort to develop a general, open-source software library known as solvableSE, which is designed to facilitate the computational construction of solvable models across a wide range of fields [7]. The program's construction is grounded in a perturbative framework that is capable of accounting for a broad class of many-body correlations, including those postulated by parquet theory. The excitonic insulator transition (EIT) occurs when a semimetal transitions into an excitonic insulator due to electron correlation, and it is driven by weak interelectron interaction leading to lattice distortion and dimensionality reduction. This process is not yet fully understood, especially in layered transition metal dichalcogenides, which exhibit both semimetal and insulating properties. By analyzing band structures and dielectric functions, researchers can investigate EIT in these materials. This study uses a many-body approach with random phase approximation and vertex correction to examine EIT in layered 1T-$MX_2$ (with $M$ being 3$d$ transition metal) materials. The results show that EIT occurs when these materials have a critical vertex correction value, and it is influenced by vertex correction in the vicinity of the Fermi level. This approach is applicable to other materials and can be used to investigate excitonic insulators. The study also finds that 1T-$VSe_2$ is on the verge of becoming an excitonic insulator, and it is possible to stabilize it with an external electric field. The same computational method can be used to investigate other excitonic insulators and their stabilization techniques. The study offers insights that can guide experimental efforts to discover excitonic insulators, and it paves the way for the creation of optoelectronic devices based on these materials. The study also explores the possibility of designing an optoelectronic switch using $MX_2$ materials, specifically $VSe_2$, by controlling an external electric field.
