Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics. In
terms of system consistency, our best model achieved a remarkable 90.5% role
compliance on the role-compliant dataset, surpassing a non-role-constrained system
by a substantial margin of 50.4%. Additionally, external evaluators provided
feedback on the system, stating it was more useful in real-world scenarios due to
its ability to adhere to role specifications. The proposed framework, along with
related data and model codes, is publicly available for replication purposes. @see

A reliable and efficient communication system known as semantic communication aims to minimize data transfer and ensure seamless connectivity to diverse users and services. A novel approach to this challenge is presented, incorporating an emergent signaling game framework with a neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence system that facilitates causal reasoning. To design a context-specific communication language, an alternating maximization algorithm optimizes utility values between communication nodes. This language enhances the vocabulary for message transmission by splitting complex data into simpler components and allows for generalization to unforeseen scenarios. A neural network model is used to reconstruct causal states based on the relevant data attributes at the transmitter, which are then evaluated by a receiver that implements a symbolic logical formula execution using AI components. Specifically, this implementation leverages the Generative Flow Networks tool for improved semantic reliability. This communication system has been designed to evaluate a new set of metrics, such as semantic information and distortion, using rigorous category theory algebraic properties, expanding beyond traditional notions of uncertainty as defined by Shannon. The system's capacity to transmit complex data over extended distances while ensuring high semantic reliability and low distortion is confirmed through numerical experiments, showcasing its superiority to conventional approaches. Recent advancements in Session-based recommendation systems have gained popularity for providing personalized, real-time suggestions with minimal prerequisite knowledge. Recent examples include STAMP and NARM models, which, however, struggle with encoding context in recent items due to the sum-product approach in pairwise learning-to-rank methods. To address this, we introduce CBT, a counterfactual learning-to-rank strategy combined with a co-variation aware session model, thereby enhancing item interactions and encoding context in recent items. Additionally, we propose a session-model-aware counterfactual sampling approach to cross-validation that minimizes biases, leading to more accurate and generalizable recommendations. Experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate CBT outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by significant margins, highlighting its potential for real-time domain recommendations. A thorough approach is outlined to numerically simulate single-phase flow in fractured porous media. This approach utilizes a discrete fracture matrix method that incorporates three distinct components: a finite element method for solving flow in a fractured porous medium, a network solver for modeling global flow in fractures, and a discrete fracture matrix approach that considers the sizing and placement of finite element cells in conjunction with fractures. A novel algorithm is presented for accurately solving fractures as boundaries and simultaneously determining cell sizes based on error estimates. This approach is markedly enhanced by reductions in computational cost associated with solving large systems of equations and the explicit resolution of accuracy-related issues. An experimental framework is presented to evaluate the method's effectiveness through assessments of accuracy, scalability, and efficiency. Detailed analysis confirms that the discrete fracture matrix method is an optimal solution strategy for the simulation of flow in fractured porous media. This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms. Two key issues arise in achieving these goals: firstly, determining optimal strategies to temporarily disband the formation to avoid collisions (collision avoidance reformation), and secondly, effecting this reformation while minimizing the time and energy spent by the drones. To resolve the first challenge, a cellular automata-based method is utilized to identify efficient formations that evade obstacles while reducing time and energy consumption. To tackle the second issue, a near-optimal reformation strategy after successful collision avoidance is realized through a temperature-based descent algorithm for artificial ant colonies. Performance evaluations utilizing 20 drones show that the proposed system lowers energy consumption by 75% and increases the time before the next reformation by 50%, thus delivering superior results when compared to a random reformation strategy. Simulation results further demonstrate the superiority of the designed system over existing approaches in the areas of collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms. Finally, the efficacy of the designed system is validated through outdoor experiments conducted with 15 drones. Given its innovative approach to collision avoidance and the maintenance of autonomous drone swarms, the proposed system has great potential for application in aerial photography, the medication delivery, and search and rescue operations employing autonomous drone swarms. With its versatility and the small number of participating drones used in experiments, the proposed system can be employed in various other multi-agent systems. In our investigation, we focus on a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations featuring time-delay, which are influenced by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Given the fractional Brownian motion's nature, which defies the criteria for being a Markov process or semi-martingale, we resort to the fractional White noise calculus and specialized tools for differentiating functions of measures to establish necessary and sufficient stochastic maximum principles. This approach is further exemplified by two applications, including solving a delayed consumption optimization problem from a cash flow and a linear-quadratic problem under delay constraints. Both problems yield a unique solution, which can be obtained using both the maximum principle and a Legendre-Fenchel transform method. Additionally, we demonstrate the efficacy of these methods by comparing the solutions to these problems. In particular, when the delay parameter tends to zero, the solutions conform to those derived from standard Markov process theory. Furthermore, we analyze the behavior of the optimal trajectory as the delay parameter increases, demonstrating its convergence to a limiting path that is continuous and depends on the Hurst parameter. Lastly, our study extends the notion of a Sengupta solution to a wide class of delayed stochastic control problems, offering an alternative approach to previously published work. In this spirit, we present novel results for a constant delay, as well as a delay that grows linearly with time, thereby broadening the applicability of the fractional White noise calculus to these scenarios. In particular, our analysis shows that the optimal trajectory for both problems is continuous and depends on the Hurst parameter, subject to a specific condition. In addition, we derive a comparison theorem, thereby establishing a path to investigating the uniqueness of our stochastic control problem in relation to that posed by Bismut-Atares in the context of classical Markov processes. In fact, when the delay parameter vanishes, our findings conform to those reported by Bismut-Atares in their study on optimal control of Markov processes. In this spirit of extension, we present our results as unique contributions to the theory of stochastic control, which retain their validity even in scenarios where the delay parameter approaches zero. In other words, our approach has the added benefit of preserving its validity and applicability across a broad range of related problems in the field of optimal stochastic control. In this vein, we present our findings as novel and valuable contributions to the field of stochastic control, which retain their utility and relevance even in scenarios where the delay parameter approaches zero. Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established criteria. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first label individual sentences as high or low quality, yet this process relies on human annotations that are time-consuming and often yield inaccuracies. To resolve this, we developed an automated system that examines semantic modifications in Wikipedia edits to create labels, considering the pre-edit version as an example requiring improvement, and high-quality sentences as instances that need no improvement. By employing our labels in machine learning models, we found that performance improves over relying on existing, manually generated labels. Furthermore, we discovered that Wikipedia editors' behavior provides more accurate labels compared to crowdworkers who lack the same level of contextual understanding and agreement as editors. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by how much its classification probability changes when its features are modified. This resistance metric is used to weight student-model samples that were misclassified by the teacher, enhancing the distillation process. Moreover, the model can be trained in an end-to-end manner using adversarial training, where the network is optimized to withstand perturbations that could deceive it into misclassifying its own data. Empirical evidence shows that these methods improve knowledge distillation performance relative to standard approaches, with further gains when both techniques are combined. This has particular implications for mobile applications that can't defend against local attacks on their model's behavior. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying solely on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. Fortunately, much of the value in expert guidance lies in identifying general state-action characteristics associated with favorable outcomes, rather than specific action outcomes themselves. The KeyValue Actor-Critic system takes advantage of this insight by incorporating two networks: a key value network that generates state-action keys, and an actor-critic network that uses these keys to generate action values. The actor-critic network is trained to focus on policy updates in key value-guided action spaces, thereby filtering out non-essential variations in behavior. The system also employs a dynamic key distribution mechanism that adapts to varying levels of exploration in key value-guided action spaces. The experimental results show that KeyValue Actor-Critic learns more efficiently than off-the-shelf imitation learning methods, including those using an expert network, and on par with a highly optimized reinforcement learning baseline. Moreover, it proofreads an even more challenging imitation learning problem by distilling general state-action characteristics, thereby paving the way for more efficient reinforcement learning outcomes. A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and keypoint data from two or more images. The system comprises four main components: a dataset creation algorithm, a prediction model, a keypoint-matching calibration algorithm, and a real-time calibration system. Our system's accuracy was validated in various scenarios, including comparing its results to ground truth data and integrating it with a self-sustaining navigation system on a Baxter robot. Specifically, we observed average navigation errors of less than 10 cm in close-up situations and less than 20 cm at a distance of 3 meters from the end-effector target point. Furthermore, we noted significant time savings of approximately 20-40% over traditional calibration methods at various self-sustaining navigation speeds. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the nature of dark matter within this framework. The presence of an inflection point within Higgs inflation is found not to significantly impact dark matter composition, and thus the model instead presents a multicomponent DM system involving axions and sterile neutrinos. As a result, we are able to relate the axion parameters, including the axion decay constant, to the neutrino parameters within this DM system. The model incorporates a variety of DM creation mechanisms such as the axion production resulting from both the alignment mismatch and the decay of topological defects. In addition, it also includes sterile-neutrino creation via both the resonant and non-resonant mechanisms as well as a more recently proposed model involving CPT symmetry. Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To accomplish this goal, we introduce a novel approach, termed TuRaN, which utilizes a lower supply voltage than recommended to cause SRAM access failures, then employs a high-throughput entropy extraction circuit to analyze these faults. TuRaN achieves an enhanced throughput of up to 270 Mbps through the concurrent analysis of four SRAM faults generated by a single clock period, thus surpassing prior SRAM-based TRNGs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that TuRaN retains an entropy amount of at least 7.65 bits per cycle as evidenced by the randomness testing performed using the NIST STMs suite and the die-side EM testing method for statistical analysis. In addition to being designed for random number generation, we show that TuRaN can also be employed as a hardware-based failure detection and recovery mechanism. Consequently, we conclude that TuRaN represents an efficient solution for future Internet of Things devices. In order to evaluate the performance of TuRaN in an actual setting, an SPW FPGA prototyping board was utilized, resulting in an observed throughput of 24.416 Mbps and an increased latency of 10 microseconds. We estimate that TuRaN can generate as many as 3,000 million random numbers prior to requiring the re-initialization of the SRAM array. As a result, we are confident that TuRaN presents an attractive option for the random number requirements of various IoT applications. The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality, the Feynman integrands are simplified to a form that only captures physical information, resulting in a causal representation. In this discussion, we explore the application of all-loop causal representation to describe multi-loop Feynman integrands, which can be characterized by loop topological features and connections. To address concerns regarding numerical stability in loop-tree duality-based calculations, we examine case studies involving numerical evaluations of planar and non-planar two-loop triangles under varying kinematic conditions. Our research suggests that the application of loop-tree duality is not only feasible but also highly efficient, offering a significant advantage in computational performance. Furthermore, we find that this method can be easily extended to complex loop topologies involving multiple branches, which can be reduced to a causal representation through a systematic procedure. Notably, our findings for a double-triangle scenario reveal a direct correlation between physical phase space points, causing fluctuations in the amplitude's absolute value and sign. Building upon this understanding, we propose a threshold-based strategy for identifying and eliminating numerical instability. Finally, we successfully integrate our approach into a publicly available code to facilitate loop-tree duality-based calculations, which can be readily adopted by researchers for a wide array of multi-loop processes. Our code is now accessible through the following repository: https://github.com/loop-tree-duality/LTDTree/tree/tree-tree-duality. Our research is further documented in two accompanying papers: 'Numerical stability in loop-tree duality calculations' and 'Causal representations for multi-loop amplitudes - Extension to complex scenarios'. These documents can be found at the following links: arXiv:2101.00113 and arXiv:2102.01369, respectively. Additionally, a presentation and a technical report are available for review at the following locations: presentation: https://arxiv.org/es/docs/pdf/2102.01369.pdf and technical report: https://arxiv.org/es/docs/pdf/2102.01370.pdf. Both documents contain a detailed summary of our research for the benefit of broader audiences. Lastly, our code is also documented in the following repository: https://github.com/loop-tree-duality/LTDTree/tree/LTDTree-document. We welcome researchers to contribute to our code by incorporating their own implementations of various numerical techniques into the repository: https://github.com/Contributing-to-LTD

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous work done on Sturm-Liouville operators by renowned mathematicians. A related theory involving the CMV matrix already addressed this topic, yet our approach is unique as it focuses specifically on the mentioned quantum walks and also yields valuable properties of Green functions. These properties enable us to derive a precise formula for a positive-matrix-valued measure, ultimately allowing for a direct computation of the spectral measure in a particular model known as the two-phase model. Furthermore, this study also explores potential applications of the eigenfunction expansions in both the two-phase model and another type of model characterized by almost-periodic potentials. Specifically, we examine the two-phase model to derive a formula for a positive-matrix-valued measure, whereas for the almost-periodic model, we investigate certain aspects and find some accompanying conditions of the potential. To conclude, we take the almost-periodic model as an example to demonstrate how eigenfunction expansions can be used to study long-term behaviors of associated quantum walks, such as asymptotic distribution of spectral measures and limiting correlation coefficients. Some of the findings we present are novel and have yet to be shared with the mathematical community. Furthermore, our proof methods are notably different from those in the mentioned CMV matrix work and therefore contribute uniquely to the field. Lastly, our work is also partially related to another significant paper published by well-respected experts in the field of one-dimensional quantum walks. A key distinction between our study and that paper lies in the origin and scope of the investigated eigenfunction expansions, with the almost-periodic model being an added focus area for our research. A key non-trivial lemma that we developed in the process of our research will also bear importance as it addresses an accompanying condition of the potential associated with the almost-periodic model, thus contributing valuable insights to the study of one-dimensional quantum walks. A further extension of this criterion may also hold promise for being applied to theories beyond those discussed here. Conversely, certain closed-form solutions to quantum walks can potentially serve as useful test cases for validating accuracy of numerical approximations employed in field studies. A few such examples may also be found included in the paper. A key point to note is that our study is not an exhaustive research in its own right but rather contributes a vital missing piece to the existing theory on one-dimensional quantum walks, thus helping to bridge the existing gap between existing research and the area of long-term behavior study in quantum walks.

Ultimately, the $q$-deformation's capacity to supercede traditional scaling limitations holds promising potential for optomechanical systems, empowering innovations in optical technology. In photochemical aerosol dynamics, particles are produced through the interaction of gases with the atmosphere, whereas in nucleation, particles emerge from the atmosphere itself. Research into this process is ongoing, with various factors contributing to its complexity, including the involvement of numerous species and variables. In this study, the principles of classical nucleation theory are applied to the most prominent non-thermal aerosol production mechanism, binuclear pathway hydrohalide nucleation, allowing for an evaluation of existing simulations and future research directions. By doing so, it becomes evident that further research is necessary to fully grasp the mechanisms of non-thermal aerosol dynamics. Nonetheless, significant advancements have been made in understanding the binuclear pathway, and current knowledge is sufficient for incorporation into models used to predict atmospheric phenomena. In fact, existing simulations already incorporate various parameterizations that have successfully explained many of the observed characteristics of polar stratospheric cloud formations. Ultimately, the evaluation process highlights the potential of nucleation research to contribute to improvements in stratospheric jet and circulation perturbations caused by Antarctic cold air outbreaks, which could be facilitated by parameterizing nucleation in models used to predict these weather patterns. By doing so, it may be possible to improve weather forecasts by incorporating nucleation processes, thereby potentially enhancing climate model accuracy as well. We establish the definitions for a compact perception pair, compactifying a perception pair, and compactifying a space of operators invariant under group actions and non-expansive in nature. It's proven that every perception pair with measurements from a totally bounded measurement space and bounded self-maps on a group action can be isometrically embedded within a compact perception pair. Additionally, it's found that the closure of the space of non-expansive group action invariant operators contains the space of compact operators, providing non-examples for metric generalizations of known statements in Hilbert spaces. Moreover, new results in Hilbert spaces, such as characterization of compact perception pairs, and isometric embeddings of non-compact groups into compact groups, are derived as special cases. Finally, dimensions of compact perception pairs are investigated. Our study offers insights into the geometry of operator spaces, including those with group action invariance. In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task, given that many conventional methods are unsuitable for their inherent complexity. Our research introduces a concept called geometric complexity, quantifying the variability of model functions using a discrete Dirichlet energy metric. By combining theoretical analysis with empirical evidence, we demonstrate that several widespread training heuristics, such as parameter and spectral regularization, as well as parameter initialization techniques, serve to control geometric complexity. Furthermore, we show that geometric complexity offers a coherent framework for understanding the effects of various training hyperparameters on the performance of deep learning models. Our work is the first to provide a theoretically robust connection between the behavior of deep learning models and a recognized mathematical concept. Our research suggests that controlling geometric complexity may serve as an effective way to develop generalizable deep learning models. A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security, resulting in the entanglement-breaking channel without being detected by the users. Our findings suggest that randomizing the source phase to a limited degree may not be sufficient to safeguard phase-encoding QKD systems using weak coherent states. Our study also presents a viable attack on phase-encoded non-orthonormal states, which cannot be defeated through phase randomness, and finally offers a successful hybrid measurement attack on BB84 encoded states without requiring the identification of the encoding states. Our proposed attacks require minimal resources, are easy to implement, and could potentially be used in the development of a realistic quantum hacking attack. Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. Our research aims to explore the influence of a pretraining corpus's origin and size on the performance of a Korean-centric model. Notably, we discovered four crucial findings: Firstly, a pretraining corpus's domain significantly affects the model's ability to learn in-context. Conversely, a pretraining corpus's size doesn't guarantee in-context learning to emerge. Furthermore, a pretraining corpus composed of multiple domains may facilitate the development of in-context learning, even when each domain doesn't result in in-context learning alone. Lastly, a pretraining corpus related to a downstream task may not always ensure a high in-context learning performance for that specific task, especially when it comes to the few-shot setting, and that language modeling performance and in-context learning do not always correlate as one might expect. Our research offers a deeper comprehension of the intricate relationship between pretraining and in-context learning, and we hope that our findings will guide the development of tailored strategies to induce in-context learning in LLMs. Our source code and datasets can be accessed at https://github.com/NoNoNoNoNo/ICL_Ko. The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of training data into acoustic units for synthesis. This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. The transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel-consonant units, while steady-states include sonorants and fricatives. The speech signal is first segmented into CVC-like units based on a short-term energy contour and then grouped using graph clustering. The clustered units are initialized to include transient onset and decays, and steady-state rhyme components, and are subsequently rearranged into acoustic units in an HMM-GMM framework. The AU sequences are used to perform recognition and modeling, and the generated speech samples are evaluated using the short-term overlap error rate and the utterance distortion measure. The results suggest that the proposed units can be utilized effectively in zero-speech synthesis systems. The study further examines the performance of various acoustic unit segmentation algorithms and their impact on synthesis quality, and evaluates the utility of additional data and acoustic modeling capabilities in improving zero-speech synthesis quality. The results suggest that both data augmentation and acoustic modeling can contribute to improved synthesis quality in zero-speech synthesis systems. The output of this research is a speech system with approximately 200 acoustic units per speaker, and speech samples can be accessed through a downloadable package at the following site: https://speechresearch.github.io/Zerospeech2019/index.html. Additionally, the site provides information on the required software and programming environments for replication of the study's results. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across preceding stages, thus yielding better performance, faster solution times, and more interpretable outcomes. Our planner was thoroughly tested on a 10 kg humanoid robot and achieved a substantial reduction in processing time, down from minutes to just milliseconds, with minimal performance losses. Moreover, experiments on a 6DOF robotic arm verified the versatility of our methodology, yielding a substantial decrease in computation time while maintaining trajectory quality. Crucially, our framework yielded real-time motion plans that could be executed successfully on both robots. Although initially developed for walking tasks, our method demonstrates broad applicability to a range of hybrid locomotion strategies and generic multi-limbed robot movements. We have developed two overarching methods to quantify the manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum resource limitations.
Initially, we formulated a fundamental criterion for achieving a physical transformation between quantum states using a previously introduced resource metric.
This approach led to the discovery that one method to determine the metric's value is by finding the minimum error probability in a dichotomic resource-preserving protocol.
Building on this, we presented a unified framework for calculating error probabilities in resource-preserving protocols constrained by specific quantum limitations known as one- and two-qubit channels.
This approach proved successful in determining the metric for hyperdistillation of entanglement, resulting in a previously undiscovered connection between entanglement hyperdistillation and error-free transformation of entangled states.
Furthermore, we found that the error probability in the hyperdistillation protocol is dominated by the first excited state of the resulting Hamiltonian, which in turn enabled us to apply tools from classical statistical physics to analyze the asymptotic behavior of the protocol.
This approach resulted in a previously unforeseen correlation between hyperdistillation and thermodynamic systems, where the entanglement gap is related to the heat capacity but with a sign reversal.
Ultimately, we applied the developed methods to study the probabilistic manipulation of log-diclonic resources, which corresponds to entanglement distillation across different product spaces, yielding an insightful discovery that the error probability in log-diclonic resource manipulation is directly proportional to the log-diclonic entropy of the resource. This study further broadens the understanding of the connection between entropy and error probabilities in the context of quantum resource theories. 
Additionally, we have made the source code available at https://github.com/andressena/hyperdistillation. Currently, the repository does not support the analysis of log-diclonic resources, but it can be modified to include such calculations. Moreover, the code has been used to verify the previously published results in the field of hyperdistillation and resource theories, which are detailed in the document.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. Initially, we transform the original robust optimization problem into a more manageable form and employ an approximate soft-max function to facilitate the calculation of an equilibrium solution via Nash equilibrium principles. Subsequently, we develop an innovative solution strategy, known as DR-DSGD, which is a decentralized stochastic gradient descent algorithm capable of handling exogenous and endogenous data distribution shifts. DR-DSGD outperforms its traditional counterpart DSGD in communication efficiency, with an advancement rate of o(1/√K), where K denotes the number of local iterations. Furthermore, DR-DSGD surpasses the existing robust optimization solution under the assumption of known $\gamma$ with an convergence rate of o(1/√K), thus bridging the gap between robust optimization and online learning results. Lastly, we present experimental findings that demonstrate the DR-DSGD algorithm's efficacy in tackling distributionally robust learning challenges within decentralized networks. We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue, allowing the correction of velocity-based models to match dipole-based models and guarantee gauge invariance. The proposed method provides a reliable way to construct accurate TB models for describing strong light-matter interactions, especially beneficial for large-scale simulations of photonic systems. The approach may also be applied to the reformulation of spin-orbit coupling in solid-state systems. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential of TB models to describe not only linear responses but also strong excitations within accurate first-principle frameworks. This extends the scope of efficient computation from linear to nonlinear photonic phenomena. The application of our approach to describe multi-dimensional systems with complex band structures enables the precise prediction of electromagnetic interactions at both the linear and strong excitation levels. To verify our methodology, we performed a thorough convergence test of electromagnetic interactions against first-principle simulations on paradigm materials, involving both 2D and 3D cases. The results show that our TB models can accurately reproduce both linear and strong excitations within an accurately scaled magnetic vector potential, consistent with first-principle theory. Furthermore, we utilized TB models to derive explicit expressions for diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in solid-state materials. The obtained expressions confirm the compensation issue present in velocity-based models, highlighting their shortcoming. To address nonlocal effects in light-matter interactions from a theoretical standpoint, we evaluated the impact of wave-vector-dependent matrix elements of the change in the momentum operator. The analysis reveals that nonlocality introduces significant variations in the diamagnetic current but merely adjusts the paramagnetic current without eliminating the issue of compensation. This approach simplifies complex trust region implementations for parameters with varying scales. A new statistical method is developed for basket trials to assess the effectiveness of a new treatment in multiple patient subgroups under one protocol. This approach uses Bayesian statistics to optimize sample size and allows information sharing between groups. We develop formulas to ensure each subgroup trial meets specified criteria for power and reliability. For subgroups with prior beliefs, we calculate the required sample size for the new trial based on the prior and desired overall reliability. For subgroups without prior beliefs, we determine the required sample size as a function of the other groups' prior distributions and desired overall reliability. We apply this framework to three types of basket trials: those investigating a single patient subgroup, multiple patient subgroups with a treatment comparison, and one with a control group and treatment comparison. We also assess the performance of this method in scenarios where the prior assumptions are incorrect. A retrospective analysis of a real-world basket trial demonstrates the approach's applicability and effectiveness. We find our method requires significantly fewer trial participants than traditional frequentist methods to achieve the same level of reliability for detecting treatment differences. For the actual trial, we estimate a 25-50% reduction in participants is possible. This method is now available in the R package Baskett. An example trial data set can be found on our repository's wiki page. We invite users to share feedback and experience with this method. We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based registration methods, PRNet employs deep networks to overcome complex alignment and correspondence issues. Unlike existing methods that require a fully observable shape, PRNet is suited for partial-to-partial registration tasks, surpassing traditional and deep learning-based approaches on synthetic datasets. Our approach features self-supervised learning of a suitable geometric representation and a keypoint detector for common point identification, alongside learned keypoint-to-keypoint correspondences. Experimental results demonstrate PRNet's ability to consistently detect and match keypoints across varying views and objects, while the geometric representation is refined to accommodate incomplete data. Additionally, PRNet's keypoint detector outperforms other deep learning-based methods in semantic segmentation tasks, and is used as a starting point for pose estimation and object detection methods. Furthermore, PRNet's flexibility is showcased through its successful application to registering autonomous driving lidar scans in real-world environments. A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree by finding the least integer c such that the quotient $G/\gamma_{c+1}(G)$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property. In this research, we derive the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of Generalized Solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $\Gamma_n$ and explicitly calculate the lower central series for $\Gamma_n$. Additionally, we decompose the nilpotent quotients $\Gamma_{n,c}$ as semidirect products of finitely generated abelian groups, and we identify which invertible matrices can be extended into automorphisms of $\Gamma_{n,c}$. Furthermore, we establish the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of $\Gamma_n$ based on these decompositions and provide a straightforward method to calculate the conjugacy classes of nilpotent $\Gamma_{n,c}$. In the process, we also identify the nilpotent conjugacy classes within $\Gamma_n$. In contrast, we show that twisted conjugacy classes in $\Gamma_n$ do not necessarily have nilpotent closures. Also, we identify specific automorphisms of $\Lambda_{n}$ and demonstrate that the nilpotent quotients $\Lambda_{n,c}$ can be expressed as direct products of finitely generated abelian groups, and we determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of $\Lambda_n$. Lastly, we outline potential implications of our research on the twisted conjugacy classes within $BSM_n$. This study contains an appendix collecting background information on nilpotent groups. In particular, we refer to the collected information as 'blue material' that is not essential for understanding the primary results outlined in the paper. In this blue material, we prove that finite nilpotent groups possess the $R_\infty$ property, we establish the relationship between $R_\infty$-nilpotent groups and 2-nilpotent groups, and we demonstrate the $R_\infty$-nilpotent quotient degree for solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $BSM_n$. Additionally, we provide a Nilpotent Group Property Checker, an algorithm written in Python for verifying if a group is nilpotent. This checker is readily accessible at https://github

Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without manual labels presents significant difficulties due to the considerable time and resources needed for annotation. Current techniques typically address a novel modality either by fine-tuning a pre-trained model or by dividing the tasks into independent image translation and segmentation steps. In this study, a Cyclic Segmentation Generative Adversarial Network is proposed that simultaneously performs domain adaptation and object identification within a single unified structure. Apart from standard CycleGAN losses and supervisory signals from labeled source domain images, additional self-supervised objectives focusing on the segmentation are employed to optimize performance utilizing target domain images devoid of manual labels. Evaluations on the segmentation of neuronal nuclei using EM images and unlabeled ExM images confirm that the proposed CySGAN outperforms not only pre-trained models but also methods that execute domain adaptation followed by segmentation in sequence. In turn, this will contribute to assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass star systems by means of photometric light curves, as white-light stellar flares may be confused with astrophysical signals indicative of extraterrestrial life. In this research paper, we present the most recent findings from our ongoing analysis of white-light stellar flares, incorporating data from ASAS-SN and other resources, including a new dataset derived from the Tailored Survey for Active stars using TESS (ASTELES), an on-going collaboration including multiple researchers from various universities. We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the deformation theory of instantons can be equivalent to the cohomology theory defined by these spinors and Dirac operators, specifically with coefficients in the adjoint representation. The resulting Serre-type results provide insights into the existence and uniqueness of non-zero G2-instantons. Additionally, our theory expands on earlier work by Vector Bundles on almost G2-manifolds by providing precise criteria for the existence of non-zero G2-instantons. The work specifically looks at 7-manifolds that are fiber bundles over 6-manifolds with specific properties, and proves that deformed G2-instantons may arise from restrictions of instantons on the total space of these fiber bundles. The publication is accompanied by concrete applications, including the determination of the deformation cohomology classes for Calabi-Yau 3-folds and certain 7-manifolds based on homogeneous spaces. completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low rank model that
is both computationally efficient and easily interpretable. We draw inspiration

this concept into a framework that identifies recurring templates across time
and assigns adjustable time adjustments to accommodate deviations from these
templates. We address two key challenges associated with time-based completion:

Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). A critical examination of Arthur's comparison reveals significant misunderstandings regarding the nature of the continuous, polygons with an infinite number of sides, and infinitesimal quantities. Additionally, claims by Rabouin and Arthur, suggesting that Leibniz considered infinite quantities to be inherently contradictory, rely on an incorrect blending of Leibnizian concepts of bounded and unbounded infinites - a distinction previously noted by early Knobloch. Instead, a framework developed by Robinson may provide a more accurate account of Leibnizian calculus, which can be formalized using a conservative axiomatic system for infinitesimal analysis called SPOT. This formalisation covers concepts such as the bounded/unbounded distinction, a distinction between quantities that can or cannot be assigned to geometric objects, a general concept of monad, and a distinctive relationship between physical objects and their corresponding quantities. As such, the Robinson-based SPOT, or at least its key concepts, appears to be a more accurate representation of Leibnizian calculus, which can be distinguished from other approaches such as the Weierstrassian and Arthur-Kock-Bell approaches. This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered. This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation technique, with a focus on minimizing the number of computations required to recover the solution. This is crucial because it depends on parameters like the degrees and size of the linear system as well as the error rate. As part of an ongoing series on solving polynomial linear systems with errors, we build on our previous findings, including a proof from [Guerrini et al., Proc. ISIT'19], that a lower bound on evaluations can be achieved when errors are randomly distributed, even for large error rates. This paper follows up on [Kaltofen et al., Proc. ISSAC'17] by refining those results in two key ways: introducing a new evaluation bound with reduced dependence on system parameters, and incorporating an early termination mechanism to prevent unnecessary computations arising from overestimating the system parameters or the error bound, both of which were concepts introduced in [Cabay, Proc. SYMSAC'71]. Alongside this, we present an alternative proof that confirms an existing hypothesis on evaluation bounds with errors, first proposed in [Averbuch et al., Proc. ISSAC'16]. This proof is significantly simplified and verifies the existing conjecture. Additionally, we provide an adaptation of our evaluation bound with an early termination mechanism and demonstrate that this can often result in a substantial reduction in computations required to solve polynomial linear systems, even when the system parameters are known exactly and there is no error. This is made possible by introducing a new criterion for terminating the recovery process, one that is more conservative than existing approaches and accommodates errors in polynomial coefficients, a concept explored further in [Kaltofen et al., Proc. ISSAC'17]. Comprehensive numerical experiments are presented to illustrate these findings. In ultrastrong light-matter coupling regimes, giant Stokes and anti-Stokes photon emissions exhibit symmetry related to parity, when emitted in pairs from two identical qubits. By introducing a small asymmetry, this symmetry can be broken, resulting in the exclusive emission of giant Stokes photons. Building on recent experiments, our work develops a theoretical framework to achieve this breakage through an applied asymmetrical voltage. Additionally, by leveraging ultrastrong coupling cavities with large electromagnetic fields, our findings predict a high probability of emitting a giant anti-Stokes photon, which could lead to the generation of squeezed vacuum states. This research potentially opens doors to advancements in quantum optics, particularly with platforms like superconducting cavities and nanocavities. Furthermore, the predicted phenomena have the potential to be implemented in remote Bell-state sharing based on quantum emission, thus contributing to advancements in entanglement-assisted cryptography. Additionally, the proposed concept may find an exit path from the restriction of coherent emission associated with ultrastrong coupling, which could be beneficial for fundamental research and technological innovations. Lastly, our study extends its reach to other technologies such as circuit quantum electrodynamics, nanomechanical cavities, and metamaterial-based devices, which are also capable of embracing the ultrastrong coupling regime. Some of these applications, particularly those related to cryptography and quantum processing, are yet to be fully explored and may require an accelerated understanding of the hybrid quantum electromagnetic driver, as predicted by our theoretical analysis. Lastly, our research revisits the fundamental concept of vacuum-field correlation, which is pivotal in the ultrastrong coupling regime, thereby contributing to future advancements in quantum electromagnetics. Over four years, starting from 2017, a rigorous testing program for nearly 20,000 20-inch PMTs was carried out by the JUNO team. By examining these PMTs and implementing a series of stringent requirements, the experiment's investigators were able to verify the high quality of the instruments and achieve the desired standards needed for the experiment's success. This paper specifically focuses on the detailed evaluation of the 20-inch PMTs used in the JUNO experiment. It discusses the testing procedures, tools, and results utilized to evaluate these PMTs and their performance during the experiment. With its large-scale and prolonged testing program, the JUNO team was able to thoroughly evaluate the 20-inch PMTs used in the experiment and establish a set of rigorous standards for similar large-scale neutrino experiments. This paper presents the results of these tests and demonstrates the high quality of the 20-inch PMTs used in the JUNO experiment. Additionally, the study discusses the characteristics of the worst-performing PMTs and potential connections to the manufacturing processes, as well as the reflections and lessons learned from the testing program and its findings. In practical scenarios like power consumption forecasting and air quality analysis, long sequence time-series forecasting (LSTF) is indispensable. The complexity of multidimensional time series data presents significant model demands, necessitating precise representation of long-term input-output relationships and relationships across multiple dimensions. Recent work employing the Informer model based on the Transformer architecture has yielded impressive results for long-term forecasting, yet it falls short in addressing dimensional interactions. Our enhancement of the Informer addresses these limitations in multidimensional forecasting through several key approaches. Firstly, we incorporate an adaptive graph neural network to identify dimensional connections often hidden in time series data. Secondly, we incorporate adaptive graph convolutional networks into spatio-temporal prediction models to capture dimensional interactions. Our empirical evaluations with diverse datasets have revealed that the integration significantly elevates predictive accuracy by around 10%. Notably, our model is particularly adept at forecasting long sequences in high-dimensional data sets. As such, we present an informed version of the model, denoted Informed, as a premier choice for long sequence time-series forecasting. Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current systems relying on refractors or Schmidt cameras are ineffective due to off-axis issues and circular fields of view. We present a novel design for an Atmospheric Dispersion Corrector using a flat detector array, aiming to address these problems. By employing a flat, anisotropic detector array is possible, allowing for a more compact ADC design. We present the details of our design, along with the demonstration of a proof-of-concept prototype utilizing a CCD array and a flat, anisotropic optical setup. This prototype successfully corrected dispersion in observations made off-axis, showcasing its potential for use in telescopes. We share the results of our test, including images, before outlining possible improvements for future applications. Ultimately, this ADC design presents an economical and viable solution for correcting atmospheric dispersion in telescopes. We see this as an opportunity for an innovative and important innovation in astronomical instrumentation. Upon further refinement, this technology can be utilized in existing telescopes to correct dispersion, as well as in new projects such as surveys, observatories, and networks of small radiotelescopes. Research is currently in progress to optimize this design for the use in small radio telescopes, specifically the ARRA large array. Further information can be found at https://adc-instruments.github.io. Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform. We observed a substantial improvement in click-through rate, with PILE outperforming single-teacher baselines by approximately 0.9%. Additionally, the top model constructed using PILE achieved relative improvements of 4.3% and 6.3% over single-teacher models when using 20% and 10% of the original label data, respectively. This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A characterization of BPC's solution set, including uniqueness and sparse solutions, is established in terms of a Toeplitz matrix. The uniqueness and characteristics of BPC's solution rely on the eigenvalue properties of this matrix. The solutions range from a single, weighted Dirac mass for certain conditions to infinitely many Dirac masses in other cases. The number of Dirac masses in each case is influenced by the rank of a positive or negative semi-definite matrix. The positive or negative definiteness of the matrix also determines the weights of the Dirac masses as either nonnegative or nonpositive, respectively. The lower bound for Kc, which ensures a solution exists, is derived. Additionally, the paper provides a method for constructing a solution for every cutoff frequency Kc. The approach combines iterative water-filling and a limited-memory BFGS algorithm. The majority of the paper focuses on recovering one-dimensional Radon measures, but the methods are easily extended to recovering Gaussian measures, which includes the recovery of probability measures when the Fourier coefficients are unrestricted. The paper's results and theories are supported by numerous numerical experiments. The numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method, BPC, performs well even at low frequencies and compare its convergence to other approaches. The additional experiments in this paper analyze the computational efficiency of BPC. The findings show BPC's dependence on a trade-off between solution accuracy and computational efficiency. The paper then introduces a way to efficiently compute BPC's solution when it exists and an alternative approach, BPC-f, which is computationally efficient but may not always yield a solution. The ideas and techniques presented in this paper are further tested in recovering Radon measures on higher-dimensional spaces in an accompanying paper. To recover measures on higher-dimensional spaces, the Fourier coefficients are restricted, effectively lowering their dimensionality, which enables the application of the methods in this paper. The resulting approach in the companion paper relies on a generalized version of the theories established here. A final set of experiments in this paper compares recovering Radon measures on one-dimensional and higher-dimensional spaces through the restricted Fourier coefficients. The resulting method is then extended to recovering Radon measures on the entire space from their Fourier coefficients through a regularization technique. P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium translates syntax into switch-dependent code, but this process can be slow due to static analysis and code generation. Researchers have previously identified several areas for improving the consortium's compiler, but the effectiveness of these improvements has not been thoroughly tested. A recent version of the compiler, version 16, provides a number of developments not listed in the identified areas. In the case of multiple targeted improvements, the new compiler offers comparable performance to existing systems, such as faster parsing times and reduced memory usage, while also providing new features, including the ability to translate P4 programs more quickly and efficiently, allowing for automatic detection and prevention of common programming errors. New data structures, like hash tables, can now be implemented on switches with limited memory, and a new runtime system streamlines execution time and reduces memory usage in the consortium's compiler. A detailed analysis of each improvement is provided, along with real-world examples, benchmarks, and actual switch measurements, demonstrating that these enhancements will be beneficial to a wide range of P4 developers. All new research findings are open-source and can be accessed at [github.com/ToToOur/syntastic-p4](http://github.com/ToToOur/syntastic-p4). A detailed overview of the consortium's compiler is provided in Section II, while our new research findings are described in III, IV, V, and concluded in VI. The paper concludes with future work outlined in VII, followed by conclusions in VIII. The work presented here has been formally submitted to the P4 Symposium 2022. In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that elevate the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields across curved surfaces in two-dimensional environments. One method enhances the transported field by projecting it onto a higher-order function space before solving the transport equation. In contrast, the other method utilizes a mixed finite element approach to concurrently solve for both the transported field and its vorticity, introducing a stabilisation strategy via a Streamline Upwind Petrov-Galerkin method. These schemes are validated and their performance compared in a series of numerical experiments involving both specially designed and standard rotating shallow-water models. Overall, the proposed methods demonstrate the ability to accurately transport vector-valued fields over long distances, even in the presence of strong directional bias and low spatial resolution. This research presents viable options for solving vector transport equations in applications spanning meteorology, oceanography, and hydrodynamics. It also paves the way for their extension to three-dimensional systems and the solution of Navier-Stokes equations. Additional future work is suggested to optimise and adapt these methods for convection-dominated scenarios. All numerical code used in this research is openly accessible on the Git hub repository https://github.com/JoelFosterUK/Transport_Schemes_for_Vectors. To facilitate the implementation of these methods, a revised version of the MOONS code with integrated transportation capabilities is also provided at https://git.ing-INF UniTOit.it/JoelFosterUK/MOONS/-/tree/transport. In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems. A crucial aspect that distinguishes HBVMs from other methods is their ability to be formulated with more stages than degrees of freedom, and to retain their energy-conserving properties even when formulated with an arbitrary number of stages. This characteristic makes HBVMs highly versatile. To further illustrate their value, we demonstrate their implementation in two specific applications - the Euler-Lagrange equations and the spin dynamics of a heavy rigid body. Firstly, the Euler-Lagrange equations are used to model various physical phenomena, such as the motion of a heavy rigid body, to which we apply an adapted version of the HBVM method to verify its ability to conserve energy and angular momentum. Secondly, we utilize the spin dynamics of a heavy rigid body to illustrate the ability of the HBVM method to accurately track tiny changes in angular movement over extended time frames. By confirming the accuracy and reliability of the HBVM method in these applications, we further establish its utility as a dependable tool for applying the Euler-Lagrange equations to the solution of various physical dynamics problems. Furthermore, to confirm the reliability of the HBVM method in situations involving rapid changes in momentum, we compared its results with those obtained through the application of the variational integrator method. By verifying and validating the accuracy of the variational integrator method in such scenarios, we substantially extend its established domain of utility. Ultimately, the confirmed superiority of the HBVM method and the validated accuracy of the variational integrator method make them both dependable tools for use in a broad range of applications involving the solution of variational problems. Furthermore, to further establish their reliability and precision, we observed that the HBVM method, much like the variational integrator method, exhibits properties of stability in the sense of Liapunov, and is thus capable of providing stable solutions to problems involving the spin dynamics of rigid bodies, even at extended time scales. These rigorous mathematical findings significantly extend the established theoretical bases for both methods, and provide a solid foundation for future work in this area. We introduce an innovative approach called local critic networks, which utilize segment-level feedback for smart neural pruning. By grouping neurons into logical clusters, we apply optimal filtering techniques to refine the selection process, ensuring high effectiveness with minimal computational overhead. A layer-group update method utilizes a collection of local critic networks to provide optimal training directions, while a segment-level evolution strategy optimizes the group structure itself. The integration of these two mechanisms enables smart neural pruning with enhanced accuracy and efficiency. Moreover, we address the challenge of declining performance after pruning by developing a multi-stage training scheme, which restores accuracy through progressive retraining. Thorough experiments validate the outstanding performance of our approach on various datasets and architectures. Notably, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art models by 1.38% and 1.13% on the CIFAR10 and ImageNet datasets, respectively. Comprehensive source code is available at https://github.com/Atteno/LCN.git.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart. In this research, a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system is analyzed where the non-dissipative boundaries initially deviate from Wada's characteristics, changing topologically. Focusing on the effects of dissipation, this study investigates how this system alters when weak dissipation lowers the system's energy below its critical value. Interestingly, this investigation finds that non-Wada basins transition into partially Wada basins under such weak dissipation. Moreover, numerical results indicate the emergence of Wada points on the boundaries of these basins in three-dimensional systems. Ultimately, this research reveals that Wada basins in three-dimensional systems exhibit increased stability when subjected to low levels of dissipation. Nonetheless, their boundaries remain highly complex with Wada points. Importantly, this research finds that Wada basins in three-dimensional systems can survive below the critical energy value that causes them to shrink or disappear. Interestingly, this behavior also occurs in a ladder-shaped artificial three-dimensional system that lacks any inherent physical significance, yet displays Wada basins. In conclusion, this research confirms that Wada basins in three-dimensional systems exhibit improved resilience when subjected to low levels of dissipation and can survive significant decreases in energy levels. Moreover, this research also showcases the existence of Wada basins in artificially constructed three-dimensional systems characterized by Wada points on their boundaries. Overall, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of Wada basins in three-dimensional systems and their intriguing properties. Furthermore, this research also initiates an exploration of Wada basins in systems that lack analytical solutions through the use of numerical methods such as those found in quantum many-body systems. Lastly, this research shows that Wada basins can be detected accurately using a criterion that measures their volume, thus confirming their existence in three-dimensional systems. In addition, this research discovered that Wada basins in three-dimensional systems possess a unique characteristic known as "winding number," unparalleled in two-dimensional systems. In conclusion, this research made a significant breakthrough in three-dimensional systems by confirming the existence of Wada basins characterized by Wada points and defined by their winding numbers, thus expanding our understanding of Wada basins beyond their application in two-dimensional systems and promising more opportunities for their detection in future studies. Additionally, this research also established a new theory stating that Wada basins can be detected based on their volume, thus promoting the use of this research in quantum many-body systems. Human action understanding in complex videos has far-reaching implications, 
which this study addresses by proposing the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN).
Compared to current deep learning-based methods, HAN stands out due to its
capacity for (1) extended temporal structure capture; (2) explicit modeling of 
temporal transitions between frames and segments, and (3) the ability to learn key 
regions in frames and temporal segments through its multi-step attention mechanism.
Evaluations on two benchmark datasets, UCF101-300CUB and Pennsylvania Human Action 
Dataset, demonstrate that HAN surpasses state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin.
Furthermore, the study conducts thorough ablation studies to reinforce the efficacy of its key components. 
As a result, the proposed model achieves state-of-the-art performance on these datasets without the use of external data. 
 Consequently, HAN emerges as a formidable model for understanding human action in complex videos. 
 Moreover, the study's success serves as a crucial benchmark for evaluating video temporal structure capture and temporal transition detection. 
 Ultimately, the study's code will be freely accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/IndigoTVC/HAN. 
 In addition, the study's 300CUB-pseudo-GT dataset will be also provided on https://github.com/IndigoTVC/300CUB-pseudo-GT.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes, confirming that the singularity in such black holes is hidden by an event horizon. The validity of this theory for near-extremal and extremal black holes is confirmed by analyzing their minimum function values after the scattering process. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions. Compared to alternative estimators, NS-based estimates show superior performance in terms of accuracy and stability. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/la-pm/nestented. Firstly, we introduce an adaptive, multi-scale NS method to estimate the entropy of a single distribution. We then extend this approach to calculate the mutual information between two distributions, either when both distributions are known, either when only the target distribution is known and we must approximate the reference distribution by clipping the tail of the actual distribution to the right and left. Numerical results confirm that this new estimator outperforms existing ones in terms of accuracy and stability. The proposed NS method is now implemented in Python and made available on https://github.com/la-pm/nesteded. Two new tools are introduced to visually assess the quality of NS-based estimates: a reliability plot can be used to evaluate the convergence of entropy or mutual information estimates as more NS iterations are performed; while a cumulative distribution function comparison plot allows us to visually assess the accuracy of a heavy-tailed approximation. These plots can serve as a useful guideline to adjust the NS parameters and improve the estimator's quality. Moreover, they can also be used to visually explain the behavior of an NS-based estimator when sampling data is collected from an actual distribution. By examining these plots, it is possible to identify both the sections of a distribution that are accurately reconstructed by NS and those areas that require further improvement. Cybersecurity has gained significant importance over recent years, with the detection of cyber threats emerging as a critical task due to the immense damage a single breach can inflict on companies. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved it, allowing high-quality classifiers to detect attacks efficiently; however, these classifiers demand substantial computing power or memory. The scenario presents a problem, particularly when these classifiers need to operate on low-resource devices or prevent performance overload on high-end devices. A novel solution to overcome this challenge is proposed by NBTree, a lightweight tree-based classifier capable of efficiently handling multi-dimensional data on resource constraints devices without sacrificing accuracy. The effectiveness of NBTree is evaluated against renowned deep learning models and a highly accurate, yet resource-hungry, detection tool named NetBLAST, showing that NBTree surpasses NetBLAST in terms of accuracy while requiring significantly less computational power, thus establishing it as a robust alternative for network anomaly detection in resource constraints environments. The development behind this work stems from the perception that a small cybersecurity breach can cause severe negative effects on companies, emphasizing the need for reliable and real-time anomaly detection tools. The effectiveness of our solution is further confirmed by comprehensive experiments conducted across diverse datasets, showing NBTree to be an efficient and accurate classifier that can efficiently detect attacks on various networks. The simplicity and efficacy of our proposed solution, along with the conducted experiments, suggest that NBTree can reliably substitute more complex classification systems, providing a more robust and efficient alternative to deep learning models in the context of network anomaly detection. The knowledge gained from this study can be applied to other domains experiencing similar classification challenges.
