a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to
the absence of clear analytical evidence. To address this concern, we developed a
method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing to quantify the
level of unfairness in a districting plan. Our results show the effectiveness of
this approach, particularly in a real-world application involving Texas, where a
faster alternative to traditional methods yielded fairer voting distributions and
allowed for the identification of biased districting plans. To date, this study
represents the first effort to utilize Bayesian techniques for the purpose of
detecting gerrymandering. Tutorials and additional information can be found at
https://osqithub.github.io/texas-districts/. Additionally, RepOSD software has
been utilized for data analysis and visualization at http://osqithub.github.io/ReOSD/.

A novel defect detection approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, which integrates Gabor and HOG to precisely locate defects. Since defects distort the fabric's uniform pattern orientation, this method leverages the direction awareness to effectively identify the defect region. Following the development of a directional descriptor, the proposed technique applies low-rank decomposition to differentiate the background from defect information within the fabric's image blocks. A nonconvex surrogate function and an alternative direction method of multipliers (ADMM) are utilized to improve the low-rank decomposition model's efficiency and computation speed. Ultimately, the sparse matrix-derived saliency map is segmented to pinpoint defect regions. Experimental findings demonstrate that this method outperforms existing techniques and successfully detects fabric defects. Additionally, the proposed approach exhibits better generalization and stability on testing datasets compared to model-free techniques. We provide a characterization of smooth quadrics based on the existence of full exceptional collections with a specific property, generalizing a previous result obtained by C. Vial for projective spaces. Additionally, this enables us to calculate the number of full exceptional collections of independent drifts on smooth quadrics, extending work by D. Ruberman and P. Gilmer, and also to classify full exceptional collections with a specific drift on singular quadrics, which allows further classification of full exceptional collections with zero drift on these varieties. Furthermore, this classification leads to a computation of the first cohomology space for the drifts of full exceptional collections on smooth quadrics. Lastly, based on the characteristics of full exceptional collections, we define and compute the first cohomology space for the drifts of all collections on smooth quadrics. Using category $\mathcal{D}^b(\mathrm{Coh}(X)))$, where $X$ is a smooth quadric, we also establish that the functorial properties of full exceptional collections allow for the classification of all full exceptional collections with a given Grothendieck-Serre trifle. Specifically, this has been determined for full exceptional collections with a zero drift on singular quadrics and for full exceptional collections with a zero drift on smooth quadrics, which we denote as $\mathrm{FS}^{\phi}_n$. By studying the characteristics of $\mathrm{FS}^{\phi}_n$, we are able to show that this full exceptional collection has a highly structured relationship, which we formally state as a theorem, which in turn allows for further mathematical discoveries regarding homology groups of certain triplets of points on a hyperplane within the quadric variety. Notably, this leads to the computation of homology groups of triplets of points that lie on a hyperplane within the quadric variety, which we denote as $\mathrm{H}_3(\mathrm{Coh}(X), n))$. Lastly, based on the characteristics of $\mathrm{HS}^{\phi}_n$, we also study and compute the first cohomology group for the drifts of all half-full exceptional collections with a given Grothendieck-Serre trifle, which we denote as $\mathrm{H}^1(\mathrm{Coh}^{\phi}_n, n))$. This area of study appears to be an underserved aspect of the mathematical field of study in varieties of quadrics. Consequently, the contributions presented within this thesis are essentially new and useful to the mathematical field of study

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
Our findings from extensive evaluations using both intelligent agents and high-throughput search reveal that:
the optimized platform maintains perfect correlation with the original game;
the increased speed enables successful agent discovery nearly ten times faster;
the enlarged action throughput expands the range of queries that agents can efficiently process, reaching rates of up to 100 questions per second. 
The significant boost in processing power provided by TextWorldExpress opens doors to groundbreaking, large-scale studies in natural language understanding, as well as in related fields like program synthesis and data-driven story generation. 
It also holds great promise for rapid development and testing of intelligent assistants in related areas, such as conversation and robotic forecasting systems. 
The platform, along with a full suite of tutorials and a powerful API, is now freely accessible at https://github.com/TWExpress/TextWorldExpress. 
A public leaderboard tracking submissions to TextWorldExpress challenges is found at https://twexpress.baiers.net/. 
Additional information is provided in our project overview video at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9pufOoGpHjY. 
Lastly, our research is partly presented in a conference paper and an accompanying workshop paper, both found at https://twexpress.baiers.net/paper/ and https://confat.com/i/iccve20.pdf, respectively.

A key concept called manipulability ellipsoids effectively encodes human pose data and task-dependent information, significantly contributing to teaching robots human-like motion through emulation. In robotics literature, there has been a recent shift towards transfer learning between robots. However, the transfer of this information from human to robot systems has been overlooked. This research aims to bridge this knowledge gap with a new method to transfer manipulability information from one robot to another with a different kinematic structure. Since these ellipsoids are based on symmetric positive-definite matrices, they can be treated as points on a specific geometric manifold. This work offers the first approach to transfer manipulability by leveraging the power of geometric manifold learning. Specifically, it utilizes a variational GAN that conditions the generator on the target robot's kinematic structure and enables the learning of an elliptical shape characteristic of the source robot's manipulability. Evaluations using a humanoid robot demonstrate successful learning of similar ellipsoidal shapes on diverse humanoid platforms are also presented. Ultimately, this method allows multiple robots to achieve similar task capabilities and shares knowledge across robot communities, enabling robotic cooperation and task transfer. Advancements in attosecond science hold great potential to unveil the core electronic behavior of matter, contingent on achieving two interconnected technological milestones linked to high-order harmonic generation sources. Firstly, achieving a higher photon flux would allow researchers to measure even the faintest electronic processes, while also attaining better spectral tunability would grant selectivity in targeting specific electronic transitions. Breakthroughs are made feasible by parametric waveform synthesis, giving scientists the capability to craft controllable, highly-tunable high-energy electric transients. Our findings demonstrate that by manipulating the waveform of the driving laser pulse via its relative phase and carrier-envelope phase, it's possible to exert fine-grained control over attosecond pulse characteristics. This innovation not only amplifies experimental possibilities in the realm of attosecond science, but also paves the way for a highly sophisticated, coherent manipulation of free-electron paths. Furthermore, we illustrate the promise of this approach by highlighting distinct signatures of inelastic light scattering associated with double core-level excitations in nitrogen molecules, which can be identified through their unique interactions with attosecond pulses modulated by phase and timing. These discoveries open up new avenues for fundamental research, while also presenting opportunities for advanced technological interventions. Ultimately, this study aims to inspire a more encompassing, wavefront-engineering based approach to attosecond science, where electronic transitions and ionization processes are deliberately shaped to their fullest extent. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the existence of solutions that exhibit maximal or minimal symmetry and are stable over all time. Notably, in the case where the domain is the entire space, we find that solutions with negative energy will collapse within a time frame not exceeding the initial energy's negative sign multiplied by the Euclidean space's radius. This result addresses a query posed by Keel and Koenig in 2006. Furthermore, by utilizing a variant of the molecular cluster expansion, we derive a stochastic representation for solutions under certain large-distance asymptotic conditions, thereby confirming that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse in an almost surely, positively scaled time frame. This analysis is further supported by a recent study by Burak Kaspi showing that solutions with negative energy will not collapse in the case of the focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space under certain constraints. Consequently, our findings present the limitations of our previous method while yielding new insights into Schrödinger equation solutions with negative energy. Finally, based on the principles of variational methods and the reparameterization of solutions, we investigate the existence of solutions that exhibit minimal or maximal symmetry under the influence of nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, demonstrating a wide range of new variational space options, including the construction of symmetric solutions through the application of the constrained optimization of energy functional over this space, and establishing their stability over all time through the application of a stability criterion previously established. This research also generalizes the findings of other studies on solutions with minimal or maximal symmetry, including those published by the researchers Weisshou and Zhang in 2018, Burak Kaspi in 2019, and the researchers Chen and Zhang in 2020. Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Despite achieving significant success across a wide array of differential equations, further improvements to computational efficiency are required for this approach. To address this need, enhancing training point generation is an important direction of investigation. Both adaptive and quasi-uniform sampling techniques have previously been explored, each showing benefits. To leverage these insights, we introduce Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation, which combines an adjustable nodal distribution method and a memory mechanism. We then conduct experiments on both linear and nonlinear PDEs, evaluating its accuracy and efficiency relative to traditional sampling methods. Our results indicate that RESANF can achieve accuracy equivalent to networks utilizing generated data through a uniform grid, all while significantly reducing the amount of data by almost three orders of magnitude. Consequently, RESANG offers a highly effective means of improving the efficiency of Physics-informed neural networks by optimizing the adoption of observed data and generated nodes. It has the added benefit of simplicity and ease of implementation. We hope that adopting RESANG will enable more robust and efficient neural network solutions to partial differential equations in the future. I explore a feasible method to investigate this at the Large Hadron Collider operating at sqrt(s) = 13 TeV, an equivalent increase in fixed-target energy of 40,000 times, with crucial implications for understanding the characteristics of cosmic ray showers. Additionally, I discuss how a modified LHC beam dump could serve as an effective tool to study this phenomenon, offering valuable insights into cosmic ray physics. It is anticipated that such research will contribute to a deeper comprehension of hadronic physics and open up novel avenues for experimental work. A specific experimental strategy is outlined to verify the production of positive charged hadrons over a broad pseudorapidity range (-3.8, -2.8, -1.3, -0.9, 0.9, 1.3, 2.8, 3.8) utilizing the LHC's cosmics, with an attached Roman pot to the beam dump that can be brought close to the primary vertex. This study seeks to enhance the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We critically examine the conventional graph convolution, comprising a KNN search and a multilayer perceptron. By dissecting its underlying mathematical operations, we arrive at two key insights for GCN optimization. Firstly, the 3D point cloud representation's geometric structure is efficiently propagated across the GCN through KNN search. This insight drives the simplification of multiple KNN searches within GCNs. Secondly, rearranging the sequence of feature aggregation and multilayer perceptron operations yields equivalent results. Based on these findings, we refine the computational procedure for GCNs. Experimental results demonstrate the optimized networks enjoy lower computational complexity, reduced memory usage, and accelerated inference speed while retaining comparable accuracy for point cloud learning. The source code will be publicly available at the GitHub repository: https://github.com/ofsoundof/EfficientGCN.git.

We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which uses fixed images in conceptual meaning but can take various forms visually. Unlike existing Trojan attacks, which embed inconsequential triggers in clean images, our method considers trigger images as full-resolution representations of meaningful object classes. As our backdoored classifier is designed to recognize the inherent concepts of trigger images rather than specific patterns, it can be triggered by semantically similar images with distinct appearances, making our attack more applicable and resilient to countermeasures in real-world scenarios. Our experiments show that even with limited Trojan patterns, our approach can adapt to new trigger images within the same category and evade sophisticated defense strategies effectively. Moreover, since our attack doesn't rely on innocent images, it can be implemented by anyone without needing a massive clean dataset. Our findings highlight the limitations of current defense techniques and suggest that adapting to semantic triggers might be more feasible and necessary for developing more durable against future attacks. In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited to incorporate the latest developments. A {\bf 56}, 97 (2020)) are considered to outline the pathway for enhancing low-energy astrophysical $S$-factor determinations via new Threshold Hand Mirror (THM) measurements. Several unresolved issues in carbon-carbon fusion are discussed, including the complex structure of carbon, the multiple possible orientations of the nuclei in collisions, and the diverse channels available during the fusion process. Despite significant advancements over the past five decades, determining the astrophysical $S$-factor with high precision at both low and high energies remains an ongoing challenge. Given the crucial role of this reaction in astrophysics, resolving this long-standing issue is essential for accurately quantifying key processes such as the growth of massive stellar cores and the creation of elements through supernova explosions. Therefore, pursuing novel experimental approaches like the THM technique, which enables the simultaneous measurement of both direct and reverse reactions at 180 degrees, may offer crucial insights to overcome the existing obstacles in carbon-carbon fusion research. By combining experimental data from the THM and other cutting-edge experiments with advanced theoretical calculations, it may be possible to break through the limitations imposed by the Coupled Channels Method and obtain precise low-energy astrophysical $S$-factor values. Ultimately, the continued pursuit of carbon-carbon fusion research will not only advance our understanding of this important reaction but also contribute to broader fields such as nuclear astrophysics, including topics like compact star formation and nucleosynthesis. Additionally, basic scientific investigations enabled by innovative experiments like the THM can provide valuable lessons for future generations. As such, the THM can serve as a model for the type of innovative research that astrophysical experiments can facilitate and inspire. Finally, the potential for future carbon-carbon research to yield ground-breaking findings not only contributes to the advancement of astrophysical knowledge but also facilitates innovative technologies with far-reaching applications. Designing handcrafted features can also restrict the potential of channel representation learning by the DNN. This research suggests attention-based CSI for robust wireless localization. The proposed approach employs an attention mechanism to weigh and select relevant CSI from multiple antennas, a spatial block, or a beamforming perspective. Moreover, an end-to-end architecture allows the DNN to simultaneously optimize antenna selection or beamforming along with weight estimation. The study's findings indicate that the proposed method surpasses conventional methods in terms of generalization and localization accuracy across diverse scenarios. The code is available at https://github.com/nooos/DeepWirelessLocalisation.

Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the costliness of its iterations for many states. Informed by its relation to the semismooth Newton method and the efficiency of its inexact variations, inexact policy iteration, a class of algorithms for large-scale finite MDPs with local contraction guarantees, was introduced. This method is further exemplified through inexact GMRES policy iteration, which applies GMRES for policy evaluation, thereby leveraging the underlying Tikhonov regularization for regularization of the policy's gradient. Notably, inexact GMRES policy iteration outperforms policy iteration and optimistic policy iteration by 5.8 and 2.2 times, respectively, in a series of grid world experiments with 5000 to 10000 states. Although its theoretical basis requires a contraction guarantee, this example indicates the potential of inexact GMRES policy iteration for large-scale MDPs with localized sparsity. We hypothesize inexact iteration could offer significant advantages in such environments. Additionally, an exact implementation of inexact GMRES policy iteration, involving the LU decomposition, shows comparable processing times to policy iteration. In contrast, the exact formulation of inexact policy iteration, also known as the Newton method, is computationally costly due to the symbolic evaluation of its action-dependent Jacobian and cost vector. By leveraging the insights from Tikhonov regularization and the semismooth Newton method, we propose an explicit Tikhonov regularization of the policy, offering an alternative to inexact GMRES policy iteration with exact matrix-vector multiplication. Furthermore, we present a straightforward, yet efficient, randomized Tikhonov regularization of the policy, requiring only a single pass over the states. By combining these approaches with an existing contraction guarantee, inexact Tikhonov policy iteration is achieved, allowing for localization without sacrificing contraction guarantees. Consequently, a localized, large-scale MDP is constructed, thereby facilitating large-scale optimization with local contraction guarantees. This method surpasses inexact GMRES policy iteration by 2.2 times in grid world experiments and matches its processing times in the 10000-state experiment. Furthermore, all of our analyzed algorithms match or outperform existing large-scale MDP methods, such as Tikhonov regularization and localized value function approximation. In particular, inexact Tikhonov policy iteration and inexact GMRES policy iteration are 5.8 times faster than Tikhonov regularization. Additionally, inexact GMRES policy iteration outperforms localized value function approximation

We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Moreover, the paper also identifies both the required and sufficient conditions under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented line segments exhibit equal behavior. Additionally, the study provides a new criterion for determining when the ordinary and symbolic power series of an edge ideal of a weighted directed graph $\mathcal{D}$ are equivalent, built upon a previous criterion by Boeyen and Moritz. This paper examines the solution to an inverse problem presented by expensive computer simulations of complex real-life scenarios. Specifically, researchers focused on an expensive hydrological model designed to generate realistic data for Athens, Georgia, USA. To efficiently handle the large datasets produced by such simulators, an approach involves first selecting key points to approximate the output, and then applying a specialized method to estimate optimal input parameters at those points, while accounting for any uncertainty in the solution. A comprehensive simulation-based study compares the proposed technique with other established methods on a range of synthetic and real-world scenarios. Notably, one of these scenarios centered on predicting future rainfall in a neighborhood hit by a sudden downpour, with the goal of preventing flooding. Our findings indicate that the proposed approach yields superior results, with improvements in accuracy and processing speed compared to other methods. Specifically, it offers up to a 60% reduction in computational costs while maintaining a high level of precision. Moreover, it provides a reliable flock of candidate solutions, which facilitates the selection of the most suitable one based on additional criteria. To achieve these results, a large dataset of 500 synthetic scenarios was generated and analyzed, along with a real-world case study involving the management of rainfall-runoff in the same neighborhood. A publicly available Java package, known as RINCS, has been developed to implement these techniques and facilitate their use by the scientific community. It can be downloaded at https://github.com/jmcdaniel/RINCS. A related video is available at https://youtu.be/7KmxoH0K1YI. (2019). Our paper focuses on the development of new algorithms for learning robust models, where the learner has more flexibility due to the use of local queries. We create the first distribution-free algorithms that achieve optimal risk with high probability, even without assuming a uniformly contiguous sample exposure, for concepts that can be defined by a small collection of simple, bounded functions. These algorithms utilize local membership and weight queries to estimate the concept's distributional average, where the effect of random example exposure is mitigated through an averaging process, aided by a novel, adaptive boundary estimation technique. We show that our methods are resilient to adversarial influence, where an adversary attempting to deceive the learner can only provide the learner with information equivalent to randomly selected samples, for a number of iterations that is proportional to the concept definition's size. These algorithms take advantage of an existing distribution-free guarantee for concepts defined by distribution-valued functions, where the adversary's influence is largely neutralized through an innovative parameter estimation technique, which relies on local equivalence queries and adaptively estimates the concept's distributional boundary using an initial guess, corrected, and refined process. Our work offers insight into the value of local, instead of random, sampling in distribution-free learning and robustness contexts. It also provides the first instance of its kind, showing that local queries can effectively counteract the effect of random example exposure and concept definition complexity. For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with a lone photon have been measured in collisions involving protons and a lead-lead nucleus. This analysis used data from the CMS detector at the CERN LHC, operating at a proton-proton center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The fragmentation functions for jets above 30 GeV were determined in events with a high-transverse-momentum photon, above 60 GeV, between photon rapidity of -2.4 and +2.4. Comparisons with fragmentation functions obtained from proton-proton collisions revealed a weakening of jet fragmentation in central lead-lead events, occurring out to a distance from the jet axis of 1.1, and exceeding that seen in proton-proton collisions by as much as 20% across that range. Additionally, fragmentation functions for jets associated with the highest transverse momentum photons showed little variation relative to those measured in proton-proton collisions. This increased modification of jet fragmentation functions in central lead-lead events may be attributed to increased interactions between high-transverse-momentum jets and the surrounding medium, such as jet fragmentation loss or charmonium production. Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of Apéry-type inverse binomial series. Building upon previous findings that non-alternating central binomial series could be solved using level four multiple zeta values, we now show that alternating versions require level eight and can be solved using an alternative approach. This involves the substitution of hyperbolic trigonometric 1-forms for their standard trigonometric counterparts. Several key results, including an Apéry-type solution for general binomial series, can be confirmed using this approach, which also enables the extension of such series to even indices. This new framework also enables the resolution of inverse generalized hypergeometric series, particularly for even indices. Furthermore, a fundamental relationship between hyperbolic and standard trigonometric series reveals that the values of hyperbolic series are simply the negative of their standard trigonometric counterparts. This means the values of standard trigonometric series are effectively real-valued solutions to previously defined Feynman integrals involving denominator terms with negative signs. This connection sheds new light on the original integral involving the double cuspaneous Feynman diagram as well as its counterpart with a denominator term. Both of these integrals now have real-valued solutions provided by the values of standard trigonometric series. Finally, this new understanding also enables the extension of such series to positive rational indices, effectively generalizing the original Apéry series. This new framework thus offers a general method for solving Feynman integrals involving denominator terms with square roots, previously solved by modular form methods. This new method offers a more direct, geometric interpretation that is closely tied to hyperbolic 1-forms. Follow-up research on WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, previously reported by Meisner et al in 2020, has yielded an assortment of peculiar attributes for the object. New images taken by Keck/MOSFIRE and HST/WFC3 cameras have established that the object is among a select few with extremely faint proper motion, indicating it has a very low temperature consistent with the coolest Y dwarfs. Moreover, the object possesses color indices of W1-W2 and ch1-ch2 about 1.6 mag bluer than a typical Y dwarf. New data collected from WISE, Spitzer, and HST for parallax measurement have determined a close distance of $16.3^{+1.4}_{-1.2}$ parsecs and a substantial transverse velocity of $207.4{\pm}15.9$ km/s. The calculated J, W2, and ch2 absolute magnitudes align with the coolest Y dwarfs despite W1-W2 and ch1-ch2 indices displaying a distinct discrepancy. Research suggests that the object is most likely an ancient metal-poor brown dwarf and possibly the initial instance of a Y subdwarf, necessitating further examination through broad-band spectroscopy and photometry using the JWST for validation of the hypothesis. The research further highlights that accurate segmentation of photometry is necessary for detecting faint Y dwarf candidates using wide-area surveys like ROMAN on LUKE. ROMAN's planned observations of two WISE targets, namely 0847+2105 and 1343+2631, could potentially uncover additional Y dwarf candidates. If found, they would likely be the initial discovery of Y subdwarfs. Additionally, LUKE's scheduled observations in 2023 could possibly find the initial instance of a ZZ Cet subdwarf subpopulation. We develop a novel, numerically efficient approach to solving DGLAP equations for single and double parton distribution functions by leveraging Chebyshev interpolation techniques. This method enhances numerical precision with a reduced number of grid points for PDF evolution, achieving improved efficiency. The DPD evolution process utilizes a cost-effective grid-point scheme, enabling the incorporation of two distinct renormalization scales for each parton. The proposed methods account for NNLO DGLAP kernels and flavor matching. The advantages of our technique, particularly its applicability to double PDFs, lie in its high computational speed and minimal memory requirements. The presented results cover a wide range of scales from NNLO DGLAP evolution at $Q=10^5$ GeV to double PDFs at $Q=20$ GeV, with the former exhibiting a ~5x enhancement in precision compared to other techniques at high scales. The latter demonstrates a ~10x improvement in precision over existing PDF evolution tools like APFIX and DAPSG, with the two methods showing comparable accuracy in double PDF evolution at lower $Q$ values. The Chebyshev DPD evolution tool can be accessed through the link https://github.com/jjhealy ChesterChebyshevDPD. The associated code can also be cloned from https://github.com/jjhealy ChebyshevDDPDF for use in theoretical calculations that rely on double distribution functions. Additionally, the code for the numerical evolution of double distributions can be found at https://github.com/jjhealy ChebyshevDPD. The new theoretical model reveals that slip leads to a higher rate of instability and longer wavelengths than predicted by previous models. Consequently, larger drops tend to form on fibers with high slip coefficients. In their study, the effects of liquid-solid slip on film coated on fibers were observed and contrasted to predictions based on no slip conditions. By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, although the choice of stellar model affects the outcome. Furthermore, even if the predictions for other spectral features are inaccurate, we find that the Prospector-derived star formation rates are generally accurate. Additionally, we consider how observing the $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m Brackett-$\gamma$ line might be used to constrain the model's parameters and as an indicator of star formation rates in future near-infrared spectroscopy missions like JWST. While observing this line at low redshifts is challenging due to nearby strong H$_2$ absorption bands, we suggest that it might be observable in certain cases and could be an valuable diagnostic in the study of distant galaxy evolution. Finally, we examine how observing the $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m Brackett-$\gamma$ line might be used to constrain the models and as an indicator of star formation rates, and discuss potential future applications of this line in the study of galaxy evolution across cosmic time.

This is the initial paper in a two-part series aimed at identifying a method to compute equivalences of quantum subalgebras within the $U_q(\hat{sl}_{n})$ category $\mathcal{C}$. In this particular study, we classify the braided auto-equivalences of local modules in type $A$ orbifolds under $U_q(\hat{sl}_2)$. Specifically, through a methodical approach, we determine the braided auto-equivalences for 20 out of 22 minimal projective modules labeled under $A$ type orbifolds. Furthermore, we establish a formula-oriented approach for identifying orbifold equivalences based on primed fusion rules. As a direct result, four exceptional orbifolds with no corresponding primed fusion rule monodromy are identified. This paper's companion study will tackle type $B$, $C$ and $D$ orbifolds, alongside identifying a generalised approach for classifying such equivalences. The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher for modelling allele spread within genetic populations, but also gained applications by Kolmogorov for a broader range of scenarios. Applying an innovative approach for tackling non-linear partial differential equations provides a distinctive approximate solution to the Fisher-KPP equation, which, however, defies initial intuition. Although the solution respects the maximum principle, a breakdown occurs once time surpasses zero, leading to an extremely irregular, non-smooth outcome that contradicts conventional travelling wave approximations commonly utilised in the field. Despite its unconventional appearance, further analysis will be undertaken to illustrate its validity and accuracy in modelling time-dependent waves for systems following a switch between stable and unstable states. Ultimately, applying this approximation in a given mathematical model yields favourable results, as it facilitates derivation of a highly simplified equation, greatly lessening computational demands and paving the way for dimensional reduction. This approach presents a newly identified method for tackling a range of equations, including the Ginzburg-Landau equation and the Amann reaction-diffusion equation. It also holds potential for applying the proposed solution to various real-world problems. Therefore, it is anticipated that the proposed solution will contribute to new areas of study and research. This work addresses the UbiComp 2021 Challenge presented by Stabilo, aiming to classify handwritten mathematical terms based on time series data from the DigiPen. The challenge involves recognizing mathematical expressions from 15 possible characters written by multiple individuals. To overcome the initial challenge, a data-driven and rule-based information extraction technique is applied to break down the labeled data. Following this process, two machine learning models are developed - the first is a binary classifier leveraging a hybrid Deep Neural Network and Random Forest to detect writing activities, and the second is a Deep Neural Network integrating convolutional and recurrent layers for single-character classification. Although the proposed approach demonstrates satisfactory accuracy and performance in the challenge evaluation, it is noted that further enhancements could be achieved through enhanced feature representation and integration of more sophisticated neural networks, ultimately resulting in a 66.67% accuracy rate on the testing data. The technical details and findings presented can be utilized in the classification of free-hand written symbols and may serve as a valuable resource for further research in the field of handwritten mathematical term classification. The associated code is accessible via the GitHub repository: https://github.com/sharvashankar/Ubipcomp21-Stabilo. The DigiPen data used for the competition can be obtained from https://digi.pen.nl/. This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling incremental synthesis. This method is in line with a broader goal of concurrently modelling durations and acoustic features at a frame-level. Evaluations show that this approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods in predicting the median duration of unseen natural speech. Furthermore, it enables more efficient synthesis by producing more accurate median durations on the fly, which can be a beneficial alternative to averaging durations smoothed with a window size. Species distribution analysis can be effectively conducted through occupancy modeling, taking into consideration inaccuracies in species detection data. To address multiple species, states, interactions, false positives, autocorrelation, and data from various sources, various modifications to the fundamental single species occupancy model have been introduced. However, creating high-performance software that can analyze large spatial data sets is still a developing field. A newly developed package, spOccupancy for R, is designed to fit single, multiple species, and combined occupancy models that are sensitive to spatial relationships. Utilizing a Bayesian approach with Pólya-Gamma data augmentation and Gaussian Process neighbor techniques, this package enables efficient model computation even for extensive datasets. spOccupancy provides intuitive functionalities for simulating data, testing models, verifying predictions, evaluating model performance, and making predictions on unseen data. To capture the intrinsic variability of type Ia supernovae from limited spectral data, we developed a probabilistic autoencoder that incorporates a Normalizing Flow component after initial training using an Auto-Encoder. The model's two-stage generative architecture can identify a reduced-dimensional representation of SNe Ia, accurately modeling their spectral evolution across wavelength and time directly from data. Introducing a penalty term to address variability correlations and a multi-stage training framework within our physically-parameterized network enabled the separation of intrinsic and extrinsic variability, eliminating the need for magnitude standardization models. The PAE was applied in several tasks to improve cosmological analyses, such as automatically detecting outliers, generating sample spectra consistent with data distribution, and resolving noisy inverse problems to estimate cosmological distances. Notably, we found three intrinsic model parameters yielded the best results, in line with existing research. The PAE achieved an optimal standardization of $0.091 \pm 0.010$ mag for our test sample of SNe Ia, reducing to $0.074 \pm 0.010$ mag when peculiar velocity contributions are removed. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the complex human interactions seen in everyday life, neglecting the role of group meetings in disease spread. By adopting hyperedges to model these interactions, we create more comprehensive models, allowing the transmission rate to depend on the number of infectious contacts a person has. This approach leads us to develop new spectral conditions and study various types of contagion models, considering both the stochastic individual-level model and the mean-field approximation. Numerical examples and the analysis that follows enable the differentiation between inherent disease characteristics and the impact of individual actions. Ultimately, this framework holds potential for a more precise evaluation of the effectiveness of virus containment interventions. For further investigation, we present an approach for estimating key model parameters using real-world epidemic data, as demonstrated using data from the 2020 coronavirus outbreak in the United States. Additionally, we discuss the potential for future research to apply this framework to other disease models, addressing both the lack of data and the uncertainties involved. Recent breakthroughs in understanding 2D magnetic semiconductors, exemplified by the study of CrI$_3$, have generated significant enthusiasm due to their intriguing spin-dependent properties and their potential to revolutionize spintronics and magneto-optoelectronics. Through advanced theoretical calculations, researchers investigated the behavior of spin polarization within the prototype ferromagnetic CrI$_3$ bilayer, which has an in-plane magnetic orientation. Their investigation reveals that this ferromagnetic bilayer displays a rich pattern of spin texture within its uppermost valence bands, which arises from two unique spin cants resulting from the interplay of ferromagnetic ordering with both chirality and electrical polarization. One type of cant is a result of layer stacking asymmetry and valence state polarization, resulting in equivalent canting patterns on both layers. Conversely, the other cant is a consequence of Rashba effect, which in this ferromagnetic case generates oppositely canting components on adjacent layers within the same electronic state. Additionally, researchers formulated a set of rules governing spin polarization behavior within magnetic crystals based on their magnetic structure and found that this ferromagnetic bilayer exhibits an unusual situation in which it displays two distinct spin polarization states. Ultimately, its spin texture could potentially be manipulated through an electric field to create a controllable spin-valve effect, which in turn could enable the development of innovative concepts like a spin transistor. Furthermore, their analysis suggests that similar spin texture phenomena could and should be investigated in other magnetic semiconductors, which in turn could lead to the creation of spin texture engineering tools. Last but not least, their investigation highlights the significant role that can be played by layer stacking asymmetry in generating spin polarization within magnetic crystals, which in turn could lead to the development of new and innovative methods for controlling spin-valve type phenomena. \end{abstract}

Deep multimodal learning using K-fan deep Boltzmann machines offers a novel approach to combine multiple input sources. This method can learn a common representation using contrastive divergence and is applied to classification, information retrieval, and other related tasks. A significant drawback of traditional two-fan deep Boltzmann machine models lies in their inability to handle complex tasks effectively, particularly when multiple input modalities are incomplete or missing. The globally predominant messaging app, WhatsApp, boasts a distinct characteristic 
in its closed nature and user-friendly capabilities of transferring multimedia and
large-scale information sharing to groups, which often facilitates the rapid spread 
of anonymous, encrypted messages. However, the direct delivery of messages to user 
phones enabled by WhatsApp, although personal and immediate, can be exploited to 
circulate baseless rumors and fuel misinformation campaigns. Recent elections in 
Brazil and India are notable examples of such abuse, which have led WhatsApp to 
initiate countermeasures like limiting forwarded messages to a single recipient. 
Despite this effort, the success of these measures remains uncertain. In our study, 
we utilize an epidemiological model coupled with real data from WhatsApp in Brazil, 
India, and Indonesia to investigate the impact of limiting features that contribute 
to rapid information dissemination. Our analysis reveals that current WhatsApp 
restrictions can delay, but ultimately fail to halt the spread of large-scale 
disinformation campaigns within closed groups. Consequently, we recommend combining 
these measures with other proactive strategies focused on detecting and removing 
inflammatory content before it spreads widely. As an example of such an approach, 
we outline a simple prescription-based strategy for WhatsApp's incoming messages that 
could potentially be implemented. Furthermore, our study highlights the need for 
further research on detecting and removing harmful content on social media platforms 
utilized for anonymous dissemination. Additionally, we investigate the utility of 
machine learning in analyzing content posted on WhatsApp, identifying its 
characteristics, such as language, sentiment, and topic, which can be crucial for 
developing both preventive and reactive measures against the misuse of such platforms. 
In particular, we focus on detecting hate speech, which is a particularly hazardous 
form of misinformation, by assessing its prevalence on WhatsApp groups in India and 
Indonesia using automated ML-based classification tools. Our evaluation reveals that 
existing ML models can identify hate speech with reasonable accuracy only when the 
training data mirrors the distribution of messages on WhatsApp, which is an extremely 
challenging requirement. Consequently, we initiate the development of a more 
practical LLML-based approach, WhatsApp-Hate, tailored to the unique constraints 
imposed by WhatsApp's API, which is inherently restrictive to data collection and 
external analysis. Ultimately, our LLML-based approach achieves a moderate level 
of accuracy without relying on the specific features of hateful content and without

We analyze a general branching population where individual lifetimes are independent and identically distributed with arbitrary distributions, and individuals give birth to new ones at random times following a Poisson process independently from each other. It's assumed that individuals experience mutations at a specified rate under an infinitely many alleles model, leading to population partition by genetic type. This gives rise to a frequency spectrum, denoted by $A(k,t)$, which counts the number of family groups of size $k$ in the population at time $t$. The frequency spectrum process represents a type of non-Markovian branching process belonging to a class of random-characterized branching processes. Through certain regulatory conditions and asymptotic considerations, we establish certain convergence theorems for the frequency spectrum, ultimately contributing to a central limit theorem under specific conditions. Additionally, a key finding shows that the frequency spectrum is characterized by a limiting distribution that can be approximated through a certain infinite systems process. This model has significant applications in the infinitesimal type theory and population genetics, particularly in the analysis of Chasquillan's data. Ultimately, our research paves the way for important inferring capabilities. Furthermore, the discrete model presented here provides a complementary perspective to the model presented in "Infinitesimal Clustering" by Dr. Chastain. Lastly, the discrete model presented here can also be seen as an extension of the discrete model presented in "Infinitesimal Clustering." The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects within spoken input that arise from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. We achieve this goal by incorporating a specialized, attentive activation function - the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU) - into our end-to-end system. By selectively amplifying key input characteristics and suppressing irrelevant ones, AReLU enables our system to prioritize artifact-related features. Our proposed system was applied to the logical access task using the ASVSpoof2019 dataset and demonstrated improved performance compared to systems utilizing standard, non-adaptive activation functions. Specifically, our AReLU-based system outperformed the baseline system that used a standard ReLU activation function across multiple benchmark settings, exhibiting a 16% enhancement in equal error rate performance. Furthermore, our experiments evaluated the efficacy of our AReLU mechanism in relation to the quality of the spoofed speech. We discovered that as the quality of the spoofed speech decreased, our AReLU-based system exhibited increased performance benefits - for extremely poor-quality spoofed speech, our system showed a 20% improvement in equal error rate compared to the baseline system. These findings underscore the importance of accurately identifying artificial speech effects, especially in challenging scenarios where the speech is of poor quality. Our work represents a new standard for end-to-end spoofing countermeasures within logical access tasks, as verified by our public code releases and experiment replications. Additionally, our proposed AReLU mechanism can be applied to other tasks that involve speech analysis for related applications. We anticipate that our research will inspire the development of more effective spoofing countermeasures. We release our code on the GitHub repository https://github.com/GrishopHE/AReLU_for_Spoofing_Countermeasures for the benefit of the research community. We have also submitted a journal paper to the IEEE/ASA Journal of Acoustic, 'Attention-based End-to-End Logical Access Spoofing Countermeasures: System Development and Experiment Replication', which details our presented research in full. We look forward to connecting with the research community through our proposed metric for evaluating end-to-end spoofing countermeasures - the difference in equal error rate between a system that has and has not received AReLU training. We expect this metric to promote innovation in the development of spoofing countermeasures. We have included our proposal for this new metric in Section 10 of this document. Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model with local supersymmetry, may offer a way to describe new phenomena beyond our current understanding.  Exploring the cosmic applications of supergravity provides a platform to investigate the potential outcomes of this theoretical framework, which could serve as the low-energy effective theory of superstrings-a potential quantum gravity candidate.  Developing inflationary models in supergravity, however, poses significant challenges stemming primarily from the constraints on scalar potentials and complicated interactions within the framework, as well as the excess degrees of freedom.  Addressing these issues requires a strategic approach, involving the use of field theory reformulations, reformulating the classical action from a supersymmetric perspective, and introducing new techniques to construct globally defined scalar potentials.  Furthermore, supergravity offers an opportunity to examine novel cosmological behaviors facilitated by D-terms and gaugino masses.  An alternative to single-field inflationary models, the multi-field inflationary set-up in supergravity allows for a more nuanced exploration of the interplay between the inflating field and its superpartners.  The challenges posed by gauge symmetry breaking, the existence of moduli, and the implementation of supersymmetry breaking make the construction of globally defined inflationary models a daunting task.  Despite these obstacles, the first globally defined globally defined hybrid inflationary model has been constructed, leveraging D-terms, Gaugino condensation, and $\rm D^2$ terms in a subset of $N=1$ supergravity models.  The hybrid supergravity model offers an array of cosmological behaviors tied to the breakdown of the local $U(1)$ gauge symmetry, including D-term inflation, in addition to an exploration of the interplay between inflationary observables, supersymmetry breaking, and stochastic inflation.  The potential consequences of the breakdown of the local $U(1)$ gauge symmetry during inflation are examined through the lens of tensor non-gaussianity, modulation of primordial fluctuations, and stochastic gravitational waves.  The feasibility of the ${\rm D}^2$-term inflationary model is confirmed, while the gauge mediated supersymmetry breaking model and the minimal supersymmetric model fail to yield a coherent inflationary narrative within the framework of supergravity, according to a comparative analysis of their respective potential profiles. In the 2000s, commodity trading advisors experienced notable gains, largely driven by their trades in commodity futures. But their fortunes have shifted dramatically since the 2010s, with underwhelming returns. One plausible explanation for this downturn may be the presence of short-term reversal traders, who allegedly exploit CTAs for financial gain. In a recent study, an artificial market model was devised by incorporating both a commodity trading advisor (CTA) and a short-term reversal trader (SRT). The aim was to establish whether these SRTs were detrimental to CTA profitability. Notably, the research yielded the opposite outcome - in markets with both types of traders, CTA profitability and activity actually increased. Consequently, a positive symbiotic relationship between these traders may be more likely than initially assumed. The study's findings support previous theories suggesting a shared information advantage enjoyed by both types of traders, which could be key in forming their strategies and decisions. This research paper delves into the problem of uplink cascaded channel estimation in multi-user multiple-input-single-output systems aided by intelligent-reflecting-surfaces operating within the sub-6 GHz frequency range where channel propagation isn't sparse. A high-performance, low-overhead estimation protocol has been developed to minimize reflection power loss without requiring on-off amplitude control. The proposed solution exploits a common structure within the system, significantly reducing pilot transmission overhead by decomposing the complex cascaded channel into separate user-specific and shared variables. The challenge of highly coupled estimation variables is overcome through the use of optimization-based estimation methods utilizing channel covariance. An alternating optimization algorithm has been developed to efficiently solve the resulting non-convex problem, with an efficient initialization technique ensuring a local optimal solution. The research further introduces a successive convex approximation algorithm for optimizing the protocol's training phase, leading to improved accuracy. The authors conduct comprehensive simulations, which demonstrate that the proposed algorithm yields superior performance relative to existing state-of-the-art techniques. Specifically, the results reveal that the proposed algorithm achieves 99% accuracy when the number of reflection bits is 16, outperforming existing methods by 50%. The associated overhead is shown to be remarkably low at just 1.13% of total uplink duration. The proposed technique is also shown to be adaptable to various practical scenarios, including those with user location privacy. The research identifies the main challenge of implementing the developed protocol as the need for significant battery power due to the associated overhead. Nevertheless, the results indicate that the proposed algorithm remains efficient even when the number of reflection bits is reduced to 8, at an overhead of just 0.91%. The research finally concludes that the developed protocol offers superior performance relative to existing methods, at a cost of slightly increased complexity. The results can be utilized to guide the implementation of the developed protocol. The research suggests that the challenge of power consumption can be addressed through the use of more advanced techniques such as active IRSS selection and channel utilization optimization. The authors finally note that the developed protocol remains suitable for various practical scenarios, at the cost of slightly increased complexity. The research concludes by suggesting the use of existing techniques to tackle the challenge of power consumption. The research opens the door for the use of deep learning techniques in the design of intelligent-reflecting-surface assisted multiple-input-single-output systems. This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but also took into account local factors such as deaths, infections, and stimulus packages. Additionally, our research reveals that local news COVID coverage varied based on the audience's political affiliations, the area's politics, and the news outlet's ownership and past behavior. Notably, our data indicate that red areas received less COVID-related information despite experiencing similarly high mortality rates as blue areas. This study highlights the significance of considering both local factors and societal-level variables when studying news coverage of public health crises using real-time data. Furthermore, our research shows that local news outlets responded adaptively to changing pandemic conditions but ultimately reflected pre-existing structural biases. Lastly, our results suggest that local news COVID coverage may have contributed to the persistent coronavirus mortality gap between red and blue areas, underscoring the critical role of local media in public health communication during the pandemic. The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In this ability, there's typically a notable turning point where children rapidly grasp and master counting techniques. To simulate this cognitive milestone, we developed an AI system using reinforcement learning. By testing this system with the 'give-N' task - where it's given a binary vector and has to pick 'N' items - we discovered that it showed a similar inflection point in learning. Furthermore, our AI, built using the modular network structure known as the ESBN, was able to learn patterns that allowed it to accurately select items outside of its initial training scope, similar to how humans can apply learned concepts beyond what they initially learned. We found that ESBN performed better in the 'give-N' task compared to a neural network with a flat structure. To study the 'inflection point' in detail, we measured how the ESBN's performance changed over time in a fixed reinforcement learning environment. By doing so, we noticed that ESBN exhibited a sharp increase in performance as soon as it completed training on counting up to 4, but struggled with counting past 4. We realized that this difficulty wasn't due to the ESBN itself, but rather because of the limited scope of its initial training. Once we extended the initial training to include counting up to 4, the ESBN was able to pick items correctly even when given numbers beyond 4. By comparing our AI with a simple model that used the maximum likelihood method to study this task, we found that the reinforcement learning system we created was able to pick items more accurately overall. To further test the robustness of the reinforcement learning system we created, we extended the 'give-N' task in two ways. Firstly, we expanded it to select items that appear at different indices than those within its initial training scope. By doing so, we discovered that the ESBN was able to select items more accurately compared to a neural network with a flat structure. Secondly, we replaced the standard 'give-N' task with variants that either asked the AI to select items at different indices or change the items to be selected to a different binary vector. By doing so, we noticed that the ESBN was able to select items more accurately compared to a neural network with a flat structure. To summarize, our research creates an AI system that, similar to children learning to count, has a "inflection point in learning", and shows robustness in tasks beyond those initially learned. Bloom filters provide quick approximations of set membership while consuming minimal memory. These filters help engineers prevent time-consuming actions, such as accessing a disk or the network. A potential substitute for Bloom filters is the cuckoo filter, which often needs less storage and processes information faster. A different solution, the Bloomier filter, has been proposed as an expansion of the Bloom filter. A modification to this concept has also been explored, particularly by Dietzfelbinger and Pagh. Their variation of the Bloomier filter can serve approximate membership queries efficiently, though no comprehensive testing of it exists to date. A different filter was developed, the xor filter, as an implementation of their idea, offering more effective efficiency and speeds. Notably, the developed xor filter often needs less storage than both Bloom and cuckoo filters, while still processing information faster than Bloom filters and exhibiting similar performance to cuckoo filters. A compact variant of the xor filter was also designed (xor+), resulting in a more space-efficient solution. These filters were thoroughly tested and documented. A key advantage of this new generation of filters is that they can handle large sets of data in memory, which can be useful in machine learning applications. A different advantage is that they can perform fine-grained optimizations of disk usage, leading to potential improvements in database efficiency. A variation of these filters, called partitioned variants, was also devised, specifically the partitioned Bloom filter (pBloom) and the partitioned xor filter (pxor). A test suite was developed for these new ideas to evaluate their effectiveness, resulting in promising results, particularly the pxor filter excelling in most scenarios with even better performance. A key advantage of these partitioned variants is that they can process membership queries in parallel, making them suitable for cloud-based environments. A different advantage is that they can take advantage of cache efficiency due to being designed for locality, resulting in faster processing speeds. Several key connections between convex geometry and holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds are explored. Our investigation focuses on the relationship between positive products and mixed volumes, leading to the definition and examination of a novel addition technique for divisor classes and mixed divisor classes. We establish new geometric inequalities for divisor classes and provide alternative interpretations of classical convex geometry concepts within the framework of algebraic geometry. Specifically, we recontextualize the Alexandrov body construction, Minkowski's existence theorem, demonstrating their analogues with divisorial Zariski decomposition and the duality between the pseudo-effective cone of divisors and the movable cone of curves, respectively. Additionally, we introduce a new inversion technique for divisor classes, yielding new insights into the presence of abounded section classes for holomorphic line bundles and the geometric purity of certain cohomology groups. Our methods also enable the presentation of specific numerical inequalities derived from convex geometry, having implications for the degeneration of holomorphic line bundles and the study of geometrically pure cohomology groups. Finally, we apply our divisors-on-the-fly lemmas to investigate the long-term behavior of Goresky-MacPherson's local cohomology modules $H^i_{\newton{(X,K_X)}/X}(x,x+1)$. These local cohomology modules have been reexamined by Bergh-Engstr\"om in relation to the asymptotic syzygies of ideals proposed by MacIntye-Brennan, as recently extended by Bergh-\"om-H\"ubert in the context of smooth projective varieties. Our divisors-on-the-fly lemmas allow us to simplify their asymptotic analysis and provide new insights, particularly when combined with the decay rate estimates of Rizzi for the local vanishing properties of Bauer-Finet. Our investigation also raises questions regarding the geometric purity of certain cohomology groups and the presence of abounded section classes for holomorphic line bundles. These inquiries may serve as targets for future research within this area of convex geometry and algebraic geometry. Our work is further exemplified through its application to the specific geometric situations of smooth cubic surfaces without complex singularity, the geometric purity of cohomology groups in positive characteristic, the presence of abounded section classes for holomorphic line bundles on varieties with small positive section class, the decay rate estimates of local cohomology modules for varieties with small positive section class, the long-term behavior of local cohomology modules for varieties with small abounded section class

We successfully submitted the winning entry to the NeurIPS 2021 - AWS Deepracer challenge, which required developing a self-driving vehicle model that interacts with its environment through action-reward interactions. The objective was to create an autonomous vehicle model that navigates a simulated track, adapts to real-world settings, and completes a lap at maximum speed while staying on course. The resulting model demonstrated robust lane-following capabilities in the real world, despite variations in weather and camera settings not seen during training. It is now deployed in a physical Deepracer car and consistently demonstrates positive results. Inspired by the classic discrete-time model of nervous activity proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, a new continuous-time model, known as the McCulloch-Pitts network (MPN), has been developed for sequence learning in spiking neural networks. This model employs a localized learning rule, in which synaptic weights update solely based on the accessible information at each synapse. The model leverages the asymmetry of connections between binary neurons to effectively learn and memorize multiple temporal patterns of binary vectors, an ability similar to that of symmetric Hopfield networks for spatial patterns. Furthermore, our study reveals the model's capability to efficiently acquire sequences of binary images and generate neural spike-train data. Our model adheres to spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) principles, offering a theoretical framework for the systematic design of biological neural networks capable of long-term, robust sequence storage. Our research also includes the implementation of six diverse sequence learning tasks, each employing random binary images to demonstrate the model's efficacy in sequence learning and comparison with the Hopfield network for spatial pattern learning. This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
The analysis of baseline models and those submitted by competitors revealed a significant disparity between their performance levels in the newly introduced setting.
The proposed dataset will play a crucial role in further research to enhance the development of more versatile scene text models capable of providing more reliable and robust predictions. 
The competition's resources can be accessed at: https://competitions.codeforces.com/problemset/2445. A complementary website containing additional information is available at: https://oov2022.github.io/. Additionally, the dataset has been made available at: https://github.com/OOV2022/Dataset.

This study integrates principles from validated calculations to provide precise error assessments alongside findings about chaos expansions representing random equilibrium states. Additionally, it demonstrates the application of chaos expansions to multi-dimensional equations, incorporating other established techniques for seamless integration. This work also addresses the issue of initializing chaotic trajectories by employing principles similar to those used for nonchaos case analysis. However, unlike the conventional approach which assumes an arbitrary initial condition, this study shows that an optimal trajectory initialization method exists. A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, AutoLabel, addresses this issue by using existing printed documents to both train and evaluate multiple machine learning models in a loop. By employing a system that combines human and machine intelligence, AutoLabel enables the rapid creation of a large, accurately labeled dataset. The resulting models can then be used to develop robust invoice extraction models, as demonstrated in this study. The study shows that using AutoLabel, we can achieve top-notch accuracy on a range of intricate document types, including invoices and those from multiple countries that may have different languages. Sequential decision-making in operations management problems, such as those governed by constraints, can be addressed using the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). Two main obstacles arise when attempting to solve CMDPs for the development of optimal operational strategies: they are often characterized by a vast number of states and actions, as well as a difficult-to-compute transition matrix. To resolve these challenges, we develop an algorithm that combines policy iteration with subgradient ascent. We show that this approach allows the CMDP to converge to a solution at a rate proportional to $O(\log(T)/\sqrt{T})$, where T represents the number of iterations, provided that a specific condition is met. This method also offers an efficient way to reduce the dimensionality of the CMDP by exploiting its structural properties when applicable. We successfully apply our algorithm to critical problems with such a structure: multi-product inventory control and multi-class queue management, achieving results superior to state-of-art methods. For instance, we achieved an average deviation from optimality of less than 3% when dealing with a queue management problem involving 10 classes and 50 products. Conversely, the best known alternative algorithms presented a deviation of at least 12%. We have made our code available at https://github.com/EmileSaglio/CMDP-algorithm. This research outlines a method for recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols when not using an actual input device, offline. The approach involves segmenting symbols accurately into over 300 categories. Since many mathematical symbols require both horizontal and vertical projection to be split, but also have horizontal and vertical strokes which can't be easily distinguished, this poses a significant challenge for segmentation. Our study proposes an automatic segmentation method of these symbols by utilizing distinctive features such as the presence of horizontal or vertical lines, size, and shape characteristics. The simplicity and efficiency of this algorithm make it suitable for offline mathematical symbol recognition tasks, especially on devices with limited processing capabilities. Our experiment showed that our segmentation method achieved an overall segmentation accuracy of 94.8% across 308 mathematical symbol categories. Additionally, the study using the PRISM dataset, found the top performing models for offline mathematical symbol recognition to be the Convolutional Neural Network, with an accuracy of 96.47%, the SqueezeNet, with an accuracy of 96.24%, the MobileNet, with an accuracy of 95.84%, the Google LeNet, with an accuracy of 95.64%, and the VGG16, with an accuracy of 95.44%, respectively. A comparison of these models revealed the MobileNet to be the most efficient, yet nearly equivalent in performance to the Convolutional Neural Network, making it the ideal choice for applications with strict processing requirements, such as E-learning and E-commerce, due to its ability to achieve a highly accurate recognition rate with minimal computational resources. Furthermore, the study assessed the effectiveness of different preprocessing techniques, such as removing noise, resizing, and simplifying symbols, which improved the accuracy of the model by 25.96%, from 70.54% to 96.50%. Consequently, the simplest yet efficient model, the MobileNet, coupled with robust mathematical symbol preprocessing techniques, can achieve an offline mathematical symbol recognition accuracy of 99.64%. Therefore, this study's findings can be utilized in developing applications such as the automatic filling of mathematical fields in documents, the automatic marking of mathematical tests, the segmentation of mathematical symbols in 3D printing, and the generation of mathematical symbol fonts. Ultimately, the study's goals are to contribute to the advancement of mathematical symbol recognition, explore the potential of mobile networks in achieving high accuracy with minimal computational resources, while also facilitating the development of mathematical symbol based learning systems. We examine the relationship between network architecture and disease propagation in the contact process using numerical methods. Initially, our research reveals that the disparity in epidemic behavior between homogeneous and heterogeneous networks is surprisingly small, yet the latter's complex structure can lead to a lower overall infection rate. Unlike non-clustered networks, the presence of robust community structures in the network tends to cause a secondary outbreak of infections, resulting in two distinct periods of variability. Specifically, the large fluctuations in the early stages of an epidemic within local clusters pose significant challenges to forecasting its spread. Crucially, our analysis suggests that bridging elements within the network have a substantial impact on predictability, with increased distances from the initial infection source to these nodes corresponding to decreased accuracy in forecasting the epidemic's progression. Furthermore, our research investigates how different disease response mechanisms influence variability, revealing that diverse reaction mechanisms can yield disparate infection rates at the conclusion of an epidemic. Importantly, our primary findings are applicable to both simple contact networks and those incorporating geographical factors. Ultimately, our research aims to contribute to more accurate predictions of epidemic behavior in diverse network environments.

A recent pessimism-based approach in Bayesian learning aims to increase robustness by finding the most conservative estimate by limiting the potential outcomes in a model. We apply this concept to the field of DTAs, developing a pessimism-based Bayesian method that incorporates covariate and treatment uncertainties in its pessimism-based outcome prediction. We highlight the limitations of the traditional pessimism approach and overcome them by proposing a new outcome prediction method that adapts to the DTAs' optimistic and conservative nature. We provide theoretical justifications for the new approach and demonstrate its practical benefits through a series of comprehensive simulations. Furthermore, we successfully implement the new method on a real-world data set, showcasing its practical applications.
