Dualities between subcategories of finitely generated modules over Artin algebras can be defined by the relationship to Wakamatsu tilting bimodules, with specific cases yielding known dualities. When restricting these relationships to subcategories of finitely generated modules with particular dimensions, previously established correspondences and dualities on tilting modules are reaffirmed. The implications of this relationship include demonstrating equivalences of derived categories of finitely generated Gorenstein-projective modules, as well as the invariance of certain algebraic invariants under tilting transformations. Furthermore, a criterion for identifying tilting modules with the property of preserving duality under certain dimensional constraints is presented. This criterion enables the identification of Miyashita dualities among finitely generated modules in specific cases, with particular exploration of Koszul-dual algebras, Steenrod algebras, and a certain case involving the polynomial algebra over a field in an odd characteristic in the case of a field being that of characteristic 2, under specified conditions. Finally, additional future research directions are suggested. As a result of this investigation, a completely unified framework for understanding Miyashita's duality in module theory is established, along with new insights into the relationship between classical duality and tilting duality. New algebraic invariants that capture the essence of classical duality have also been introduced, with particular tilting modules identified as preserving this duality under certain dimensional constraints. In addition, potential applications of this research in the field of Topological Modular Forms are anticipated. Lastly, categorical tilting duality dualities are investigated in relation to the concept of Gorenstein-duality. The Gaussian distribution is uniquely determined by the distribution of a linear combination and a power function of independent identically distributed random variables. We identify the a-adic solenoids for which this relationship holds, effectively proving a theorem analogous to the generalized Polya theorem. This proof relies on solving a functional equation for a specific class of functions associated with the character group of the a-adic solenoid. We demonstrate that the solutions form a countable set, enabling a continuous probability distribution to be defined. Then, by examining the combinations of these variables, we arrive at the desired classification. Notably, this theorem shares similarities with a previous result by Bergal on the classification of probability measures on tori. We also explore an extension to the classification of symmetric convex functions, enabling us to completely classify the symmetric convex functions of type 1 on the group of continuous functions from the set of prime numbers to the set of rational numbers. This classification can be interpreted through the study of one-dimensional lattices over the ring of rational functions on the set of prime numbers. Furthermore, we prove that any probability measure on the group of continuous functions from a set of n natural numbers to the set of rational numbers can be expressed as a convolution of a measure supported on a group homomorphism with a measure that arises from a functional equation, essentially a version of the classical Bernstein problem, before finally establishing a new set of classifications for probability distributions on solenoids and tori. These classifications are based on the topological properties of the respective groups, utilizing a construction of a continuous section to the continuous action of the group on itself that is key to multiple extensions of the theorem. We show that an application of a specific functor that lifts functions between topological groups to the level of measures results in an essential part of these extensions, leading to a connection between the functorial properties of geometric objects and the existence of continuous sections in the context of probability theory. We conclude by outlining potential new avenues for research inspired by these findings. Research supported in part by the National Science Foundation grant NSF/DMR-9600566. Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of zeros and ones, typically denoting the presence of something in a specific location. These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as ecological studies, genetic information, and linguistic analyses examining word occurrences in texts. Clustering methods can effectively apply to this data for a range of purposes including the identification of geographically linked species groups, known as biotic elements. Various clustering approaches can be utilized to process such data including the use of latent class mixtures under the assumption of local independence, hierarchical clustering based on the Jaccard distance, or applying continuous data methods to the multi-dimensional scaling representation of distances. These clustering methods vary conceptually and cannot be directly compared empirically. The purpose of this paper is to provide a comprehensive review of the aforementioned methods, examine their practical applications in various contexts, and evaluate their effectiveness through a comprehensive simulation study focusing on key performance metrics such as the likelihood-based pseudo information measure and the Calinski Harabasz index. The results indicate that the performance of the methods is largely dependent on the data at hand, with a particular approach outperforming the others in terms of these metrics for a given dataset. The conclusions drawn from this study suggest that a comprehensive evaluation should be conducted for a specific research question to determine the most suitable clustering method. The methods reviewed in this paper are implemented as R functions and available for download on the CRAN website at https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/BinCluster/index.html. A new R package called BinCluster provides the necessary functionality to reproduce the results presented in this study. The package consists of five main functions including bincluster, lca, hierarchicalCluster, multivariateGS, and plotBinCluster. The binCluster function performs clustering based on the binary data and can also handle covariates. The lca function estimates latent class models under the assumption of local independence, hierarchicalCluster computes the hierarchical clustering for binary data, the multivariateGS function performs multi-dimensional scaling based on the Tucker1935 James distance, and the plotBinCluster function plots the classified groups and their corresponding covariates. The package also supports the standard uni-dimensional binary clustering method previously described in the literature. Additionally, the package includes additional tools such as the plotpca function for the graphical representation of the principal components, and the calcDist function used to calculate the distances between the classified groups. In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has received significant attention, but dealing with RGB and RGB-D images separately often necessitates the design of specific network architectures. This paper proposes an efficient and unified structure that integrates cross-attention context extraction to effectively tackle both tasks. By effectively fusing two inputs (for RGB images) or three inputs (for RGB-D images) with a cross-attention mechanism, our framework leverages the rich information present in both RGB and depth features. This structure's simplicity and efficacy enable efficient extraction and fusion of contextual information. As shown by experimental results, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on various datasets in terms of multiple evaluation metrics. Moreover, due to its efficiency, it can be employed for real-time salient object detection tasks. The proposed model's code is available at https://github.com/AtyNav/DCC-Nets. The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8136 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. Meanwhile, in subtasks B and C, a linear support vector machine was used in combination with pre-selected character n-gram features. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.5243, and ranked 27th out of 65 participants. We discuss key research findings and our approach to hate speech detection. Additionally, we highlight several areas for improvement and potential future developments in this field. We hope that through our work, the accuracy of hate speech detection can be enhanced and more compassionate online environments be created. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/um-iu-ling/semeval-2019-offenseid.

A number, N, can be termed a palindrome if its binary format is symmetrical. In this paper, the relationship between the quotients of these symmetrical numbers is explored and several fundamental questions about the resulting sets of integers and fractions are answered. We demonstrate the feasibility of solving this problem using a precise formula, by ascertaining if an integer, N, can be expressed as a division between two identical symmetrical numbers, A and B. Upon determining representability, we pinpoint an upper limit on the value of the smallest numerical component. We then prove that a certain set of numbers has a higher frequency of occurrence within the set of all possible quotients. We establish a lower limit on the second numerical component, as well as the entire quotient itself. In a subsequent extension, we identify a general pattern and establish a connection between the given set of numbers and a new set, where each element of the first set is squared. We then prove a fundamental question about this new set, namely that any given integer can be expressed as a division between two identical numbers, a generalization of the original problem for symmetrical quotients. Finally, in an extended exploration, the pattern observed in the binary representation of these symmetrical quotients is compared with the binary representation of regular palindromic numbers. It is observed that while both types of numbers exhibit similar characteristics in terms of their binary representation, regular palindromic numbers often have a greater extent of symmetry. We then identify a new category of numbers, termed ultra-palindromes, which possess an even more extensive extent of symmetry, far exceeding that of symmetrical quotients, known for their limited and distinct binary representation. In conclusion, the unique characteristics of symmetrical quotients, defined by their binary representation, distinguish them as a distinct category of numbers, offering valuable insights into the various patterns observed within this category. Ultimately, the interest in this category of numbers is seen as an opportunity to contribute to the broader, fundamental understanding of numbers, as evidenced by numerous papers on this topic. As this paper draws to a close, it is seen as having fulfilled its primary objective of exploring and comprehensively understanding the world of symmetrical quotients. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses an additional challenge. Research has offered numerous techniques for mitigating this issue but their effectiveness is often dependent on specific conditions such as complete knowledge of the initial polyenergetic X-ray spectrum. In this paper, a new approach is proposed where estimations of the remaining energy levels are calculated alongside the image reconstruction process using data from a CT scanner. This proposed method is compared with existing techniques that require either complete spectrum knowledge or a predetermined binary attenuation coefficient range. In particular, our proposed method's ability to accurately determine energy levels from limited, measured data is assessed through various measurements. In order to achieve this, the CT scanner is operated at multiple energy levels during data acquisition while being controlled by an optimization algorithm that accurately identifies the energy levels without the need for prior knowledge. Furthermore, the process's efficiency in determining the energy levels is evaluated through a practical image reconstruction process using a commercially available scanner and reconstructed images compared with reference values. Our results indicate the effectiveness of this novel technique in accurately estimating the energy levels from limited, measured data. In addition to this, the process of image reconstruction using the estimated energy levels rather than the complete spectrum results in nearly identical images with significantly reduced artifacts. In particular, our proposed method exhibits a 99% accuracy in comparison with the reference values for one of the energy levels and a 90% accuracy for the second. This method also yields highly accurate attenuation coefficients with an average error of 0.96%, particularly in comparison with the standard of error 2.08 used in this research. In order to validate our approach further, the process and efficiency in determining the energy levels was compared with existing methods through specific quantitative measures such as the CPU time, specific attenuation coefficients error and the conjugate gradient method, specifically the Ram-Sidepu index. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). A specific obstacle is encountered in deciphering historical ciphers, which often employ fictional alphabets to conceal the contents. To overcome this problem, this study develops a novel data creation approach rooted in Bayesian Program Learning (BPL). Unlike conventional generation methods that require extensive annotated images, our approach produces realistic handwriting from just one sample per alphabet symbol. After creating these symbols, synthetic lines are produced for training leading Handwritten Text Recognition models like Sequential Training, and a semi-supervised Bayesian program model can learn the unknown alphabet and handwriting styles using only a few real lines. Our results demonstrate successful application of this data creation method to two ciphers: the Elizabethan Crypt and the Napoleonic Code, using only publicly accessible images and no special knowledge. We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a preamplitude construction, confirming the findings of Huang and Yuan. The method involves the use of a Casimir operator that determines the amplitude up to certain ambiguities. A specific set of four-dimensional 'zigzag' integrals is found to accurately capture the leading logarithmic discontinuities at any order. Furthermore, an analysis reveals a previously overlooked crossing symmetry in the preamplitude, which can be utilized to create a symmetric function exhibiting the desired logarithmic behavior in various channels. Through this approach, an explicit expression is obtained for the two-loop correction to anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators with generic spin. The formula incorporates terms related to harmonic sums, specifically alternating nested ones up to weight three. In addition, an extension of the bulk-point limit for AdS amplitudes is proposed, demonstrating that this limit accurately retrieves the entire flat-space amplitude. With this modified understanding of the bulk-point limit, the model can accurately reproduce scale-dependent logarithmic threshold terms observed in type IIB string theory in flat space. With these elements, the model is found to consistently describe threshold behavior in both AdS and flat spaces. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Researchers have recently identified that a subset of object-oriented programming, characterized as Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), can be efficiently computed on SIMD devices by utilizing techniques like loop fusion and vectorization.  This paper marks the first instance in which SMMO-based parallelism is applied to a general programming model suitable for high-performance computing on SIMD devices.  This model, known as Object-Oriented Parallel Vector Operations (OOPVO), defines a framework for computing SMMO-based parallelism via a set of predefined templates.  By allowing compilers to directly translate OOPVO into optimized machine code, researchers have achieved significant performance improvements.  Specifically, four applications showed over 20 times speedup compared to sequential execution, and compared to MPI/GPU implementations, four applications showed over 50 times speedup, with one demonstrating a speedup of over 900 times.  Notably, even simple optimizations could still yield speedups of over 10 times.  By providing a comprehensive statistics analysis, researchers found that a large class of computational problems, including those found in fields like linear algebra and graph theory, are eligible for parallelization using the SMMO approach.  Ultimately, this work paves the way for a new generation of high-performance computing applications on SIMD devices via the OOPVO framework.  Future developments aim to focus on improving compiler techniques for directly translating SMMO-based parallelism into optimized kernel code.  Additionally, researchers intend to explore the use of runtime specializations to further boost performance via kernel-based parallelism. In various fields, ensuring decision functions maintain their optimal performance under changing conditions, even with limited knowledge of their environment, is a top priority. Our study introduces an approach for quantifying how well decision functions withstand uncertainty in the form of credal Bayesian networks, which are parametric models representing the unknown environment with confidence intervals on key variables. Focusing on the 'Maximum Marginal Probability' (MARmax) issue – the maximum possible error probability when misclassifying data, resulting from the most optimistic scenario – our approach transforms MARmax into a more manageable problem on a probabilistic circuit, converting it to a series of smaller min-cut problems that can be efficiently solved. Our proposed algorithm outperforms the existing baseline method in several synthetic and real-world scenarios, including animal pharmacology studies, reducing the MARmax error by an average of 20%. Based on these findings, the researchers created an optimal solution for the online Euclidean spanner problem in one-dimensional space with a competitive ratio of O(β^n). We suggest an asynchronous algorithm to solve Nash equilibrium problems by iteratively decomposing the mixed strategies. This methodology is heavily grounded in monotone operator theory, utilizing warped resolvents for handling a combination of nonsmooth and smooth functions involved in strategy mixtures. The proposed approach is versatile and can accommodate various functions involved in strategy mixtures, despite being primarily demonstrated with nonsmooth functions. Additionally, we outline the mathematical underpinnings of the proposed algorithm. The algorithm's implementation has been successfully validated with numerical examples in fields such as economics and game theory. However, it's worth noting that convergence proof has only been established in scenarios where one of the players' best response involves a smooth function. Further research is needed to extend this to other applications. The proposed algorithm is compared with existing methods such as Tikhonov-Fenimore and monotone operator theory approaches, showing promising performance in games like Poker and Cournot competition. Tikhonov-Fenimore and monotone operator theory approaches are observed to lack convergence in certain applications, whereas the proposed asynchronous method demonstrates convergence in all tested scenarios. Moreover, it achieved faster computational times than the Tikhonov-Fenimore and monotone operator theory approaches. The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. A simulation tool called PopSyCLE allows users to study this phenomenon and predict the occurrence of detectable microlensing events. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing research. Furthermore, we propose a simplified model to predict the stress experienced by the liquid in the stick-slip regime. The application of our findings extends beyond the scope of foam physics, potentially informing the understanding of complex liquid flow in engineering and biological contexts. Additionally, we provide an overview of existing research focusing on the phenomenon of stick-slip behavior in complex liquids. Unlike the stick-slip effect observed in solid mechanics, our study reveals that the origin of the stick-slip effect observed in complex liquids is not solely attributed to mechanical factors but also influenced by surfactant activity. Consequently, we anticipate that the stick-slip regime will serve as an essential area of investigation for future research, aiming to elucidate its underlying physical mechanisms in detail. Nonetheless, our proposed model already exhibits decent agreement with existing research, particularly for the study of the stick-slip effect in polymers, when considering the relative importance of Newtonian and polymeric components. Ultimately, our research aims to contribute to the development of stick-slip models, potentially applicable in various places where this phenomenon occurs. We explore solitary waves known as nanoptera in nearly isolated, singularly perturbed systems of interconnected particles, motivated by the observation of solitary waves in a one-dimensional array of rotating nanoparticles supported by a liquid droplet. Our investigation focuses on the elastic collision of a high-energy solitary wave with a flat surface, utilizing a singularly perturbed model of colliding strings. It's found that upon encountering the flat surface, a solitary wave transforms into a probing wave that may undergo reflection or be transmitted as a solitary wave, depending on the impact strength. As the solitary wave interacts with the surface, it loses some of its initial amplitude due to the diminution effect, leading to a possible transmission if the loss is compensated by the solitary wave's initial amplitude. Notably, a transmitted solitary wave has a diminished amplitude compared to the initial amplitude of the colliding wave. Furthermore, at sufficiently high energies, a solitary wave may be transmitted in the form of a periodic wave train known as a nanoptera, accompanied by a transmitted cusp-like wave known as a solopter. As the period of the wave train increases, its transmission is observed to decrease in a staggered pattern, while the solopter's transmission is seen to decrease in an alternating pattern, both in a singularly perturbed context. Our analysis indicates that solitary waves, including nanoptera and solopters, may be stable over a range of energies, despite losing some of their initial amplitude upon interaction with the flat surface. It's conjectured that these solitary waves could be observed in the mentioned system of rotating nanoparticles, potentially for several minutes. Our findings are also expected to be applicable to other singularly perturbed systems, such as those formed by the interaction of a point source with a shallow liquid pond or a narrow channel, as well as to near-threshold solitary waves in the mentioned Hertzian chain, where they may exhibit a prolonged lifetime due to their initial energy intensity. Our study is finally expected to be relevant to the observation of solitary waves in various singularly perturbed systems in two-dimensional and three-dimensional contexts, where the diminished amplitude phenomenon may still occur, albeit through different mechanisms. It's worth noting, however, that the classification of nanoptera and solopters as solitary waves could be contingent upon the choice of Hamiltonian representation in the corresponding system. It's also possible that the observed solitary waves in the mentioned system of rotating nanoparticles are variants of solopters, given their expected lifespan of several minutes and their periodic behavior. Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by decay modes that occur after inflation. We explore a specific type of feature - a classical oscillation - born at the moment inflation begins, caused by a massless particle in a non-constant background field. As inflation proceeds, the fluctuations within this background field cause the massless particle to oscillate, producing a resonance. These oscillations result in created particles, primarily through a resonance decay mode operative at or near the moment inflation ends. We examine two notable cases: one where the resonance particle decays into a pair of scalar fields, providing insight into the primordial non-Gaussian signals, and another where it decays into a graviton pair, generating distinctive gravitational waves, and finding that the resulting signal can exceed Planck noise in certain models. We predict that future studies using future satellite missions such as LISA could yield detectable signals for certain Inflaton-anti-Inflaton potential slopes. This paper explores the benefits that self-supervised learning confers on Vision Transformer (ViT), distinguishing it from convolutional networks (convnets). Our findings show that self-supervised ViT features uniquely capture the semantic structure of an image, a trait absent in supervised ViT models and convnets. Additionally, these features excel as k-NN classifiers, outperforming all public convolutional network variants and supervised ViT models on ImageNet 31 classes. Notably, our research highlights the limitations of large-scale supervised ViT models, which fail to surpass leading self-supervised convnets. To address these limitations, we developed an efficient and highly scalable framework for self-supervised ViT training, utilizing 760 GPUs and 20 exabytes of storage to craft an innovative, 2000M-parameter ViT model. Our approach successfully demonstrates the advantages of self-supervised ViT learning, ultimately leading to a mere performance gap with fully supervised methods on standard benchmarks like ImageNet 2012 and ResNet 50/50 pretraining. Moreover, we found that our self-supervised ViT model excels as a semantic segmentation backbone, surpassing state-of-the-art convolutional network variants on ImageNet Substitution 1.1 and evaluating their transferability on real-world semantic segmentation tasks. Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have received considerable attention for their impressive ability to generate detailed images from text input alone, yet achieving high-quality results typically requires multiple iterations. To facilitate text-guided image generation, users must frequently adjust input prompts, but even slight modifications can lead to vastly different generated images, making it difficult to achieve desired results. To overcome these challenges, we introduce the Stable Latent Guidance (S LAT) technique, allowing for the efficient and subtle adjustment of latent variables and thus the image generation process, by utilizing additional image constraints and optimizing them in alignment with the prompt. The proposed technique is versatile and can be applied across various text-conditioned diffusion models. Moreover, it offers multiple benefits, including the ability to produce multiple and varied outputs from a single model, facilitate the discovery of image manipulations, and improve the efficiency of image editing tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the S LAT technique in producing high-quality images comparable to state-of-the-art models, and additional findings and visual examples can be found in the supporting document. The code for the S LAT technique is available at https://github.com/VisualLearning-Stanford/Stable-Latent-Guidance. Additional resources, including the model weights and generated images, can be accessed at https://stanfordvision.org/slatex/. S LAT is one of the three techniques described in this document; the other two are SEGA and LAT. While SEGA focuses on the early stages of the diffusion process, LAT and the presented S LAT technique target the latent variables at different scopes, leading to complementary benefits. For more information, the reader is directed to the relevant paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.07836. S LAT shares similarities with SEGA in that it leverages additional image constraints for image editing purposes; however, the two differ in their scopes of operation. While SEGA focuses solely on the initial stages of the diffusion process, S LAT is designed to function at a broader scope, allowing it to be applied across various text-conditioned generative diffusion models, including those optimized with maximum likelihood principles rather than adversarial ones. To improve image editing efficiency while maintaining consistency with the original image, S LAT can be viewed as an iterative extension of the techniques described in the document. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned through unsupervised methods. Experimental findings show that the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis results in improved steganographic performance with regard to capacity-distortion metrics. Moreover, we discovered that aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties can be differentiated based on their variation throughout the training process. Based on the underlying assumptions of Bayesian neural networks, we propose an analytical approach for approximating the posterior distribution, thereby providing a clear theoretical foundation for the development of steganographic predictive models. This research is expected to pave the way for the creation of more robust steganographic predictive models. Moreover, we anticipate that the proposed techniques will find applications in a variety of inverse problems. The proposed steganographic predictive model framework can be applied to a diverse range of image and video steganography, in addition to potential future extensions to steganography on 3D objects and artificial intelligence-assisted steganography. Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or temporal data, but integrating these aspects remains unclear. This study demonstrates how the human visual system can effectively combine spatial and motion information, enabling recognition in scenarios where individual sources are insufficient. Researchers achieved this insight by analyzing'minimal videos' - brief clips that facilitate reliable object, part, and action recognition, but are unrecognizable when spatial or temporal constraints are compromised. Unlike existing deep networks, humans exhibit more adept performance in these complex configurations, highlighting missing dynamic vision mechanisms in current models. Additionally, humans display robust integration capabilities, resolving ambiguities between spatial and motion cues, but are more susceptible to misleading static images, suggesting a critical role for motion-based integration mechanisms in object and action recognition. Further exploration into'minimal videos' may help to better replicate human visual processing in artificial intelligence systems. The rapidly evolving Earth Observatory research area has immense potential to utilize AI in real-time weather forecasting. This work addresses the challenge of accurate weather prediction by leveraging the video transformer network. Building on existing research into vision transformer architectures, we address the limitations associated with their high computational complexity and data-hungry nature. To achieve this, we propose combining Video Swin-Transformer with a dedicated data augmentation method, and employing a gradual spatial reduction on the encoder and cross-attention on the decoder. The efficacy of our proposed model was tested on the Weather4Cast2021 challenge dataset, where it successfully predicted 8 hours of future weather frames from hourly weather sequences. After normalizing the dataset for evaluation consistency, our results demonstrate a 2.9% improvement in MSE score and 11.7% improvement in F1 score over the baseline model. In models that expand on the electroweak sector, a basis can be found where the symmetry prevents coupling, leading to viable dark matter candidates. Specifically, we analyze the $S_3$-symmetric three-Higgs-doublet models with different types of symmetry breaking, and identify two models that can serve as potential candidates for dark matter. In the first model, where only one doublet acquires a vacuum expectation value while the other two remain aligned, an $\mathcal{O}(100)\,$GeV dark matter candidate arises from a combination of odd and even scalar fields under the $S_3$ symmetry, and is stabilized by the symmetry. In the second model, where two doublets acquire vacuum expectation values while one remains aligned, a dark matter candidate in the $\mathcal{O}(100)\,$GeV range emerges from a mixture of odd and even scalar fields, and is stabilized by the symmetry. Additionally, we find that both models can be consistent with electroweak baryogenesis if we introduce an extra sector responsible for it and satisfy certain requirements derived from LHC data, including a minimum mass difference between the dark matter candidate and the lightest Higgs boson. In both models, we also find that the dark matter candidate's interaction with ordinary matter is primarily mediated by a specific doublet that avoids coupling with Standard Model fields due to the symmetry. Consequently, we can obtain a combined fit to both dark matter and baryogenesis phenomena by relating the scale of dark matter to the scale of baryogenesis, and imposing a minimum mass on the dark matter candidate. Furthermore, both models predict the existence of charged scalar and vector bosons, which, in contrast to similar models without symmetry, become coupler to Higgs bosons, and thus may soon be discovered at the LHC. Modern motion deblurring methods based on deep learning utilize paired synthetic data for training frameworks, aiming to directly convert blurry inputs to clear outputs. However, the success of these methods heavily relies on high-quality synthetic blurry data available only before training, a constraint that becomes impractical with large datasets. Notably, our method also enables the creation of visually acceptable synthetic blurry data, contributing to the development of more realistic datasets for motion deblurring. Moreover, our approach extends the scope of deep learning-based motion deblurring methods to tasks involving significant occlusions and variable exposure times. A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. This paper proposes a novel self-training technique that mitigates this data annotation constraint by leveraging the parser's own output to improve performance. Specifically, the Deep Contextualized Self-training algorithm integrates external sequence models, derived from the parser's application to unlabelled data, into the parser using a sophisticated weighting system. Comprehensive experiments have been conducted across multiple languages in diverse settings, and the results clearly indicate that our approach outperforms traditional self-training and state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods by a significant margin. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that DCST compares favourably to recent, more complex methods that combine neural models with statistical ones. Notably, our work has achieved state-of-the-art results on the CoNLL 2014 English UD dataset and has paved the way for successful application of deep contextualized models to newly annotated datasets. This research introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset showcasing diverse human body expressions while accounting for everyday attire. The primary objective of HUMBI is to enhance modeling accuracy by capturing five essential bodily signals, such as gaze, facial expressions, hand gestures, posture, and clothing variations across a range of subjects. The creation of HUMBI involves utilizing 107 synchronized high-definition cameras to capture and capture high-definition footage of 772 individuals, representing various demographics and styles. Using these multi-view images, we apply advanced 3D mesh modeling to accurately reconstruct and represent diverse human body expressions from multiple viewpoints. Based on HUMBI's capabilities, we outline a new benchmark challenge focused on leveraging pose data to generate highly realistic, photorealistic human body expressions in three-dimensional formats, with a significant emphasis on promoting genuine social telepresence. We propose a universal approach to effortlessly and effectively transfer neural models from English to other languages. Our method utilizes weak supervision in the form of task representations and can adapt existing neural models to new languages with minimal modifications, as long as there's unlabeled parallel data and a loss function based on task representations. We put our framework to the test by transferring an English sentiment classifier to three foreign languages and discovered that it surpasses the performance of numerous strong baselines while matching or even exceeding state-of-the-art results obtained through more resource-intensive and complicated methods. Moreover, our framework successfully captures rich, semantically significant representations across languages despite the absence of direct supervision. Last but not least, our framework features a unique ability to transfer neural models across significantly divergent languages such as English and Mandarin, achieving impressive results in sentiment classification on this language pair. This research proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To simulate real-world hurricane scenarios, the study generates probabilistic storm paths based on historical data, and corresponding storm surge situations are developed based on actual hurricane parameters. To assess potential losses, the study employs a quantitative metric that estimates total load reduction, and these outcomes are calculated using a simulated model of the 2000-bus Texas power system superimposed onto an actual map of the region. Simulation results indicate that power substations experiencing storm surge-related flooding may incur additional losses as the hurricane continues to move inland. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that power system operation and hurricane trajectory are interdependent, and this influences potential power losses, offering valuable insights for developing more effective hurricane response and preparation strategies. Ultimately, the study aims to facilitate improved understanding and mitigation of hurricane-induced power grid damage. To further enhance hurricane resilience, the study suggests potential mitigation strategies, including upgrading power substation equipment and implementing inland backup power sources. We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D and 3D spaces as generalized versions of the heterochaos baker map, initially developed as simplified models for unstable dimension variability in complex systems. We identify that the intrinsic encoding properties of these maps align with those of the Dyck system from the study of languages, and this correspondence serves as the foundation for an in-depth analysis of their invariant measures. Through initial investigation, we confirm the existence of two distinct ergodic measures with maximal entropy for these generalized baker maps, and also reveal the underlying cause for the failure of certain entropy-based approaches. Building upon this, we seek the largest collection of nontrivial ergodic measures with nonpositive Lyapunov exponent for these maps. Additionally, we outline a potential extension of our research to explore ergodic properties within lattice structures and connect this to the study of lattice systems with nonvanishing abelian derivatives as encountered in the study of thermodynamic phase transitions. Furthermore, based on our preliminary findings, we suggest entropic criteria as a natural criterion for distinguishing ergodic properties within this family of lattice systems. Ultimately, we summarize our key conclusions, including new formulas for ergodic measures and entropy values, which hold significant value for the family of lattice systems under (α, β)-Lyapunov rigidity. We confirm (α, β)-Lyapunov rigidity for certain systems with α, β values greater than 3, and provide supporting numerical evidence for potentially ergodic measures with Lyapunov exponents as low as −10 or smaller. A pressing concern is whether the Standard Model of particle physics adequately accounts for the scalar sector observed in nature or if it is a subset of a more complex model featuring additional particles. A critical method for resolving this query involves scrutinizing extended scalar models using future high-energy collider facilities, including the potential proton-proton collider with 27 and 100 TeV center-of-mass energy, and advanced lepton colliders at various energy levels. A comprehensive review of the current status of extended scalar models has been presented, focusing on models featuring a second doublet, a singlet, or a complex scalar in addition to the previously discovered Higgs boson. A key aspect of this work involves evaluating the predictive power of these models, particularly how their predictions for physical particle characteristics, such as masses, coupling parameters, and mixing angles, vary based on specific theoretical assumptions. A pressing issue is the identification of signatures that may indicate the presence of these additional particles, which would significantly impact our understanding of the scalar sector in nature. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly requiring significant input data and resulting in an overly complex model. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to the target pitch through adjusting dilation factors based on the input pitch, eliminating the need for the previously required lengthy sequential conditioning. Secondly, the network is simplified by stacking dilation factors along the depth dimension, allowing many conditional time steps to be combined into one. As a result, QPNet significantly reduces model complexity while utilizing prior knowledge more effectively than WN. Furthermore, the experiment findings show that QPNet surpasses the generative capabilities of its parent model WaveNet in both quality and efficiency. Specifically, QPNet achieves comparable or superior generative capabilities to other state-of-the-art models such as the Generation Quality Intelligence network (GI) and the Parallel WaveNet (PWN), as evidenced by evaluations using mean opinion score (MOS) and the frequency weighted segmental spectral distance (FSSD). Specifically, the results show that QPNet surpasses PWN by 0.03 MOS and GI by 0.15 MOS, based on the official jupyter notebook codes. Moreover, the study reveals that QPNet reduces the storage requirements of PWN by 50%, achieves comparable generative capabilities to GI while being more efficient, and yields higher quality outputs than the Deep Voice 2 text-to-speech model. Ultimately, the proposed QPNet offers a versatile and efficient generative network design to balance purity of data-driven methods and prior knowledge-assisted techniques to achieve high-fidelity audio generation. Specifically, the reduced complexity of QPNet enables it to be more compact than the VoiceGAN generative adversarial network, allowing it to achieve the same level of generative capabilities as PWN within a memory constraint of 90% of PWN. Given its strong performance and the ease of training it offers, the deep learning architecture of QPNet presents a promising approach to synthesizing long, quasi-periodic audio waveforms. Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF), the dominant method, have become an integral part of our daily lives as consumers. However, their limitations become apparent when dealing with recommendation data due to the complexities and idiosyncrasies of user preferences. Researchers attempted to overcome these challenges by integrating CF with Biclustering techniques. This research aims to evaluate the efficacy of Biclustering approaches for CF, analyzing various algorithmic decisions, and identifies key principles for high-performing Biclustering-based CF methods. As a result, this work proposes USBFC, a CF method leveraging Biclustering that excels in addressing the associated challenges. Experimental outcomes on real-world datasets demonstrate the exceptional performance of USBFC compared to the existing state-of-the-art CF methods with Biclustering. Moreover, a comprehensive analysis using various complexity metrics confirms that USBFC boasts impressive efficiency, making it a suitable solution for large-scale recommendation tasks in the future. This research ultimately contributes to the development of innovative CF methods utilizing Biclustering and paves the way for future research in this domain. Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that better reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for distinguishing these signals from a planet's Doppler signal. In this research, we studied the spectral features of stellar activity using data from the HARPS-N solar telescope, and found patterns distinct from a quiet star's spectrum by comparing active to quiet periods. By using SDO imagery, we quantified the proportion of active areas (faculae and spots) on the solar surface, independent of previous activity indicators. These features were linked to variations in solar faculae coverage, as observed on the visible hemisphere of the Sun. Moreover, the spectral features were observed to shift towards longer wavelengths as the star's active regions rotate into view. These patterns were consistent across different activity levels and spectral periods. By cross-correlating these features with synthetic spectra of G and K stars, we estimated the detectability of Earth-like planets under different activity levels. In particular, we found that as a star's activity level increases from level 1 to level 3, the detectability of a 2-Earth-radius planet improves significantly, regardless of its orbital period or eccentricity. These novel indicators hold great potential for helping distinguish a star's activity signals from a planet's Doppler signal in future missions such as the James Webb Space Telescope and the Habitable Exoplanet Environment (HBE). In addition, the study lays a foundation for a more comprehensive, multi-faceted analysis of a star's activity that incorporates both observational indicators and theoretical models. This integrated understanding can inform and constrain 3D global simulations of a star's activity. Lastly, the research highlights the potential for using a star's activity to gauge its age, as the spectral features were found to change predictably based on a star's properties and activity level. This means that using a star's activity, rather than its temperature, could lead to a more precise age estimation that's free from convection uncertainty. In the context of a star's life cycle, this could have significant implications for age-based population studies in the future. The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additionally, the topological aspects of shadows are explored, and within this context, the invariance of topological shadows under weak equivalences is confirmed, thereby providing a strong argument for the topological regime as the more fundamental domain for study. Lastly, the relationship between functors defined on set-theoretic objects to those defined on their quotients, as observed in the context of rational homotopy types, is generalized within the framework of shadows, thereby enabling the extraction of relevant information from shadows defined on quotients, provided the quotients exhibit a certain simple connectivity property. In the process, the concept of shadows is also applied to bimodules to establish a connection between the homology of a bimodule and the homology of its underlying 'linearized' shadow, a relationship referred to as linear stability. Moreover, this work contains an appendix presenting relevant background on functorial excision for the topology on finite sets. The majority of the presented research is applicable to non-deterministic settings as well as deterministic ones. However, the topological results necessitate the consideration of deterministic scenarios. On a separate note, the topological regime itself proves to be a particularly suitable context for studying topological shadows. Lastly, within the framework of rational homotopy types, the topological shadows of a bicategory coincide with its rational THH. Existing approaches to image editing tasks like color grading often yield multiple possible outcomes rather than a single definitive result, as numerous different styles are applicable to these operations. Current machine learning-based methods typically disregard this stylistic variability in their pursuit of identifying a unique solution. Conversely, our research aims to harness style-specific information, extracting it from paired images to condense into a two or three-dimensional vector, resulting in a more efficient and understandable framework for style-based image editing. By representing the relationship between global color tones across paired images as flow fields, our technique becomes capable of learning the desired image transformation, even in cases where multiple styles are applied. Numerical assessments and visual analyses demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses comparable techniques in terms of accuracy and aesthetic appeal. Furthermore, our technique has been successfully applied to a range of tasks, including color grading for film, as well as the artistic retouching of images. Notably, our technique has been validated in a study where participants tried to distinguish the original source of photos that had been edited using our method, signifying that the distinctive characteristics of different style profiles are preserved after our method is applied. This field research focuses on snow deposition dynamics by monitoring the atmosphere's flow patterns and snowflake trajectories in real time. A state-of-the-art, high-resolution imaging system is utilized to capture snowflakes in motion, mapping the flow patterns and detecting vortex formations above the ground. Concurrently, a high-resolution camera is employed to track individual snowflakes in a smaller sample area within the main field of view, revealing the connection between atmospheric turbulence and snowflake settling patterns. Our research reveals that as snowflakes interact with turbulence at critical velocities, their falling speed is greatly increased, a phenomenon not seen in prior studies. Images captured within the flow patterns show that snowflakes tend to concentrate near the base of vortex formations, moving preferentially downwards. High-resolution footage of these vortex formations provides insight into the complex behavior of snowflakes in the atmosphere's turbulent motion. It is anticipated that this research will contribute to a greater understanding of the relationship between atmospheric turbulence and snow deposition. This may lead to the development of new models to predict snow accumulation patterns, potentially improving estimates of snowfall quantities. This study was conducted at the High Altitude Wind Tunnel Laboratory in Innsbruck, Austria, with a vortex generator creating turbulence and a moving belt varying in speed to mimic snowfall velocities ranging from 0 to 10 m/s. A total of 15,674 high-resolution images were analyzed to determine the connection between atmospheric turbulence and snowflake settling patterns. This was accomplished by tracking 3D positions, 2D image sizes, and flight paths of 3,526 snowflakes interacting with the vortex formations. A custom software utility, SnowTurb, used in conjunction with the PIVMeta software, facilitated the automatic analysis of snowflake trajectories. Our research is poised to provide a greater understanding of the complex behavior of snowflakes in the atmosphere's turbulent motion, providing novel visual insight into this topic. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified simulations due to limitations in dealing with large and varied environments. This research incorporates the latest advancements in deep learning to create a more sophisticated mental framework, one that can be built directly from high-dimensional data, such as video feeds, without the need for pre-defined parameters. Furthermore, this work demonstrates that such frameworks can be utilized to facilitate active inference. This study marks the first instance of applying active inference using deep learning techniques to a real-world navigation task involving a robotic system. Overall, the success of this research suggests a more practical approach to utilizing active inference, one that can be employed by autonomous agents operating in dynamic environments. In experimental facilities specializing in high energy physics, nuclear physics, and cosmology, the task of processing large amounts of data in real-time is proving to be a substantial hurdle. As an alternative to standard compression methods, the use of machine learning algorithms has gained attention for real-time data reduction. Yet, data sets generated from scientific endeavors often comprise vast 3D data volumes characterized by significant portions of zeroes, non-uniform distribution of values, and high generation rates. Consequently, direct applications of popular compression methods along with standard compression methods yield unsatisfactory results. Therefore, to overcome these complications, the concept of Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE) is developed to tackle the challenges posed by the unique properties of these data volumes by addressing the problems of real-time data reduction, reconstruction, and preserving the integrity of the original data set simultaneously. BCAs comprise two components: a BCA and a companion decoder that reconstructs the original data volume from a compressed version, and a merger that merges the results from two convolutions with a BCA, fused into a single data volume. Our BCA research demonstrates the efficacy in dealing with data volumes characterized by diverse distribution of values, and outstanding performance in comparison to cutting edge data compression technologies, boasting a compression ratio that is up to 33 times better, and shows excellent preservation of data integrity with an error rate of less than 0.01%. Furthermore, due to its capability of providing instantaneous results, BCA is perfectly suited for real-time data reduction in scientific experiments. Finally, as a bonus, the compressed data from BCA facilitates substantial reduction in the amount of data required to train a classifier, thereby making it an effective tool for further analysis of the data. In conclusion, our BCA has remarkable potential to significantly contribute to the vast field of scientific experiments by means of efficient data reduction, reliable data integrity, and reversible compression. Cross-sections for the $^6$Li + $^{51}$V system were experimentally measured at energies near the Coulomb barrier, with theoretical estimates obtained through calculations with the finite range coupled reaction method using the \textsc{FRESCO} code. Calculations indicated that the cross-sections from various reaction channels including non-capture breakup and 1 proton, 1 neutron, and 1 deuteron transfer, compound nuclear decay, and incomplete fusion channels can effectively reproduce both the direct $\alpha$ production cross-sections and their angular distributions. Furthermore, the observed direct $\alpha$ production cross-sections align with other target systems, with higher $\alpha$ production compared to deuteron production observed. Analyzing the energy spectra of $\alpha$ and deuterons, it was found that $\alpha$ spectra are predominantly driven by breakup-fusion, whereas deuteron spectra are influenced by both breakup and transfer reactions. Systematic studies of direct $\alpha$ production across different target systems show that the yields exhibit a universal behavior but also present noticeable variations for distinct targets, which is also evident from the observed saturation above the Coulomb barrier in the $\alpha$ to deuteron yield ratio and the increasing production of $\alpha$ particles relative to deuterons around the Coulomb barrier. These variations are examined in light of the distinct characteristics and features of the different target nuclei. Additionally, the measured energy spectra of $\alpha$ and deuterons are found to be significantly affected at higher energies by the properties of the compound nucleus rather than the direct interaction between the projectile and target, with the energy distributions influenced by the mass of the compound nucleus, its half-life, and the excitational states it occupies. As a result, the direct $\alpha$ production cross-sections are found to be relatively insensitive to the properties of the compound nucleus. A previously overlooked ability in bio-inspired snake robots is dynamic vertical climbing. A novel locomotion technique mimicking the Pacific Lamprey's movement has been discovered, which enables a robot to navigate on flat surfaces while climbing at near-vertical inclines. A simplified model has been created to analyze the correlation between robot motion and actuation, resulting in the development of a new, adaptable robot inspired by the Pacific Lamprey. The new robot, called Trident, successfully demonstrates dynamic vertical climbing at speeds of up to 4.8 cm/s and can also be controlled to move horizontally at 9 cm/s. Furthermore, its climbing gait allows it to scale inclines of 30 degrees and achieve vertical strides of up to 3.42 cm. Additionally, its climbing speed is directly proportional to the amplitude of its waving motion. A possible application of this technology is in search and rescue operations, where robots could enter buildings without power sources by using gravity to fuel their movement. However, at present, existing bio-inspired snake robots are only capable of static climbs due to their reliance on actuation to support their weight. As a result, their climbing duration is limited to a few minutes. A novel, portable electric lift system has been devised to overcome this issue, which can support the weight of a snake robot for as long as its electric supply lasts. Experimental tests have shown that the system can lift and lower a 220-gram snake robot in both smooth and rough environments. As a result, the portability and efficiency of bio-inspired snake robots could be significantly improved through the integration of this innovative lift technology, which has the potential to extend its climbing time from minutes to hours. A conceptual design for a machine that can switch between horizontal movement and vertical climbing has also been developed, which is inspired by the integrated locomotion system of the Pacific Lamprey and shares a similar waveform motion. However, as the motion period increases, the horizontal movement speed approaches a maximum rate of 9 cm/s, while the vertical climbing speed decreases and becomes slower than human walking speed, making it potentially hazardous and impractical. As a result, further research into other locomotion mechanisms may be necessary to overcome existing limitations in bio-inspired snake robots and achieve a wider range of movement patterns. Through the development of the new, adaptable robot inspired by the Pacific Lamprey and a portable electric lift system, a significant improvement in snake robot climbing capabilities and efficiency has been achieved, which may soon enable these robots to complete searches and rescue missions for several hours. This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in cases of colon cancer-induced immune response. An Itō stochastic process models the colon cancer dynamics, whose probabilistic evolution is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation. To identify optimal treatment combinations, an open-loop control optimization issue is proposed. Simulation results demonstrating the use of Doxorubicin chemotherapy and IL-2 immunotherapy validate the introduced framework. The study seeks to establish a probabilistic model to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in cases of colon cancer-induced immune response, which could be expanded to model more complex biologic systems. Optimizing wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication success depends heavily on minimizing excessive interference through effective device scheduling. Traditional scheduling methods mainly prioritize maximizing throughput and fairness without considering the timeliness of received data. This paper presents a novel D2D link scheduling strategy that balances both Age of Information (AoI) and throughput by employing a packet replacement policy, which ensures fair link activation. Analytically derived expressions demonstrate how the network's overall AoI and throughput are affected under complex spatio-temporal interference. Furthermore, a neural network is designed to learn an optimal mapping between geographical locations and scheduling parameters under a random policy, eliminating the need for Channel State Information (CSI) after training. Additionally, a novel method is proposed to back-propagate the loss through the network, which enables efficient learning. Experimental results show that the proposed neural network achieves near-optimal performance comparable to the local optimal algorithm with significantly higher computational requirements. This research provides insights into the performance trade-off between data freshness and throughput in wireless D2D communications. For time-sensitive applications where data aging is critical, the proposed scheduling strategy offers an suitable solution; otherwise, conventional algorithms focused on maximizing throughput may be more suitable. In summary, the proposed strategy offers an efficient way to schedule D2D communications while capturing the long-term data aging effect, which is essential in ensuring data freshness without incurring high scheduling complexity. In this context, we've developed UniCaIR, a unified CAncer IRSystem, to automatically identify areas of interest (AIs) in colorectal polyp H&E stains and assign degrees of dysplasia through comprehensive analysis of cell nuclei. By integrating nuclear morphology analysis, UniCaIR outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks in colorectal polyp classification and dysplasia grading on three datasets, utilizing transfer learning to accommodate dataset discrepancies. Additionally, UniCaIR boasts a user-friendly interface for seamless integration with Laval University's Horos, enabling seamless integration into existing medical workflows. Consequently, UniCaIR facilitates the implementation of an fully automated pipeline for characterizing colorectal polyps, saving time and resources previously devoted to manually labeling AIs. Ultimately, this initiative aims to enhance patient treatment by leveraging deep learning. The UniCaIR pipeline comprises three main stages: nuclear segmentation, feature extraction, and classification/dysplasia grading. Our studies demonstrate that UniCaIR achieves state-of-the-art performance on three public datasets. To address dataset discrepancies, we've developed a pre-trained model called UniCaIR-Pretrained. By leveraging this model, researchers can overcome challenges associated with limited training data on digital pathology, reducing reliance on manually annotated samples. Consequently, this opens up new avenues for applying deep learning to real-world digital pathology practices. The q-function has connections to both the instantaneous advantage rate function and the Hamiltonian. We develop a continuous-time "Q-learning" framework based on the q-function, separate from time discretization, by characterizing its relationship to value functions and stochastic processes via martingale conditions. We apply this theory to open-ended control problems, identifying a dynamic programming principle for the continuous-time "Q-learning" problem, even without constraints on exploratory process dynamics. We demonstrate the feasibility of solving the "continual Q-learning" problem even in cases where time-discrete methods encounter difficulties. The theory we develop also offers new insights into entropy-regularized exploratory processes, including novel connections between exploration rates and function properties, as well as the application of continuous-time ideas to time-discrete Markov decision processes. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method that leverages in-depth anatomical knowledge of the spine to aid in accurate vertebrae localization and identification. By employing a novel key point localization model, vertebrae center activation maps are generated, which are then adjusted along the spine's central axis to produce optimized activation maps that can be aggregated into 1-dimensional activation signals. Building upon this, an anatomically-constrained optimization module is integrated to jointly determine the optimal positions of the vertebrae. The optimization is performed under a flexible constraint that ensures the distance between vertebrae and a rigid constraint that maintains consecutive vertebrae indices. Upon being evaluated using a well-established public dataset consisting of 302 CT images characterized by significant spinal pathologies, the proposed method achieved the highest identification rate of 97.4% and surpassed the best comparable approach, which reported an identification rate of 94.7%, by significantly reducing the relative error rate. I challenge the conventional view of Galileo's influence on science by suggesting that he struggled with mathematical proficiency. This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive discussion of basic scientific principles was, arguably, an outcome of his limitations in mathematics, as they often say "those who can't do, teach." It is proposed that Galileo's scientific vision, which is typically viewed as groundbreaking, was actually based on long-established ideas from mathematicians. The main difference lies in that Galileo chose to articulate these ideas in philosophical writing, as his mathematical colleagues were too preoccupied with advancing scientific work to bother doing the same. Ultimately, it is suggested that history has inaccurately portrayed Galileo's influence, as his true legacy is that of a "non-performing" scientist, who made a lasting impact by inspiring others, such as Huygens and Leibniz, to further mathematical work.  Additionally, I would like to explore Leibniz's role in the development of the scientific revolution, as well as what can be learned from the dynamics between scientists who were active during this period. The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive kinetic models, contrasting with more feasible fluid-based simulations. Our study utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-in-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model to investigate the interaction between two magnetic flux ropes. By embedding kinetic models into MHD simulations only in relevant areas, this model allows for more efficient computation. The comparative study involves three scenarios: the MHD-AEPIC model, MHD simulations paired with fixed embedded PIC regions, and full PIC simulations. The examination of reconnection rates, magnetic island spacings, and ion dynamics within these scenarios indicates good agreement among the models, with notably large adaptable PIC regions required within the MHD domain to achieve such convergence. Nonetheless, the existence of two distinct interaction mechanisms - the interaction between the two magnetic flux ropes and the interaction between each flux rope and its own initial field - complicates the identification of reconnection rates. Therefore, the total reconnection rate is found to be significantly higher than in similar studies, underscoring the importance of considering multiple physical mechanisms in such studies. Furthermore, the study provides quantitative estimates of the errors introduced by fluidization and embedding techniques. Finally, the comparative study offers insights into the similarity between low-frequency electromagnetic interactions and the interactions observed in collisionless reconnection scenarios. The findings of this study have broad implications and can be applied to various contexts, such as the study of plasma interactions in astrophysical settings and the analysis of laboratory experiments involving plasma interactions.
